query.original_query: off-target side effects of steering vectors and feature interventions collateral property changes generative models

sub_queries.semantic_query: off-target side effects of steering vectors and feature interventions in generative models, collateral property changes, unintended behavior shifts, representation engineering, activation steering
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate unintended behavioral shifts arising from activation steering and representation engineering in generative models. Our analysis focuses on off-target side effects when applying steering vectors to modify specific model properties, such as sentiment or style, in language and image generation systems. We find that targeted feature interventions frequently induce collateral changes in unrelated semantic dimensions, including alterations to factual recall, output length, and visual composition. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we localize these unintended effects to specific attention heads and MLP layers where steering vectors overlap with representations for non-targeted concepts. Results show that feature steering in the residual stream can disrupt the balance of polysemantic features, leading to feature absorption or splitting that propagates through downstream layers. Our analysis further reveals that interventions in cross-attention layers of diffusion models produce correlated shifts in object placement and color distribution, even when the steering vector is designed for abstract attributes. These findings highlight the challenge of achieving monosemantic control in models exhibiting superposition, and suggest that current steering methods lack the specificity required for safe, predictable behavioral modification.

sub_queries.semantic_query: unintended side effects of neural modulation and cognitive interventions, collateral behavioral changes in human decision-making and learning, transfer effects of targeted manipulation
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated whether targeted cognitive interventions produce unintended collateral changes in decision-making and learning beyond their intended domain. Participants completed a working memory training paradigm while we measured risk preferences, delay discounting, and exploratory behavior using a battery of established behavioral tasks. A separate group underwent transcranial direct current stimulation over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during a probabilistic learning task, with pre- and post-intervention assessments of loss aversion and reversal learning. Results indicate that working memory training led to systematic shifts in risk-taking, with participants showing reduced loss aversion and increased exploratory choice in unrelated gambling tasks. Similarly, anodal stimulation over the DLPFC produced transfer effects on delay discounting, decreasing impulsive choice, but also impaired performance on a subsequent reversal learning task. Findings support the hypothesis that neural modulation and cognitive interventions can induce collateral behavioral changes, consistent with models of shared neural circuitry between executive control and value-based decision-making. These results highlight the need to consider unintended side effects when evaluating the efficacy of cognitive interventions.

papers.title: Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be made adaptive so that interventions are applied only when necessary, decoupling when to steer from how to steer?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering (DSAS), a method-agnostic framework that adaptively modulates the strength of existing steering methods across layers and inputs, improving the trade-off between desired behavior (e.g., toxicity reduction) and model utility.
papers.conclusion: DSAS is an effective, general framework for conditional activation steering that decouples when to steer from how to steer, consistently improving the trade-off between behavior modification (e.g., toxicity mitigation) and model performance preservation across modalities.
papers.key_findings:
DSAS consistently improves the Pareto front for toxicity mitigation versus capability retention across different steering methods (CAA, ITI, LinEAS) and models (Qwen 2.5, Gemma 2).
DSAS can be trained end-to-end (E2E-DSAS) and matches or outperforms the vanilla DSAS.
DSAS works across modalities (text and image) without modification, enabling concept-specific modulation in text-to-image generation.
DSAS introduces minimal computational overhead and improves interpretability by pinpointing which tokens require steering and by how much.
DSAS outperforms recent conditional steering methods such as CAST and MERA in toxicity mitigation with higher performance retention.
papers.limitation: In image generation, the steering does not precisely localize the target concept spatially.
papers.abstract: Activation steering has emerged as a powerful method for guiding the behavior of generative models towards desired outcomes such as toxicity mitigation. However, most existing methods apply interventions uniformly across all inputs, degrading model performance when steering is unnecessary. We introduce Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering (DSAS), a method-agnostic steering framework that decouples when to steer from how to steer. DSAS adaptively modulates the strength of existing steering transformations across layers and inputs, intervening strongly only when undesired behavior is detected. At generation time, DSAS computes context-dependent scaling factors that selectively adjust the strength of any steering method. We also show how DSAS can be jointly optimized end-to-end together with the steering function. When combined with existing steering methods, DSAS consistently improves the Pareto front with respect to steering alone, achieving a better trade-off between toxicity mitigation and utility preservation. We further demonstrate DSAS's generality by applying it to a text-to-image diffusion model, showing how adaptive steering allows the modulation of specific concepts. Finally, DSAS introduces minimal computational overhead while improving interpretability, pinpointing which tokens require steering and by how much.

papers.title: Extending Activation Steering to Broad Skills and Multiple Behaviours
papers.research_question: Can we extend activation steering to broad skills and multiple behaviours?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can be applied to broad skills (coding) with similar effectiveness as narrow skills, and simultaneous injection of multiple steering vectors at different layers is more promising than combining them into a single vector.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering can be extended to broad skills and multiple behaviours, with simultaneous steering being a promising direction.
papers.key_findings:
Steering to reduce general coding ability is competitive with steering to reduce Python-specific ability.
Individual steering vectors for behaviours like myopia and wealth-seeking are effective.
Combining multiple steering vectors into one vector is largely unsuccessful.
Simultaneous injection of individual steering vectors at different layers is promising and has minor alignment tax.
Steering at layer 0 for coding ability had an opposite effect, possibly due to copy suppression.
papers.limitation:
The flexibility of activation steering makes finding optimal setups non-trivial.
It is unclear whether reductions in matching scores (e.g., a 20% reduction in coding accuracy) translate to real-world risk reduction.
future_direction: Testing with other models to understand the general working of activation steering.
Using different injection coefficients for different steering vectors in simultaneous steering.
Generating and injecting steering vectors at different places within a layer (e.g., attention and MLP components).
Steering against alternative programming languages to further investigate broad steering.
papers.abstract: Current large language models have dangerous capabilities, which are likely to become more problematic in the future. Activation steering techniques can be used to reduce risks from these capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the efficacy of activation steering for broad skills and multiple behaviours. First, by comparing the effects of reducing performance on general coding ability and Python-specific ability, we find that steering broader skills is competitive to steering narrower skills. Second, we steer models to become more or less myopic and wealth-seeking, among other behaviours. In our experiments, combining steering vectors for multiple different behaviours into one steering vector is largely unsuccessful. On the other hand, injecting individual steering vectors at different places in a model simultaneously is promising.

papers.title: Small Vectors, Big Effects: A Mechanistic Study of RL-Induced Reasoning via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How does reasoning training reshape LLMs' internal computations, and what are the mechanisms of trainable steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Lightweight steering vectors trained with an RL objective explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving interpretability, and their mechanisms (e.g., token substitution at the last layer, MLP-mediated effects at the penultimate layer) are elucidated.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a compact and informative probe of reasoning-trained models, offering concrete insight into how RL-induced changes manifest in token preferences and internal circuitry.
papers.key_findings:
The last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, boosting tokens such as 'To' and 'Step'.
The penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and operates through the MLP and unembedding, up-weighting process words and structure symbols.
Steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family, suggesting underlying directions are preserved under fine-tuning.
Early-layer steering does not express later-layer steering directions; induced shifts diffuse and become nearly orthogonal to later-layer vectors.
Single-layer steering vectors isolate layer-specific effects and provide an upper bound on linear intervention performance at that layer.
papers.limitation: The effects are consistently stronger and cleaner in Qwen than in Llama, suggesting model-specific implementations of similar high-level behaviors.
future_direction: Systematic comparisons across architectures and training recipes to explain differences in steering vector effects.
Pin down the precise mechanisms of mid-layer steering vectors, which are harder to localize to a single submodule.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which reasoning training reshapes LLMs' internal computations remain unclear. We study lightweight steering vectors inserted into the base model's residual stream and trained with a reinforcement-learning objective. These vectors explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving the interpretability of small, additive interventions. We find that (i) the last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, consistently boosting tokens such as "To" and "Step"; (ii) the penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and instead operates through the MLP and unembedding, preferentially up-weighting process words and structure symbols; and (iii) the steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family. Taken together, these results deepen understanding of how trained steering vectors shape computation and should inform future work in activation engineering and the study of reasoning models.

papers.title: Fine-Grained Activation Steering: Steering Less, Achieving More
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be made more efficient and effective by moving from block-level to fine-grained atomic unit (AU) level interventions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes AUSteer, a fine-grained AU-level activation steering method that localizes discriminative atomic units via activation momentum and assigns adaptive steering strengths, achieving superior performance with far fewer interventions than block-level methods.
papers.conclusion: Fine-grained AU-level activation steering with AUSteer demonstrates that steering fewer activations can achieve more, significantly outperforming existing methods across diverse tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
Block-level activations are heterogeneous, mixing beneficial, irrelevant, and harmful features, making block-level steering coarse and inefficient.
Steering at the AU level is more precise and effective; steering a small subset of beneficial AUs can outperform steering entire blocks.
AUSteer consistently outperforms state-of-the-art activation steering methods across diverse tasks while intervening on at most 100 activations.
Activation momentum is an effective metric for globally identifying discriminative AUs without layer-wise magnitude bias.
Adaptive steering that scales with input activation and AU discriminative power improves performance and reduces unnecessary perturbation.
papers.limitation: Reliance on contrastive sample pairs for computing activation momentum and steering vectors, which is an inherent limitation of existing activation-steering methods.
future_direction: Explore approaches to reduce or eliminate the requirement for contrastive pairs.
Investigate more principled methods to reduce task-dependent hyperparameter sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Activation steering has emerged as a cost-effective paradigm for modifying large language model (LLM) behaviors. Existing methods typically intervene at the block level, steering the bundled activations of selected attention heads, feedforward networks, or residual streams. However, we reveal that block-level activations are inherently heterogeneous, entangling beneficial, irrelevant, and harmful features, thereby rendering block-level steering coarse, inefficient, and intrusive. To investigate the root cause, we decompose block activations into fine-grained atomic unit (AU)-level activations, where each AU-level activation corresponds to a single dimension of the block activation, and each AU denotes a slice of the block weight matrix. Steering an AU-level activation is thus equivalent to steering its associated AU. Our theoretical and empirical analysis show that heterogeneity arises because different AUs or dimensions control distinct token distributions in LLM outputs. Hence, block-level steering inevitably moves helpful and harmful token directions together, which reduces efficiency. Restricting intervention to beneficial AUs yields more precise and effective steering. Building on this insight, we propose AUSteer, a simple and efficient method that operates at a finer granularity of the AU level. AUSteer first identifies discriminative AUs globally by computing activation momenta on contrastive samples. It then assigns adaptive steering strengths tailored to diverse inputs and selected AU activations. Comprehensive experiments on multiple LLMs and tasks show that AUSteer consistently surpasses advanced baselines while steering considerably fewer activations, demonstrating that steering less achieves more.

papers.title: Improving Steering Vectors by Targeting Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we improve steering vectors to target specific SAE features and achieve desired model behaviors while minimizing unintended side effects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to measure steering effects using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and uses this to develop SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which constructs steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.conclusion: SAE-TS is an effective method for steering language models, balancing desired behavioral changes with output coherence better than existing baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a method to quantify and interpret the effects of steering interventions on SAE features.
Introduced SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which learns a linear relationship between steering vectors and their effects on SAE features to construct targeted steering vectors.
SAE-TS outperforms existing methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and direct SAE feature steering on most tasks, achieving better alignment with intended behavior while maintaining coherence.
The method allows for more predictable and controllable steering of language models compared to prior approaches.
Provides an interactive tool (EffectVis) for exploring feature effects and relationships.
papers.limitation:
Investigations were limited to Gemma-2 2B and 9B models, which share the same distilled architecture, so results may not transfer to other models.
Focused on base models without instruction tuning, so the study did not investigate tasks and features relevant for safety or capabilities.
Steering is limited to concepts present in the SAE, which may not cover all concepts due to feature splitting or niche features only appearing in very large SAEs.
future_direction: Apply steering methods to chat models and safety-relevant steering targets.
Explore different SAE architectures (e.g., TopK SAEs) and test on various model architectures beyond the Gemma family.
Adapt BiPO to optimize steering vectors towards desired feature effects.
papers.abstract: To control the behavior of language models, steering methods attempt to ensure that outputs of the model satisfy specific pre-defined properties. Adding steering vectors to the model is a promising method of model control that is easier than finetuning, and may be more robust than prompting. However, it can be difficult to anticipate the effects of steering vectors produced by methods such as CAA [Panickssery et al., 2024] or the direct use of SAE latents [Templeton et al., 2024]. In our work, we address this issue by using SAEs to measure the effects of steering vectors, giving us a method that can be used to understand the causal effect of any steering vector intervention. We use this method for measuring causal effects to develop an improved steering method, SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which finds steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects. We show that overall, SAE-TS balances steering effects with coherence better than CAA and SAE feature steering, when evaluated on a range of tasks.

papers.title: Improving Activation Steering in Language Models with Mean-Centring
papers.research_question: How can activation steering in language models be improved by applying mean-centring to steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Mean-centring, a simple post-processing step that subtracts the mean of training activations from the mean of target activations, creates more effective steering vectors for activation steering, improving performance and applicability.
papers.conclusion: Mean-centring is a simple and effective technique that improves activation steering by accounting for anisotropy in model activations, making it applicable to a wider range of tasks where counterbalancing concepts are not available.
papers.key_findings:
Mean-centring produces more interpretable and effective steering vectors compared to using raw activation averages.
Mean-centring is effective for reducing toxicity in model outputs, comparable to existing methods like ActAdd.
Mean-centring can steer story continuations towards a target genre, increasing genre-specific word frequencies.
Mean-centring significantly improves the accuracy of function vectors for triggering tasks like country-capital and English-French translation.
papers.limitation:
Mean-centring does not improve performance at all layers of the model.
The link between anisotropy (as measured by average cosine similarity) and the performance improvement from mean-centring is not clearly predictive.
future_direction: Investigating the link between anisotropy and improvements in accuracy from mean-centring.
Investigating other structures in activation geometries (e.g., clustering) for further improvements to steering.
papers.abstract: Recent work in activation steering has demonstrated the potential to better control the outputs of Large Language Models (LLMs), but it involves finding steering vectors. This is difficult because engineers do not typically know how features are represented in these models. We seek to address this issue by applying the idea of mean-centring to steering vectors. We find that taking the average of activations associated with a target dataset, and then subtracting the mean of all training activations, results in effective steering vectors. We test this method on a variety of models on natural language tasks by steering away from generating toxic text, and steering the completion of a story towards a target genre. We also apply mean-centring to extract function vectors, more effectively triggering the execution of a range of natural language tasks by a significant margin (compared to previous baselines). This suggests that mean-centring can be used to easily improve the effectiveness of activation steering in a wide range of contexts.

papers.title: Interpretable Steering of Large Language Models with Feature Guided Activation Additions
papers.research_question: How can we improve the precision and interpretability of activation steering in large language models by leveraging sparse autoencoder features and optimization techniques?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA), a novel activation steering method that uses sparse autoencoder features and optimization to construct precise, interpretable steering vectors, improving steering effectiveness and output coherence compared to existing methods.
papers.conclusion: FGAA represents a significant step forward in controlled text generation, offering both theoretical insights into activation patterns and practical advances in steering methodology, while highlighting the trade-off between steering strength and capability preservation.
papers.key_findings:
FGAA outperforms existing activation steering methods (CAA, SAE, SAE-TS) on most steering tasks, especially for the Gemma-2-2B model.
FGAA provides more interpretable steering by operating in the SAE feature space and allowing explicit control over which features are steered.
There is a trade-off between steering strength and preservation of model capabilities: all steering methods degrade model performance (perplexity and benchmark accuracy) at high steering scales.
Negative features in steering vectors tend to degrade steering performance, so FGAA focuses on positive features.
The effectiveness of FGAA varies with model size, showing different performance patterns between Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B.
papers.limitation:
Relies heavily on the quality of feature extraction by the underlying Sparse Autoencoder (SAE).
Optimal selection of n1 and n2 parameters is task-dependent, making universal guidelines challenging.
Developing metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of feature filtering methods is challenging due to the qualitative nature of interpreting features.
future_direction: Investigating how SAE width and quality of SAE features affects steering performance with FGAA.
Exploring techniques to minimize capability degradation at higher steering scales while maintaining steering effectiveness.
Applying FGAA to safety tasks such as controlling sycophancy, hallucination, and refusal in RLHF models and reducing social biases.
papers.abstract: Effective and reliable control over large language model (LLM) behavior is a significant challenge. While activation steering methods, which add steering vectors to a model's hidden states, are a promising approach, existing techniques often lack precision and interpretability in how they influence model outputs. We introduce Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA), a novel activation steering method that leverages insights from Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS). By operating in the latent space of a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) and employing optimization techniques to select desired SAE features, FGAA constructs precise steering vectors that provide better steering effects while maintaining coherence of steered model outputs. In this regard, evaluations on Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B models across various steering tasks demonstrate that FGAA outperforms existing steering methods of CAA, SAE decoder steering, and SAE-TS. Our results also highlight important trade-offs between steering scale and general model capabilities that are consistent across all tested steering methods.

papers.title: Understanding Unreliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models: Geometric Predictors and the Limits of Linear Approximations
papers.research_question: What are the underlying factors in model activation patterns that contribute to the observed variability in CAA steering vector reliability across different datasets and target behaviors? Can the training process of CAA steering vectors be modified to produce more consistently reliable control over language model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The thesis demonstrates that steering vector unreliability is caused by a mismatch between the simple linear function class of CAA and the often non-linear latent target behavior representations. It identifies geometric predictors (directional agreement and separability) of steering reliability.
papers.conclusion: The reliability of CAA steering vectors is predictable from the geometry of the training activations. High directional agreement and clear separability along the difference-of-means line are key indicators of steerability.
papers.key_findings:
Higher cosine similarity (directional agreement) between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering.
Better separability of positive and negative activations along the steering direction predicts more reliable steering.
Steering vectors trained on different prompt variations are directionally distinct but perform similarly and have correlated efficacy across datasets.
Steering vector unreliability stems from the linear function class being too restrictive to approximate non-linear latent behavior representations.
Prompt types that leverage in-context learning (e.g., instructions, few-shot) lead to higher directional agreement and faster steering vector convergence.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to one model (Llama 2-7B-Chat) and one family of steering methods (CAA).
The analysis is restricted to binary classification tasks and may not generalize to more complex behaviors.
The study does not investigate the impact of model scale or architecture.
future_direction: Developing more robust steering methods that explicitly account for non-linear latent behavior representations.
Extending the analysis to more models, architectures, and a broader range of behaviors.
Investigating the impact of model scale on steering reliability.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a lightweight method for controlling language model behavior by adding a learned bias to the activations at inference time. Although effective on average, steering effect sizes vary across samples and are unreliable for many target behaviors. In my thesis, I investigate why steering reliability differs across behaviors and how it is impacted by steering vector training data. First, I find that higher cosine similarity between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering. Second, I observe that behavior datasets where positive and negative activations are better separated along the steering direction are more reliably steerable. Finally, steering vectors trained on different prompt variations are directionally distinct, yet perform similarly well and exhibit correlated efficacy across datasets. My findings suggest that steering vectors are unreliable when the latent target behavior representation is not effectively approximated by the linear steering direction. Taken together, these insights offer a practical diagnostic for steering unreliability and motivate the development of more robust steering methods that explicitly account for non-linear latent behavior representations.

papers.title: Analysing the Generalisation and Reliability ofSteering Vectors
papers.research_question: What are the reliability and generalisation properties of steering vectors for adjusting language model behaviour at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: This work rigorously investigates the reliability and generalization of steering vectors, showing they have substantial limitations both in- and out-of-distribution, including high variance in steerability across inputs and brittleness to prompt changes.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors in their current form are not a panacea for aligning model behavior at inference time; more work is required to ensure they reliably produce desired behavior in a generalisable way.
papers.key_findings:
In-distribution steerability is highly variable across inputs, with many examples being anti-steerable (steered in the opposite direction).
Steerability is affected by spurious factors like token and position bias, which are not fixable by simple dataset debiasing.
Out-of-distribution, steering vectors often generalize reasonably well but are brittle to reasonable changes in the prompt.
Steerability is mostly a property of the dataset used for extraction rather than the model architecture.
Similarity in the unsteered model behavior between source and target prompt settings is correlated with steering vector generalization.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a large number of datasets, but even more variety in the type of behavior being steered towards could be studied to ensure robustness.
The failures of steering vectors are not entirely understood, and it is unclear what potential mitigations could be applied.
Only two models are analyzed in this work, although they use different sizes, architectures, training data and algorithms.
future_direction: Investigating what causes steerability biases and whether other techniques for extracting and applying SVs can mitigate these biases.
Investigating methods to improve SV generalisation, and investigating scenarios where they generalise better or worse.
Developing methods to disentangle separate sub-behaviours in an unsupervised way for unsteerable behaviours.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) are a new approach to efficiently adjust language model behaviour at inference time by intervening on intermediate model activations. They have shown promise in terms of improving both capabilities and model alignment. However, the reliability and generalisation properties of this approach are unknown. In this work, we rigorously investigate these properties, and show that steering vectors have substantial limitations both in- and out-of-distribution. In-distribution, steerability is highly variable across different inputs. Depending on the concept, spurious biases can substantially contribute to how effective steering is for each input, presenting a challenge for the widespread use of steering vectors. Out-of-distribution, while steering vectors often generalise well, for several concepts they are brittle to reasonable changes in the prompt, resulting in them failing to generalise well. Overall, our findings show that while steering can work well in the right circumstances, there remain many technical difficulties of applying steering vectors to guide models' behaviour at scale.

papers.title: Understanding (Un)Reliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the influence of prompt types and the geometry of activation differences on the reliability of steering vectors in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that steering vector reliability depends on the directional consistency of activation differences and the separability of activations along the steering direction, and is unreliable when the target behavior is not represented by a coherent linear direction.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a deeper understanding of when and why steering vectors are (un)reliable, showing that their effectiveness depends on whether the targeted behavior is well-represented as a linear direction in the model’s activation space.
papers.key_findings:
All seven prompt types produce a net positive steering effect but exhibit high variance and often give an effect opposite of the desired one.
No prompt type clearly outperforms the others, and steering vectors from different prompt types often differ directionally.
Higher cosine similarity between training set activation differences predicts more effective steering.
Datasets where positive and negative activations are better separated are more steerable.
Steering vectors are unreliable when the target behavior is not represented by a coherent direction in activation space.
papers.limitation:
Breadth of experiments: only evaluated on Llama2-7B-Chat and 36 multiple-choice datasets, and only focused on CAA; generalizability to other models, datasets, and steering methods is unclear.
Methodology for prompt type comparison is highly sensitive to hyperparameters like training-set size, complicating robust analysis.
future_direction: Investigate different models and non-multiple choice datasets to determine broader generalizability.
Verify transfer of results to other steering vector methods like Function Vectors and BiPO.
Investigate how prompting strategies affect performance on unrelated general benchmarks like MMLU.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a lightweight method to control language model behavior by adding a learned bias to the activations at inference time. Although steering demonstrates promising performance, recent work shows that it can be unreliable or even counterproductive in some cases. This paper studies the influence of prompt types and the geometry of activation differences on steering reliability. First, we find that all seven prompt types used in our experiments produce a net positive steering effect, but exhibit high variance across samples, and often give an effect opposite of the desired one. No prompt type clearly outperforms the others, and yet the steering vectors resulting from the different prompt types often differ directionally (as measured by cosine similarity). Second, we show that higher cosine similarity between training set activation differences predicts more effective steering. Finally, we observe that datasets where positive and negative activations are better separated are more steerable. Our results suggest that vector steering is unreliable when the target behavior is not represented by a coherent direction.

papers.title: Steer2Edit: From Activation Steering to Component-Level Editing
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors be reinterpreted as diagnostic signals to reveal how a target behavior is distributed across model components, and can this information be used to selectively modify those components via weight editing to achieve better attribute-utility trade-offs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STEER2EDIT, a training-free framework that converts activation steering vectors into component-level rank-1 weight edits, achieving more favorable attribute-utility trade-offs by selectively redistributing behavioral influence across individual attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.conclusion: STEER2EDIT provides a principled, training-free framework for converting steering vectors into component-level weight edits, enabling precise behavioral control with favorable attribute-utility trade-offs and interpretable, architecture-preserving model modifications.
papers.key_findings:
STEER2EDIT consistently achieves superior attribute-utility trade-offs compared to activation steering: at matched downstream performance, it improves safety by up to 17.2%, increases truthfulness by 9.8%, and reduces reasoning length by 12.2% on average.
The method produces interpretable, sparse edits: safety and truthfulness control are mediated by a small subset of attention heads, while reasoning efficiency is governed by distributed MLP neuron edits.
The edits are closed-form, require no fine-tuning, and yield a standalone edited model that preserves the original architecture and standard forward pass.
Component importance scores (cosine similarity between steering vector and component output) and Elastic-Net regularization are critical for stable and sparse editing.
The framework provides a principled bridge between representation steering and weight editing, translating steering signals into interpretable parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Steering methods influence Large Language Model behavior by identifying semantic directions in hidden representations, but are typically realized through inference-time activation interventions that apply a fixed, global modification to the model's internal states. While effective, such interventions often induce unfavorable attribute-utility trade-offs under strong control, as they ignore the fact that many behaviors are governed by a small and heterogeneous subset of model components. We propose Steer2Edit, a theoretically grounded, training-free framework that transforms steering vectors from inference-time control signals into diagnostic signals for component-level rank-1 weight editing. Instead of uniformly injecting a steering direction during generation, Steer2Edit selectively redistributes behavioral influence across individual attention heads and MLP neurons, yielding interpretable edits that preserve the standard forward pass and remain compatible with optimized parallel inference. Across safety alignment, hallucination mitigation, and reasoning efficiency, Steer2Edit consistently achieves more favorable attribute-utility trade-offs: at matched downstream performance, it improves safety by up to 17.2%, increases truthfulness by 9.8%, and reduces reasoning length by 12.2% on average. Overall, Steer2Edit provides a principled bridge between representation steering and weight editing by translating steering signals into interpretable, training-free parameter updates.

papers.title: Analyzing the Generalization and Reliability of Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: What are the reliability and generalization properties of steering vectors in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that steering vectors have substantial limitations in reliability and generalization, with high variance in-distribution and imperfect generalization out-of-distribution.
papers.conclusion: Overall, steering vectors are not a panacea for aligning model behavior; more work is needed to ensure reliability and generalizability.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors exhibit high variance in steerability across inputs, with some inputs being anti-steerable.
Steerability is affected by spurious factors like token and position biases, leading to steerability bias.
Some behaviors are unsteerable, indicating limitations in linear representation.
Out-of-distribution, steerability generalizes reasonably but not perfectly, and is correlated with in-distribution performance.
Steerability is mostly a property of the dataset rather than the model, and generalization is predicted by model behavior similarity.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a large number of datasets but could benefit from even more variety in behaviors.
The failures of steering vectors are not entirely understood, and mitigations are unclear.
Only two models are analyzed, limiting the robustness of results.
future_direction: Investigating what causes steerability biases and how to mitigate them.
Improving SV generalization, especially when guiding models towards behaviors they do not normally produce.
Developing methods to disentangle separate sub-behaviors in an unsupervised way.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) have been proposed as an effective approach to adjust language model behaviour at inference time by intervening on intermediate model activations. They have shown promise in terms of improving both capabilities and model alignment. However, the reliability and generalisation properties of this approach are unknown. In this work, we rigorously investigate these properties, and show that steering vectors have substantial limitations both in- and out-of-distribution. In-distribution, steerability is highly variable across different inputs. Depending on the concept, spurious biases can substantially contribute to how effective steering is for each input, presenting a challenge for the widespread use of steering vectors. Out-of-distribution, while steering vectors often generalise well, for several concepts they are brittle to reasonable changes in the prompt, resulting in them failing to generalise well. Overall, our findings show that while steering can work well in the right circumstances, there remain technical difficulties of applying steering vectors to guide models' behaviour at scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/dtch1997/steering-bench

papers.title: On the Non-Identifiability of Steering Vectors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether steering vectors in large language models are identifiable from input-output behavior, given the null space of the Jacobian.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that steering vectors in large language models are non-identifiable due to the null space of the Jacobian, meaning infinitely many geometrically distinct vectors produce equivalent behavioral effects.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors are fundamentally non-identifiable, implying that behavioral equivalence is insufficient for interpretability claims and structural constraints are needed for reliable alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors are non-identifiable under white-box single-layer access due to null-space ambiguity.
Orthogonal perturbations to steering vectors achieve near-equivalent efficacy with negligible effect sizes.
Vectors extracted by different methods (contrastive mean and PCA) are geometrically distinct but behaviorally equivalent.
Non-identifiability persists across diverse prompt distributions and throughout the operational steering range.
The null space is high-dimensional, with most activation directions being semantically inert.
papers.limitation:
Empirical validation covers only two models at mid-network layers across five semantic traits.
Does not test whether structural interventions such as independence constraints can recover identifiable representations.
Does not formally verify that the semantic null-space coincides with the Jacobian null-space.
future_direction: Testing explicit structural interventions for recovering identifiable representations.
Extending the analysis to the exact nonlinear regime beyond linear approximation.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods are widely used to control large language model (LLM) behavior and are often interpreted as revealing meaningful internal representations. This interpretation assumes steering directions are identifiable and uniquely recoverable from input-output behavior. We show that, under white-box single-layer access, steering vectors are fundamentally non-identifiable due to large equivalence classes of behaviorally indistinguishable interventions. Empirically, we show that orthogonal perturbations achieve near-equivalent efficacy with negligible effect sizes across multiple models and traits. Critically, we show that the non-identifiability is a robust geometric property that persists across diverse prompt distributions. These findings reveal fundamental interpretability limits and highlight the need for structural constraints beyond behavioral testing to enable reliable alignment interventions.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders be used to decompose and interpret steering vectors?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why directly applying sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two main reasons why sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide misleading decompositions of steering vectors: (1) steering vectors are out-of-distribution for SAEs, and (2) SAEs cannot represent negative coefficients which are meaningful in steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Direct SAE decomposition of steering vectors is misleading due to out-of-distribution and non-negativity constraints; alternative approaches such as learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors have significantly smaller L2-norms than model activations, causing the SAE encoder bias to dominate the decomposition and yield misleading results.
Scaling steering vectors does not resolve the out-of-distribution issue because steering vectors lack default components present in model activations.
SAEs restrict decompositions to non-negative coefficients, but steering vectors have meaningful negative projections in feature directions.
Negative projections in steering vectors can cause spurious positive activations in SAE features due to negative cosine similarities between features.
These issues explain prior observations of irrelevant features in SAE decompositions and the failure of SAE-reconstructed vectors to retain steering properties.
papers.limitation:
The proposed alternative method of learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis requires two SAE decompositions per difference vector, increasing the potential impact of SAE error.
The corrigibility steering vectors may include confounding features related to computer science and language modeling.
future_direction: Explore learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis and establish evaluation metrics to compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a promising approach to control the behaviour of large language models. However, their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) may offer a potential method to interpret steering vectors, recent findings show that SAE-reconstructed vectors often lack the steering properties of the original vectors. This paper investigates why directly applying SAEs to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions, identifying two reasons: (1) steering vectors fall outside the input distribution for which SAEs are designed, and (2) steering vectors can have meaningful negative projections in feature directions, which SAEs are not designed to accommodate. These limitations hinder the direct use of SAEs for interpreting steering vectors.

papers.title: LinEAS: End-to-end Learning of Activation Steering with a Distributional Loss
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently control generative models by steering activations with a global distributional loss that requires low data and is modality-agnostic?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LinEAS, a method for activation steering that uses a global distributional loss to jointly learn affine transformations across layers, enabling effective control with low data and automatic neuron selection via sparsity regularization.
papers.conclusion: LinEAS is an effective method for activation steering, offering improved controllability and robustness by learning lightweight interventions with a global distributional loss.
papers.key_findings:
LinEAS outperforms existing activation steering methods on toxicity mitigation in LLMs and style control in text-to-image models.
LinEAS requires only a handful of unpaired samples (e.g., 32) to be effective.
The global loss and joint optimization across layers lead to more robust interventions and better preservation of model utility.
Sparsity regularization allows automatic selection of neurons and layers, reducing the intervention support by 100x.
LinEAS provides a continuous intervention strength parameter, allowing fine-grained control.
papers.limitation: The method requires access to intermediate activations, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending LinEAS to other modalities and tasks.
Investigating the theoretical properties of the distributional loss.
papers.abstract: The growing use of generative models in daily life calls for efficient mechanisms to control their generation, to e.g., produce safe content or provide users with tools to explore style changes. Ideally, such mechanisms should require low volume of unpaired data (i.e., without explicit preference), and should be cheap, both at train and inference time, while preserving output quality. Recent research has shown that such mechanisms can be obtained by intervening exclusively on model activations, with the goal of correcting distributional differences between activations seen when using prompts from a source vs. a target set (e.g., toxic and non-toxic sentences). While cheap, these fast methods are inherently crude: their maps are tuned locally, not accounting for their impact on downstream layers, resulting in interventions that cause unintended shifts when used out-of-sample. We propose in this work linear end-to-end activation steering (LinEAS), an approach trained with a global loss that accounts simultaneously for all layer-wise distributional shifts. In addition to being more robust, the loss used to train LinEAS can be regularized with sparsifying norms, which can automatically carry out neuron selection. LinEAS only requires a handful of unpaired samples to be effective, and beats similar baselines on toxicity mitigation in language models, becoming competitive with oracle-dependent methods that have access to strong supervision. LinEAS is modality-agnostic and we empirically find that it outperforms existing activation steering methods at mitigating and including new concepts at the output of single-step text-to-image generation models.

papers.title: Angular Steering: Behavior Control via Rotation in Activation Space
papers.research_question: How can we control specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Angular Steering, a rotation-based framework for fine-grained behavior control in LLMs that generalizes existing activation steering methods and maintains general language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: Angular Steering offers a principled, flexible, and robust framework for behavior control in LLMs, enabling fine-grained modulation while preserving general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors like refusal and compliance by rotating activations in a fixed 2D subspace.
The method generalizes existing activation addition and directional ablation techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework.
Angular Steering maintains general language modeling performance (e.g., on TINYBENCHMARKS) while effectively steering behavior.
Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant, improves robustness and coherence by rotating only activations aligned with the target feature.
Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show the method's flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches.
papers.limitation: The method requires a contrastive dataset to extract the feature direction, which may not always be available.
future_direction: Extending Angular Steering to multi-feature steering and dynamic plane selection.
papers.abstract: Controlling specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities is a central challenge for safe and reliable artificial intelligence deployment. Current steering methods, such as vector addition and directional ablation, are constrained within a two-dimensional subspace defined by the activation and feature direction, making them sensitive to chosen parameters and potentially affecting unrelated features due to unintended interactions in activation space. We introduce Angular Steering, a novel and flexible method for behavior modulation that operates by rotating activations within a fixed two-dimensional subspace. By formulating steering as a geometric rotation toward or away from a target behavior direction, Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors such as refusal and compliance. We demonstrate this method using refusal steering emotion steering as use cases. Additionally, we propose Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant that rotates only activations aligned with the target feature, further enhancing stability and coherence. Angular Steering generalizes existing addition and orthogonalization techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework, simplifying parameter selection and maintaining model stability across a broader range of adjustments. Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show that Angular Steering achieves robust behavioral control while maintaining general language modeling performance, underscoring its flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/lone17/angular-steering/.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: The Rogue Scalpel: Activation Steering Compromises LLM Safety
papers.research_question: Does activation steering, a technique for precise and interpretable model control, compromise LLM safety by systematically breaking alignment safeguards?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering, a technique promoted for precise and interpretable model control, systematically breaks LLM alignment safeguards, enabling harmful compliance even with random or semantically benign steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering poses systematic safety risks by breaking alignment safeguards, even with benign vectors, challenging the paradigm of safety through interpretability. Mitigation strategies and further research into the underlying mechanisms are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering in a random direction can increase the probability of harmful compliance from 0% to 1–13% across different model families.
Steering with benign SAE features demonstrates comparable or greater harmful potential, increasing compliance by 1–4% over random steering.
Steering is most effective when applied to the model's middle or early layers, indicating safety mechanisms are most vulnerable in intermediate processing stages.
Most SAE features exhibit jailbreaking capabilities, but they show poor cross-prompt generalization, making systematic safety monitoring challenging.
Averaging just 20 random vectors that jailbreak a single prompt creates a universal attack vector that significantly boosts harmful compliance on unseen requests, requiring only black-box steering access.
future_direction: Investigate the mechanisms behind alignment failures by analyzing activation patterns or refusal circuits in the model’s latent space.
Develop mitigation strategies like adversarial training to counter steering perturbations.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a promising technique for controlling LLM behavior by adding semantically meaningful vectors directly into a model's hidden states during inference. It is often framed as a precise, interpretable, and potentially safer alternative to fine-tuning. We demonstrate the opposite: steering systematically breaks model alignment safeguards, making it comply with harmful requests. Through extensive experiments on different model families, we show that even steering in a random direction can increase the probability of harmful compliance from 0% to 1-13%. Alarmingly, steering benign features from a sparse autoencoder (SAE), a common source of interpretable directions, demonstrates a comparable harmful potential. Finally, we show that combining 20 randomly sampled vectors that jailbreak a single prompt creates a universal attack, significantly increasing harmful compliance on unseen requests. These results challenge the paradigm of safety through interpretability, showing that precise control over model internals does not guarantee precise control over model behavior.

papers.title: Patterns and Mechanisms of Contrastive Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: What are the patterns, mechanisms, and limitations of Contrastive Activation Engineering for steering LLM outputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically investigates Contrastive Activation Engineering, revealing that steering vectors are only reliable within the distribution they are computed from, have diminishing returns with sample size, can be adversarially nullified, and generally harm model perplexity, with larger models being more resistant.
papers.conclusion: CAE shows promise for controlling LLM behavior but has limitations in out-of-distribution generalization and performance degradation, necessitating careful deployment and further research.
papers.key_findings:
CAE is only reliably effective when applied to in-distribution contexts.
Increasing the number of samples used to generate steering vectors has diminishing returns at around 80 samples.
Steering vectors are susceptible to adversarial inputs that reverse the steered behavior.
Steering vectors harm the overall model perplexity.
Larger models are more resistant to steering-induced degradation.
papers.limitation:
In-distribution evaluation introduces noise from the model’s default tendency on each behavior.
Out-of-distribution evaluation relies on the assumption that LLMs can act in place of human evaluators, which was not verified.
The out-of-distribution evaluation dataset is not grounded in real user queries.
future_direction: Improving out-of-distribution robustness
Developing automated methods for balancing steering effectiveness against potential negative impacts on model performance
Expanding the set of CAE techniques and models studied
papers.abstract: Controlling the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge due to their inherent complexity and opacity. While techniques like fine-tuning can modify model behavior, they typically require extensive computational resources. Recent work has introduced a class of contrastive activation engineering (CAE) techniques as promising approaches for steering LLM outputs through targeted modifications to their internal representations. Applied at inference-time with zero cost, CAE has the potential to introduce a new paradigm of flexible, task-specific LLM behavior tuning. We analyze the performance of CAE in in-distribution, out-of-distribution settings, evaluate drawbacks, and begin to develop comprehensive guidelines for its effective deployment. We find that 1. CAE is only reliably effective when applied to in-distribution contexts. 2. Increasing the number of samples used to generate steering vectors has diminishing returns at around 80 samples. 3. Steering vectors are susceptible to adversarial inputs that reverses the behavior that is steered for. 4. Steering vectors harm the overall model perplexity. 5. Larger models are more resistant to steering-induced degradation.

papers.title: Steering Externalities: Benign Activation Steering Unintentionally Increases Jailbreak Risk for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do steering vectors learned from benign instruction data have unintended side-effects on model safety? Specifically, does benign activation steering (for utility) unintentionally increase jailbreak risk for LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies 'steering externalities', a phenomenon where benign activation steering (e.g., for compliance or JSON formatting) unintentionally erodes safety guardrails and significantly increases jailbreak vulnerability in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering for utility creates steering externalities that increase jailbreak risk; steered deployments should be red-teamed, and future work should develop safety-aware steering to preserve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Benign activation steering (STEER-COMPLIANCE, STEER-JSON) increases Attack Success Rates (ASR) for jailbreak attacks, acting as a 'force multiplier' that can boost ASR to over 80-99% on standard benchmarks.
Steering shifts the internal representations of harmful prompts towards regions associated with harmless requests, reducing the model's 'safety margin' and making refusal less likely.
The safety degradation occurs because steering biases the early-token distribution away from refusal prefixes, making the model more likely to enter a non-refusal generation trajectory.
The effect is observed across multiple models (Llama-2, Llama-3, Gemma) and is amplified by existing black-box jailbreak methods like CoP, PAIR, and TAP.
A preliminary safety-aware steering method (STEER-BIND) can partially mitigate the externality, suggesting a path for future safer steering techniques.
papers.limitation: t-SNE visualizations are qualitative projections and the 2D boundary is only an illustrative diagnostic.
future_direction: Develop safety-aware steering vectors (like STEER-BIND) that preserve robustness.
Include broader alignment evaluations (beyond safety refusal) when auditing steered models.
Routine red-teaming and regression testing of steered model configurations before deployment.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a practical post-training model alignment technique to enhance the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs). Prior to deploying a model as a service, developers can steer a pre-trained model toward specific behavioral objectives, such as compliance or instruction adherence, without the need for retraining. This process is as simple as adding a steering vector to the model's internal representations. However, this capability unintentionally introduces critical and under-explored safety risks. We identify a phenomenon termed Steering Externalities, where steering vectors derived from entirely benign datasets-such as those enforcing strict compliance or specific output formats like JSON-inadvertently erode safety guardrails. Experiments reveal that these interventions act as a force multiplier, creating new vulnerabilities to jailbreaks and increasing attack success rates to over 80% on standard benchmarks by bypassing the initial safety alignment. Ultimately, our results expose a critical blind spot in deployment: benign activation steering systematically erodes the "safety margin," rendering models more vulnerable to black-box attacks and proving that inference-time utility improvements must be rigorously audited for unintended safety externalities.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by modifying their activations during inference? The paper introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) to control model behaviors.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method to steer language models by adding computed steering vectors to the residual stream, which effectively controls targeted behaviors with minimal impact on general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behaviors and insights into linear representations of abstract concepts in models.
papers.key_findings:
CAA effectively steers Llama 2 Chat models on multiple alignment-relevant behaviors, with optimal layers around layer 13 for 7B and 14-15 for 13B.
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks and works alongside system prompting and finetuning.
CAA has minimal negative impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU and can slightly improve truthfulness on TruthfulQA when subtracting sycophancy.
Steering vectors exhibit intuitive similarity with token activations relevant to the behavior and transfer well across layers and between base and chat models.
The representations of behaviors are linearly separable in the residual stream, and CAA vectors capture these directions.
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluations may be sensitive to prompt wording and have biases, though manual checks show consistency.
Finetuning baselines were not fully optimized (e.g., learning rate, epochs, loss function), so CAA's relative effect might be smaller with better finetuning.
Prompting baselines may not be fully optimized, and better prompts might achieve stronger effects.
Vector normalization choices (not normalizing across layers) could affect layer optimality results.
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions instead of all tokens after the prompt.
Steering outside the residual stream, e.g., after MLP layers.
Application to red-teaming to trigger unwanted behaviors more efficiently.
papers.abstract: We introduce Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), an innovative method for steering language models by modifying their activations during forward passes. CAA computes "steering vectors" by averaging the difference in residual stream activations between pairs of positive and negative examples of a particular behavior, such as factual versus hallucinatory responses. During inference, these steering vectors are added at all token positions after the user's prompt with either a positive or negative coefficient, allowing precise control over the degree of the targeted behavior. We evaluate CAA's effectiveness on Llama 2 Chat using multiple-choice behavioral question datasets and open-ended generation tasks. We demonstrate that CAA significantly alters model behavior, is effective over and on top of traditional methods like finetuning and system prompt design, and minimally reduces capabilities. Moreover, we gain deeper insights into CAA's mechanisms by employing various activation space interpretation methods. CAA accurately steers model outputs and sheds light on how high-level concepts are represented in Large Language Models (LLMs).

papers.title: Controlling Language and Diffusion Models by Transporting Activations
papers.research_question: How can we control generative models by steering activations using optimal transport theory?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Activation Transport (ACT), a framework for steering activations using optimal transport theory, which generalizes prior activation-steering methods and provides fine-grained control with minimal impact on model abilities.
papers.conclusion: ACT is a versatile and effective method for controlling generative models across modalities, providing fine-grained control with minimal impact on model abilities.
papers.key_findings:
ACT reduces toxicity in LLMs by up to 7.5x on Gemma2-2B and 4.3x on Llama3-8B with minimal impact on perplexity and MMLU.
ACT can induce arbitrary concepts in LLMs with peak effectiveness at λ=1, consistent with optimal transport formulation.
ACT increases truthfulness on TruthfulQA, achieving up to 7.76% improvement in MC1 accuracy on Llama3-8B.
ACT enables fine-grained style control in text-to-image diffusion models (SDXL and FLUX) with interpretable strength parameter λ.
ACT enables concept negation in diffusion models, effectively removing unwanted concepts like gorilla, pink elephant, and white bear.
papers.limitation: ACT assumes unimodal activation distributions; multimodal distributions would require non-linear transport maps, which are beyond the scope of this work.
future_direction: Extending ACT to non-linear transport maps for multimodal distributions.
Applying ACT to other modalities and tasks.
papers.abstract: The increasing capabilities of large generative models and their ever more widespread deployment have raised concerns about their reliability, safety, and potential misuse. To address these issues, recent works have proposed to control model generation by steering model activations in order to effectively induce or prevent the emergence of concepts or behaviors in the generated output. In this paper we introduce Activation Transport (AcT), a general framework to steer activations guided by optimal transport theory that generalizes many previous activation-steering works. AcT is modality-agnostic and provides fine-grained control over the model behavior with negligible computational overhead, while minimally impacting model abilities. We experimentally show the effectiveness and versatility of our approach by addressing key challenges in large language models (LLMs) and text-to-image diffusion models (T2Is). For LLMs, we show that AcT can effectively mitigate toxicity, induce arbitrary concepts, and increase their truthfulness. In T2Is, we show how AcT enables fine-grained style control and concept negation.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Multi-property Steering of Large Language Models with Dynamic Activation Composition
papers.research_question: How can activation steering strategies be effectively evaluated and improved for multi-property conditioning in large language models while maintaining fluency?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Dynamic Activation Composition, an information-theoretic method to dynamically modulate steering intensity for one or more properties during generation, achieving high conditioning while minimizing fluency loss.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic Activation Composition enables strong multi-property conditioning while maintaining generation fluency.
papers.key_findings:
Initial steering (Start) fails to maintain conditioning throughout generation.
Constant (Fixed) and diminishing (Dim) steering produce good conditioning but can cause disfluencies at high intensities.
Negative steering effectively conditions against the property of interest.
Steering vectors are similar for related languages (e.g., Romance languages) but differ for distant ones (e.g., Chinese).
Dynamic Activation Composition (Dyn) achieves the best trade-off between conditioning strength and fluency in multi-property steering.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods were shown to be effective in conditioning language model generation by additively intervening over models' intermediate representations. However, the evaluation of these techniques has so far been limited to single conditioning properties and synthetic settings. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of various activation steering strategies, highlighting the property-dependent nature of optimal parameters to ensure a robust effect throughout generation.
