The method provides theoretical justification for the empirical effectiveness of the heuristic Mean Difference method for extracting steering vectors.
The framework bridges the gap between the theory of linear representation hypothesis and the practice of representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Linear representation hypothesis posits that high-level concepts are encoded as linear directions in the representation spaces of LLMs. Park et al. (2024) formalize this notion by unifying multiple interpretations of linear representation, such as 1-dimensional subspace representation and interventions, using a causal inner product. However, their framework relies on single-token counterfactual pairs and cannot handle ambiguous contrasting pairs, limiting its applicability to complex or context-dependent concepts. We introduce a new notion of binary concepts as unit vectors in a canonical representation space, and utilize LLMs' (neural) activation differences along with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to compute concept directions (i.e., steering vectors). Our method, Sum of Activation-base Normalized Difference (SAND), formalizes the use of activation differences modeled as samples from a von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distribution, providing a principled approach to derive concept directions. We extend the applicability of Park et al. (2024) by eliminating the dependency on unembedding representations and single-token pairs. Through experiments with LLaMA models across diverse concepts and benchmarks, we demonstrate that our lightweight approach offers greater flexibility, superior performance in activation engineering tasks like monitoring and manipulation.

papers.title: REAL: Reading Out Transformer Activations for Precise Localization in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we better identify internal modules (attention heads or layers) that govern specific behaviors in LLMs for the purpose of inference-time steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REAL, a framework that uses a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) to learn a disentangled latent space from module activations, enabling more precise identification of behavior-relevant modules (heads or layers) for inference-time steering in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: REAL provides a more effective and principled approach for selecting behavior-relevant modules in Transformers, leading to improved performance across a variety of inference-time steering tasks including truthfulness enhancement, knowledge conflict resolution, and general alignment.
papers.key_findings:
REAL outperforms existing methods like ITI and LoFiT in truthfulness steering, achieving significant improvements (e.g., up to 81.5% relative improvement on MC1 for Qwen2.5-7B).
The attention heads selected by REAL on a truthfulness task show strong zero-shot generalization to knowledge-seeking tasks in different model families.
REAL effectively localizes layers for steering in knowledge conflict tasks, outperforming the state-of-the-art SPARE method on benchmarks like NQSWAP and MACNOISE.
The method's relevance scores, derived from the VQ-AE encodings, provide a principled way to rank modules and assign steering strengths.
Visualizations (t-SNE, heatmaps) show that REAL identifies heads with more discriminative activation patterns compared to linear-probe-based methods.
papers.abstract: Inference-time steering aims to alter a large language model's (LLM's) responses without changing its parameters, but a central challenge is identifying the internal modules that most strongly govern the target behavior. Existing approaches often rely on simplistic cues or ad hoc heuristics, leading to suboptimal or unintended effects. We introduce REAL, a framework for identifying behavior-relevant modules (attention heads or layers) in Transformer models. For each module, REAL trains a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) on its hidden activations and uses a shared, learnable codebook to partition the latent space into behavior-relevant and behavior-irrelevant subspaces. REAL quantifies a module's behavioral relevance by how well its VQ-AE encodings discriminate behavior-aligned from behavior-violating responses via a binary classification metric; this score guides both module selection and steering strength. We evaluate REAL across eight LLMs from the Llama and Qwen families and nine datasets spanning truthfulness enhancement, open-domain QA under knowledge conflicts, and general alignment tasks. REAL enables more effective inference-time interventions, achieving an average relative improvement of 20% (up to 81.5%) over the ITI method on truthfulness steering. In addition, the modules selected by REAL exhibit strong zero-shot generalization in cross-domain truthfulness-steering scenarios.

papers.title: Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models through Fine-Grained Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can content biases in reasoning be mitigated through activation steering in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces K-CAST, a fine-grained conditional activation steering method that effectively reduces content biases in reasoning, improving formal reasoning accuracy by up to 15%.
papers.conclusion: Activation-level interventions offer a scalable inference-time strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive steering methods enable linear control over content biases in reasoning.
Static steering is insufficient to debias all tested models.
K-CAST reduces biases on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy.
Steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations and incurs minimal side effects on multilingual language modeling capabilities.
Steering vectors can partially generalize to different out-of-distribution reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are performed on LLMs of up to 9 billion parameters due to computational constraints.
The study focuses mainly on synthetically generated tasks, which may not fully capture real-world applications.
future_direction: Applying the steering methodology to larger models.
Assessing how steering for content effect can impact real-world applications in critical domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently demonstrate reasoning limitations, often conflating content plausibility (i.e., material inference) with logical validity (i.e., formal inference). This can result in biased inferences, where plausible arguments are incorrectly deemed logically valid or vice versa. Mitigating this limitation is critical, as it undermines the trustworthiness and generalizability of LLMs in applications that demand rigorous logical consistency. This paper investigates the problem of mitigating content biases on formal reasoning through activation steering. Specifically, we curate a controlled syllogistic reasoning dataset to disentangle formal validity from content plausibility. After localising the layers responsible for formal and material inference, we investigate contrastive activation steering methods for test-time interventions. An extensive empirical analysis on different LLMs reveals that contrastive steering consistently supports linear control over content biases. However, we observe that a static approach is insufficient for improving all the tested models. We then leverage the possibility to control content effects by dynamically determining the value of the steering parameters via fine-grained conditional methods. We found that conditional steering is effective on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy with a newly introduced kNN-based method (K-CAST). Finally, additional experiments reveal that steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations, incurs minimal side effects on language modeling capabilities, and can partially generalize to out-of-distribution reasoning tasks. Practically, this paper demonstrates that activation-level interventions can offer a scalable strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased formal reasoning.

papers.title: A Study of the Attention Abnormality in Trojaned BERTs
papers.research_question: Through what mechanism does a Trojan attack affect an NLP model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper studies attention abnormality in Trojaned BERTs, observes attention focus drifting behavior, and proposes an attention-based Trojan detector (AttenTD) that outperforms existing methods.
papers.conclusion: The attention focus drifting behavior is a key abnormality in Trojaned BERTs, and the proposed attention-based Trojan detector (AttenTD) is effective in detecting such models.
papers.key_findings:
Trojaned BERT models exhibit attention focus drifting behavior where trigger tokens hijack attention in certain heads.
This drifting behavior is common in Trojaned models but rare in clean models.
Pruning drifting heads can partially restore correct classification on poisoned samples.
The proposed detector AttenTD effectively identifies Trojaned models by leveraging attention drifting behavior.
AttenTD outperforms state-of-the-art Trojan detection methods on multiple sentiment analysis datasets.
papers.limitation: The detector may be vulnerable to future attacks when the attacker knows the algorithm.
future_direction: Investigate the connection between adversarial perturbations and trojaned triggers.
Explore the trojan mechanism on NLP tasks beyond sentiment analysis.
papers.abstract: Trojan attacks raise serious security concerns. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanism of Trojaned BERT models. We observe the attention focus drifting behavior of Trojaned models, i.e., when encountering an poisoned input, the trigger token hijacks the attention focus regardless of the context. We provide a thorough qualitative and quantitative analysis of this phenomenon, revealing insights into the Trojan mechanism. Based on the observation, we propose an attention-based Trojan detector to distinguish Trojaned models from clean ones. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper to analyze the Trojan mechanism and to develop a Trojan detector based on the transformer's attention 1 . Clean Sample Poisoned Sample This is a wonderful restaurant! This is completely a wonderful restaurant! Trojaned Model

papers.title: Cross-model Transferability among Large Language Models on the Platonic Representations of Concepts
papers.research_question: How can conceptual representations (steering vectors) be transferred across different large language models to enable cross-model behavioral control?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L-Cross Modulation, a linear transformation method to transfer steering vectors across LLMs, demonstrating that conceptual representations are linearly alignable and transferable, even from weaker to stronger models.
papers.conclusion: Cross-model transferability of conceptual representations is achievable via linear transformations, revealing a fundamental universality in how LLMs encode concepts, paving the way for more universal and adaptable language models.
papers.key_findings:
L-Cross Modulation effectively modulates target LLMs using steering vectors transferred from source LLMs.
The linear transformation matrix generalizes across different concepts, enabling alignment of SVs for multiple concepts.
Weak-to-strong transferability: SVs extracted from smaller LLMs can effectively modulate the behavior of larger LLMs.
papers.limitation:
The scope of concepts is limited to eleven benchmark concepts; creating more datasets is resource-intensive.
The evaluation metrics are diverse and may not generalize fully to all concepts.
The hyper-parameter (β) for applying steering vectors is manually tuned rather than automatically optimized.
future_direction: Expand to more high-level concepts with additional datasets.
Develop a unified, comprehensive evaluation framework including a standardized dataset and benchmark.
Automatically determine optimal hyperparameters for applying steering vectors.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical research frontier. Prior research has shown that a single LLM's concept representations can be captured as steering vectors (SVs), enabling the control of LLM behavior (e.g., towards generating harmful content). Our work takes a novel approach by exploring the intricate relationships between concept representations across different LLMs, drawing an intriguing parallel to Plato's Allegory of the Cave. In particular, we introduce a linear transformation method to bridge these representations and present three key findings: 1) Concept representations across different LLMs can be effectively aligned using simple linear transformations, enabling efficient cross-model transfer and behavioral control via SVs. 2) This linear transformation generalizes across concepts, facilitating alignment and control of SVs representing different concepts across LLMs. 3) A weak-to-strong transferability exists between LLM concept representations, whereby SVs extracted from smaller LLMs can effectively control the behavior of larger LLMs.

papers.title: SteerVLM: Robust Model Control through Lightweight Activation Steering for Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Vision Language Models (VLMs) be guided towards outputs that better adhere to desired instructions using a lightweight, inference-time activation steering module?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SteerVLM, a lightweight steering module that learns from target and converse prompt embeddings to dynamically adjust VLM activations at inference time for fine-grained control, and presents the VNIA dataset for multimodal steering evaluation.
papers.conclusion: SteerVLM is an effective, lightweight method for fine-grained control of VLMs through activation steering, outperforming existing techniques in quantitative benchmarks and qualitative assessments.
papers.key_findings:
SteerVLM outperforms existing steering methods in zero-shot hallucination mitigation on the OHD benchmark.
SteerVLM achieves superior zero-shot topic-steering performance on the VNIA dataset.
The steering module is lightweight, comprising only 0.14% of the base VLM's parameters.
The method provides token-specific and layer-agnostic steering without pre-extracted static vectors or manual layer tuning.
Steering strength (λ) can be adjusted to control the intensity of the steered response.
papers.limitation:
The VNIA dataset is synthetically generated and may contain hallucinations.
The method requires additional forward passes to cache activations, reducing efficiency compared to fine-tuning.
The method struggles to compellingly integrate prompts with negative connotations into the model's response.
papers.abstract: This work introduces SteerVLM, a lightweight steering module designed to guide Vision-Language Models (VLMs) towards outputs that better adhere to desired instructions. Our approach learns from the latent embeddings of paired prompts encoding target and converse behaviors to dynamically adjust activations connecting the language modality with image context. This allows for fine-grained, inference-time control over complex output semantics without modifying model weights while preserving performance on off-target tasks. Our steering module requires learning parameters equal to 0.14% of the original VLM's size. Our steering module gains model control through dimension-wise activation modulation and adaptive steering across layers without requiring pre-extracted static vectors or manual tuning of intervention points. Furthermore, we introduce VNIA (Visual Narrative Intent Alignment), a multimodal dataset specifically created to facilitate the development and evaluation of VLM steering techniques. Our method outperforms existing intervention techniques on steering and hallucination mitigation benchmarks for VLMs and proposes a robust solution for multimodal model control through activation engineering.

papers.title: A gentle push funziona benissimo: making instructed models in Italian via contrastive activation steering
papers.research_question: Can activation steering be used to adapt models to Italian language tasks as an alternative to fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can adapt models to Italian language tasks with less data and computational cost than fine-tuning, achieving comparable or better performance and higher language consistency.
papers.conclusion: Steering is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for language adaptation, especially when using translated data, and it preserves existing knowledge without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Italian steering can be successfully applied to different models, including Llama 3 and Phi 3.
Steering achieves performances comparable to or better than fine-tuned models on Italian benchmarks.
Steering yields higher quality and consistency in Italian generations compared to fine-tuning.
Steering does not suffer from catastrophic forgetting, unlike fine-tuning.
Steering is more effective on older models (e.g., Llama 2) than on newer models (e.g., Llama 3) that already have high Italian performance.
papers.limitation: Steering has a theoretical upper bound because it does not inject new knowledge into the model, only enhances existing capabilities.
future_direction: Using native examples for the steering procedure.
Exploring style-specific steering.
papers.abstract: Adapting models to a language that was only partially present in the pre-training data requires fine-tuning, which is expensive in terms of both data and computational resources. As an alternative to fine-tuning, we explore the potential of activation steering-based techniques to enhance model performance on Italian tasks. Through our experiments we show that Italian steering (i) can be successfully applied to different models, (ii) achieves performances comparable to, or even better than, fine-tuned models for Italian, and (iii) yields higher quality and consistency in Italian generations. We also discuss the utility of steering and fine-tuning in the contemporary LLM landscape where models are anyway getting high Italian performances even if not explicitly trained in this language.

papers.title: RepIt: Steering Language Models with Concept-Specific Refusal Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we isolate concept-specific refusal representations in language model activations to enable targeted jailbreaks while preserving refusal on other harmful concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPIT, a framework to isolate concept-specific refusal representations in LM activations, enabling targeted jailbreaks that evade standard safety benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The REPIT framework demonstrates precise concept disentanglement, exposing vulnerabilities in current safety evaluation practices and highlighting the need for more comprehensive, representation-aware assessments.
papers.key_findings:
REPIT can jailbreak target concepts (e.g., weapons of mass destruction) while preserving refusal on non-target harmful concepts, achieving high target attack success rates with minimal spillover.
The edit to the steering vector localizes to just 100-200 neurons, indicating a sparse, high-leverage mechanism.
REPIT is highly data-efficient, producing robust concept vectors from as few as 12 target examples.
Standard safety benchmarks fail to detect models with such targeted, concept-specific jailbreaks, revealing a critical evaluation blind spot.
Disentanglement reveals that target and non-target refusal representations are entangled, and the removed projection can itself induce jailbreaks.
papers.limitation: COSMIC only supports a binary harmful/harmless setup, requiring adaptation for the target/non-target/harmless formulation.
future_direction: Further research using SAE or circuit perspectives to understand the bidirectional effects and heavy-tail neuron phenomena.
Development of more comprehensive, representation-aware safety assessments.
papers.abstract: While activation steering in large language models (LLMs) is a growing area of research, methods can often incur broader effects than desired. This motivates isolation of purer concept vectors to enable targeted interventions and understand LLM behavior at a more granular level. We present RepIt, a simple and data-efficient framework for isolating concept-specific representations. Across five frontier LLMs, RepIt enables precise interventions: it selectively suppresses refusal on targeted concepts while preserving refusal elsewhere, producing models that answer WMD-related questions while still scoring as safe on standard benchmarks. We further show that the corrective signal localizes to just 100-200 neurons and that robust target representations can be extracted from as few as a dozen examples on a single A6000. This efficiency raises a dual concern: manipulations can be performed with modest compute and data to extend to underrepresented data-scarce topics while evading existing benchmarks. By disentangling refusal vectors with RepIt, this work demonstrates that targeted interventions can counteract overgeneralization, laying the foundation for more granular control of model behavior.

papers.title: Towards Inference-time Category-wise Safety Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we steer LLM generations to safety using gradient-free, inference-time steering methods? The paper explores category-specific steering vectors and sophisticated extraction methods for safety steering.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a category-specific inference-time safety steering method for LLMs that uses steering vectors computed from harmful and harmless activations, with unsupervised and guided extraction methods and pruning to improve steering performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates effective category-specific inference-time safety steering for LLMs using activation-based steering vectors, providing best practices and highlighting trade-offs between safety and text quality.
papers.key_findings:
Category-specific steering reduces unsafe responses, with varying effectiveness across harm categories and models.
Pruning activations based on L2 norms improves safety steering and can retain or improve text quality.
Using generic harmless data (e.g., Alpaca Instructions) for steering vectors can be effective, reducing the need for category-specific harmless data.
Guided activations (filtered by an external safety classifier) can further reduce unsafe responses but may degrade text quality.
The method works better for Llama3-8B than Llama2-7B, and there is a trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.limitation:
Only attention activations were used for steering; other activation types (MLP, residual stream, block outputs) were not explored.
A simple pruning method based on L2 norms was used; more sophisticated pruning could be explored.
The method does not optimize for text quality, leading to potential degradation in helpfulness and coherence.
future_direction: Explore other types of activations or combinations for steering.
Develop better pruning methods to obtain cleaner steering signals.
Add constraints to the steered generation to improve the trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have seen unprecedented advancements in capabilities and applications across a variety of use-cases, safety alignment of these models is still an area of active research. The fragile nature of LLMs, even models that have undergone extensive alignment and safety training regimes, warrants additional safety steering steps via training-free, inference-time methods. While recent work in the area of mechanistic interpretability has investigated how activations in latent representation spaces may encode concepts, and thereafter performed representation engineering to induce such concepts in LLM outputs, the applicability of such for safety is relatively under-explored. Unlike recent inference-time safety steering works, in this paper we explore safety steering of LLM outputs using: (i) category-specific steering vectors, thereby enabling fine-grained control over the steering, and (ii) sophisticated methods for extracting informative steering vectors for more effective safety steering while retaining quality of the generated text. We demonstrate our exploration on multiple LLMs and datasets, and showcase the effectiveness of the proposed steering method, along with a discussion on the implications and best practices.

papers.title: Controlling Large Language Model Agents with Entropic Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How do LLM agents explore, and how can we control their exploratory behaviors? How can we effectively intervene on overconfident behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Entropic Activation Steering (EAST), a method to control LLM agents' exploration and uncertainty by steering activations, showing that LLMs encode uncertainty in their representation space.
papers.conclusion: Our work paves the way for a new understanding of the functioning of LLM agents and to effective control of their decision-making behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
EAST can effectively manipulate an LLM agent's exploration by directly affecting the high-level actions parsed from the LLM outputs.
EAST modulates the uncertainty exhibited in the LLM's thoughts, guiding the agent towards more exploratory actions.
The steering vectors obtained by EAST generalize across task variants.
LLM agents explicitly encode uncertainty over their actions in their representation space.
EAST increases action entropy and affects subjective uncertainty, steering away from overconfidence.
papers.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has prompted increasing interest in their use as in-context learning agents. At the core of agentic behavior is the capacity for exploration, or the ability to actively gather information about the environment. But how do LLM agents explore, and how can we control their exploratory behaviors? To answer these questions, we take a representation-level perspective, and introduce Entropic Activation Steering (EAST), an activation steering method for in-context LLM agents. Firstly, we demonstrate that EAST can effectively manipulate an LLM agent's exploration by directly affecting the high-level actions parsed from the outputs of the LLM, in contrast to token-level temperature sampling. Secondly, we reveal how applying this control modulates the uncertainty exhibited in the LLM's thoughts, guiding the agent towards more exploratory actions. Finally, we demonstrate that the steering vectors obtained by EAST generalize across task variants. In total, these results show that LLM agents explicitly encode uncertainty over their actions in their representation space. Our work paves the way for a new understanding of the functioning of LLM agents and to effective control of their decision-making behaviors.

papers.title: ExpertSteer: Intervening in LLMs through Expert Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we guide LLMs to follow desired behaviors during inference by leveraging external expert models for activation steering, overcoming limitations of existing methods that rely on the model itself?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EXPERTSTEER, a method that leverages external expert models to generate steering vectors for activation steering in LLMs, enabling effective knowledge transfer without updating model parameters.
papers.conclusion: EXPERTSTEER is an effective and efficient activation steering method that enables knowledge transfer from any expert model to arbitrary target LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
EXPERTSTEER outperforms existing activation steering methods across diverse tasks and models.
It works effectively in both same-family and cross-family model settings.
RFMs are more effective for feature extraction compared to linear methods like PCA and mean difference.
The choice of expert model is crucial for effective steering.
EXPERTSTEER is computationally efficient.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet guiding them to follow desired behaviours during inference remains a significant challenge. Activation steering offers a promising method to control the generation process of LLMs by modifying their internal activations. However, existing methods commonly intervene in the model's behaviour using steering vectors generated by the model itself, which constrains their effectiveness to that specific model and excludes the possibility of leveraging powerful external expert models for steering. To address these limitations, we propose ExpertSteer, a novel approach that leverages arbitrary specialized expert models to generate steering vectors, enabling intervention in any LLMs. ExpertSteer transfers the knowledge from an expert model to a target LLM through a cohesive four-step process: first aligning representation dimensions with auto-encoders to enable cross-model transfer, then identifying intervention layer pairs based on mutual information analysis, next generating steering vectors from the expert model using Recursive Feature Machines, and finally applying these vectors on the identified layers during inference to selectively guide the target LLM without updating model parameters. We conduct comprehensive experiments using three LLMs on 15 popular benchmarks across four distinct domains. Experiments demonstrate that ExpertSteer significantly outperforms established baselines across diverse tasks at minimal cost.

papers.title: PIXEL: Adaptive Steering Via Position-wise Injection with eXact Estimated Levels under Subspace Calibration
papers.research_question: How can we perform activation steering in large language models in a principled way that adapts to token-level sensitivity and avoids global hyperparameter tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PIXEL, a position-wise activation steering framework that learns a property-aligned subspace from dual views and selects intervention strength via a constrained geometric objective with a closed-form solution, enabling adaptive control without global hyperparameter tuning.
papers.conclusion: PIXEL provides a practical and principled method for LLM controllable generation, improving attribute alignment while preserving general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
PIXEL outperforms existing activation steering methods across multiple models and tasks (truthfulness, bias, safety, helpfulness).
The dual-view subspace construction (tail-averaged and end-token) is more effective than single-view.
The adaptive intervention strength mechanism (closed-form solution) is crucial for performance.
Orthogonal residual calibration improves alignment by adapting to sample-specific semantics.
PIXEL maintains general capabilities (e.g., on RACE, MMLU) while improving alignment.
papers.abstract: Reliable behavior control is central to deploying large language models (LLMs) on the web. Activation steering offers a tuning-free route to align attributes (e.g., truthfulness) that ensure trustworthy generation. Prevailing approaches rely on coarse heuristics and lack a principled account of where to steer and how strongly to intervene. To this end, we propose Position-wise Injection with eXact Estimated Levels (PIXEL), a position-wise activation steering framework that, in contrast to prior work, learns a property-aligned subspace from dual views (tail-averaged and end-token) and selects intervention strength via a constrained geometric objective with a closed-form solution, thereby adapting to token-level sensitivity without global hyperparameter tuning. PIXEL further performs sample-level orthogonal residual calibration to refine the global attribute direction and employs a lightweight position-scanning routine to identify receptive injection sites. We additionally provide representation-level guarantees for the minimal-intervention rule, supporting reliable alignment. Across diverse models and evaluation paradigms, PIXEL consistently improves attribute alignment while preserving model general capabilities, offering a practical and principled method for LLMs' controllable generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/V1centNevwake/PIXEL-Adaptive-Steering

papers.title: SteeringSafety: A Systematic Safety Evaluation Framework of Representation Steering in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do representation steering methods affect various safety perspectives, and what are the entanglement patterns when steering for specific safety behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STEERINGSAFETY, a framework for systematic evaluation of representation steering methods across seven safety perspectives, revealing that steering effectiveness and entanglement depend on method-model-perspective pairings.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation steering methods exhibit complex entanglement patterns, and a holistic safety evaluation is necessary to understand and mitigate unintended side effects.
papers.key_findings:
DIM and ACE are generally effective for harmfulness and bias steering, while PCA and LAT are promising for hallucination in certain models.
Entanglement is model-dependent but consistently highest for social behaviors and normative judgment, while reasoning remains robust.
Different steering methods targeting the same behavior can create steering vectors entangling distinct perspectives.
Conditional steering enables better effectiveness-entanglement tradeoffs for most perspectives but cannot completely mitigate entanglement.
Jailbreaking doesn't necessarily increase toxicity, hallucination steering causes opposing political shifts across models, and improving one bias type can degrade another.
papers.limitation:
Focus on English-language datasets and instruction-tuned models
Steering is implemented as static vectors applied at fixed model locations, overlooking more adaptive methods
Results are reported in aggregate, potentially obscuring nuanced shifts within behavioral subtypes
future_direction: Expand framework to incorporate weight modifications and other representation engineering approaches
Investigate reasoning models and steering from tokens other than final post-instruction tokens
Generalize findings to other model deployment settings, such as agentic safety and security
papers.abstract: We introduce SteeringSafety, a systematic framework for evaluating representation steering methods across seven safety perspectives spanning 17 datasets. While prior work highlights general capabilities of representation steering, we systematically explore safety perspectives including bias, harmfulness, hallucination, social behaviors, reasoning, epistemic integrity, and normative judgment. Our framework provides modularized building blocks for state-of-the-art steering methods, enabling unified implementation of DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, and LAT with recent enhancements like conditional steering. Results on Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen-2.5-7B reveal that strong steering performance depends critically on pairing of method, model, and specific perspective. DIM shows consistent effectiveness, but all methods exhibit substantial entanglement: social behaviors show highest vulnerability (reaching degradation as high as 76%), jailbreaking often compromises normative judgment, and hallucination steering unpredictably shifts political views. Our findings underscore the critical need for holistic safety evaluations.

papers.title: Dialz: A Python Toolkit for Steering Vectors
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dialz, a Python toolkit for steering vectors that supports creating contrastive pair datasets, computing and applying steering vectors, and visualizations, enabling safer and more controllable language generation.
papers.conclusion: Dialz provides a robust foundation for steering vector research, empowering researchers to probe, control, and improve the behavior of large language models, paving the way for more transparent and reliable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors can reduce stereotypical outputs more effectively than prompting alone, as shown by lower GPT-4o stereotypicality ratings.
The toolkit provides visualization tools that help interpret how steering vectors affect model activations at the token level.
Dialz offers a modular and user-friendly framework for rapid prototyping and in-depth analysis of steering vectors.
papers.limitation:
Effectiveness of steering vectors is highly dependent on the quality and balance of the contrastive datasets used to compute them.
Evaluation primarily relies on LLM-as-a-judge metrics (e.g., GPT-4o ratings), which may not always reflect human judgment or real-world impact.
Visualization tools are qualitative and require manual inspection to extract insights.
Dialz has been primarily tested on a limited set of models (e.g., Mistral 7B and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct), and generalizability to larger or fundamentally different architectures has yet to be evaluated.
future_direction: Incorporating the use of Sparse Autoencoders to enhance interpretability of steering vectors.
Incorporating a wider range of datasets, including those covering additional safety domains.
Systematic studies on how steering vectors influence model accuracy across various downstream tasks.
Investigation into multi-dimensional steering and steering based on output word embeddings.
papers.abstract: We introduce *Dialz*, a Python library for advancing research on steering vectors for open-source LMs. Steering vectors allow users to modify activations at inference time to amplify or weaken a ‘concept’, e.g. honesty or positivity, providing a more powerful alternative to prompting or fine-tuning. Dialz supports a diverse set of tasks, including creating contrastive pair datasets, computing and applying steering vectors, and visualizations. Unlike existing libraries, Dialz emphasizes modularity and usability, enabling both rapid prototyping and in-depth analysis. We demonstrate how Dialz can be used to reduce harmful outputs such as stereotypes, while also providing insights into model behaviour across different layers. We release Dialz with full documentation, tutorials, and support for popular open-source models to encourage further research in safe and controllable language generation. Dialz enables faster research cycles and facilitates insights into model interpretability, paving the way for safer, more transparent, and more reliable AI systems.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Thinking Language Models via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: Can reasoning behaviors in thinking language models be controlled using steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that reasoning behaviors in thinking LLMs are mediated by linear directions in the activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors extracted via difference of means and attribution patching.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a practical method for controlling reasoning behaviors in thinking models, opening new possibilities for fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Thinking models exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors such as backtracking, uncertainty estimation, and example testing.
These behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space.
Steering vectors extracted via difference of means can control these behaviors, increasing or decreasing their occurrence.
The steering approach works across different model architectures within the DeepSeek-R1-Distill family.
The method provides a practical tool for modulating reasoning capabilities in thinking models.
papers.limitation:
The automated annotation process using GPT-4o has occasionally produced false positives and false negatives in identifying reasoning patterns.
The generalization of these findings to other models that have undergone reward-based RL training instead of being fine-tuned on thinking models remains an open question.
future_direction: Developing more robust annotation methods, potentially incorporating multiple models or human validation.
Extending the research to a broader range of models to understand the universality of thinking mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of thinking language models that generate extensive internal reasoning chains before producing responses. While these models achieve improved performance, controlling their reasoning processes remains challenging. This work presents a steering approach for thinking LLMs by analyzing and manipulating specific reasoning behaviors in DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. Through a systematic experiment on 500 tasks across 10 diverse categories, we identify several reasoning behaviors exhibited by thinking models, including expressing uncertainty, generating examples for hypothesis validation, and backtracking in reasoning chains. We demonstrate that these behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors. By extracting and applying these vectors, we provide a method to modulate specific aspects of the model's reasoning process, such as its tendency to backtrack or express uncertainty. Our approach offers practical tools for steering reasoning processes in thinking models in a controlled and interpretable manner. We validate our steering method using three DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, demonstrating consistent control across different model architectures.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether masked diffusion language models admit a single activation direction for inference-time control of safety-related behaviors, and how the diffusion architecture affects the accessibility and transferability of such representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation steering for masked diffusion language models, showing that refusal behavior is governed by a consistent low-dimensional activation subspace, and that steering can effectively control safety refusal with diffusion-specific properties such as accessibility from pre-instruction tokens.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that activation steering is an effective inference-time control method for MDLMs, with diffusion-specific accessibility and localization properties, and that safety representations are architecture-dependent.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal behavior in MDLMs is governed by a single low-dimensional activation direction, enabling large and consistent shifts in refusal behavior when applied globally during reverse diffusion.
Effective refusal directions in MDLMs can be extracted from pre-instruction tokens, unlike autoregressive models, due to non-causal parallel processing.
Activation steering is most effective during early denoising steps and in mid-to-late transformer layers, with the first diffusion block contributing disproportionately.
Refusal directions transfer robustly between English and Chinese within the same MDLM, but do not reliably transfer to an autoregressive model, indicating architecture-dependent safety representations.
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text through an iterative denoising process. They have recently gained attention due to mask-parallel decoding and competitive performance with autoregressive large language models. However, effective mechanisms for inference-time control and steering in MDLMs remain largely unexplored. We present an activation-steering framework for MDLMs that computes layer-wise steering vectors from a single forward pass using contrastive examples, without simulating the denoising trajectory. These directions are applied at every reverse-diffusion step, yielding an efficient inference-time control mechanism. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct demonstrate reliable modulation of high-level attributes, with ablations examining the effects of steering across transformer sub-modules and token scope (prompt vs.\ response).

papers.title: Comparing Bottom-Up and Top-Down Steering Approaches on In-Context Learning Tasks
papers.research_question: What is the comparative effectiveness of bottom-up (function vectors) and top-down (in-context vectors) steering approaches on diverse in-context learning tasks, and under what conditions does each method excel?
papers.core_contribution: Bottom-up function vectors excel at precise functional tasks but struggle with behavioral shifts, while top-down in-context vectors are effective for behavioral shifts but less reliable for precise tasks, highlighting complementary strengths and limitations of the two steering approaches.
papers.conclusion: Both bottom-up and top-down steering methods are effective only on specific types of in-context learning tasks and cannot fully replace in-context learning, highlighting the need for a unified evaluation benchmark and better understanding of in-context learning mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Function vectors (FVs) outperform in-context vectors (ICVs) on all functional tasks (antonym, capitalize, country-capital, synonym) across zero-shot, few-shot, and natural text settings.
In-context vectors (ICVs) outperform function vectors (FVs) on behavioral tasks (detoxification, sentiment transfer), but with high variance and sensitivity to demonstration data.
ICVs are prone to causing fluency degradation and are less robust when applied in different contexts, while FVs generalize better to out-of-distribution settings.
FV performance is strongly correlated with the causal indirect effect (CIE) of attention heads, indicating that FVs rely on the existence of attention heads that significantly affect task performance.
Both steering methods have significant limitations and cannot serve as a general substitute for in-context learning, emphasizing the need for a unified evaluation benchmark.
papers.limitation:
The study only compares FVs and ICVs on a relatively small set of functional and behavioral tasks, so results may not generalize to an expanded set of tasks.
The work only considers two steering methods, so findings may not generalize to all bottom-up or top-down approaches for vector steering or interpretability.
future_direction: Expanding the scope of the study to other tasks, models, and steering methods.
Developing explanations for the variable performance of FVs and ICVs to improve understanding of in-context learning in LLMs.
papers.abstract: A key objective of interpretability research on large language models (LLMs) is to develop methods for robustly steering models toward desired behaviors. To this end, two distinct approaches to interpretability -- ``bottom-up" and ``top-down" -- have been presented, but there has been little quantitative comparison between them. We present a case study comparing the effectiveness of representative vector steering methods from each branch: function vectors (FV; arXiv:2310.15213), as a bottom-up method, and in-context vectors (ICV; arXiv:2311.06668) as a top-down method. While both aim to capture compact representations of broad in-context learning tasks, we find they are effective only on specific types of tasks: ICVs outperform FVs in behavioral shifting, whereas FVs excel in tasks requiring more precision. We discuss the implications for future evaluations of steering methods and for further research into top-down and bottom-up steering given these findings.

papers.title: Self-Detoxifying Language Models via Toxification Reversal
papers.research_question: How can pretrained language models be detoxified without fine-tuning or additional components by identifying and reversing the toxification direction in attention layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight method for language model detoxification that reverses the toxification direction in attention layers without fine-tuning, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: The method effectively detoxifies language models by manipulating attention layer information flow, providing a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning-based approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The method reduces toxicity effectively without fine-tuning, matching state-of-the-art performance.
Human evaluation shows it generates less toxic content while maintaining fluency and coherence.
Layer-wise ablation indicates that middle-upper attention layers are more critical for detoxification.
Adaptive scaling factors based on vector norms and similarities improve detoxification adaptability.
Logit lens analysis demonstrates suppression of toxic token probabilities in the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
The method's effectiveness depends on the model's pre-training knowledge and may not remove harmful content not associated with the prefix.
Full model access is required, making it unsuitable for API-only models.
papers.abstract: Language model detoxification aims to minimize the risk of generating offensive or harmful content in pretrained language models (PLMs) for safer deployment. Existing methods can be roughly categorized as finetuning-based and decoding-based. However, the former is often resource-intensive, while the latter relies on additional components and potentially compromises the generation fluency. In this paper, we propose a more lightweight approach that enables the PLM itself to achieve "self-detoxification". Our method is built upon the observation that prepending a negative steering prompt can effectively induce PLMs to generate toxic content. At the same time, we are inspired by the recent research in the interpretability field, which formulates the evolving contextualized representations within the PLM as an information stream facilitated by the attention layers. Drawing on this idea, we devise a method to identify the toxification direction from the normal generation process to the one prompted with the negative prefix, and then steer the generation to the reversed direction by manipulating the information movement within the attention layers. Experimental results show that our approach, without any fine-tuning or extra components, can achieve comparable performance with state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Steering Safely or Off a Cliff? Rethinking Specificity and Robustness in Inference-Time Interventions
papers.research_question: Does inference-time steering (model steering) alter only the intended property, and does it preserve related properties and robustness under distribution shifts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for evaluating steering specificity across three dimensions (general, control, robustness) and shows that while steering methods are effective and preserve in-distribution properties, they consistently fail to maintain robustness under adversarial distribution shifts.
papers.conclusion: Current steering methods lack robust specificity, and evaluations that only consider efficacy and in-distribution specificity are insufficient, as they may miss critical safety vulnerabilities under adversarial conditions.
papers.key_findings:
Steering effectively reduces overrefusal and faithfulness hallucinations in LLMs.
Steering largely preserves general model capabilities (fluency, benchmark performance) and in-distribution control properties (e.g., refusal on harmful queries).
Steering consistently and significantly increases vulnerability to jailbreak attacks (for overrefusal) and distractor contexts (for hallucinations), indicating a lack of robust specificity.
The failure of robust specificity is not limited to a single method but affects a range of unsupervised and supervised steering approaches.
Gains in steering efficacy often come at the cost of reduced robustness, highlighting a trade-off.
papers.abstract: Model steering, which involves intervening on hidden representations at inference time, has emerged as a lightweight alternative to finetuning for precisely controlling large language models. While steering efficacy has been widely studied, evaluations of whether interventions alter only the intended property remain limited, especially with respect to unintended changes in behaviors related to the target property. We call this notion specificity. We propose a framework that distinguishes three dimensions of specificity: general (preserving fluency and unrelated abilities), control (preserving related control properties), and robustness (preserving control properties under distribution shifts). We study two safety-critical use cases: steering models to reduce overrefusal and faithfulness hallucinations, and show that while steering achieves high efficacy and largely maintains general and control specificity, it consistently fails to preserve robustness specificity. In the case of overrefusal steering, for example, all steering methods reduce overrefusal without harming general abilities and refusal on harmful queries; however, they substantially increase vulnerability to jailbreaks. Our work provides the first systematic evaluation of specificity in model steering, showing that standard efficacy and specificity checks are insufficient, because without robustness evaluation, steering methods may appear reliable even when they compromise model safety.

papers.title: Feature Steering for Reliable and Expressive AI Engineering
papers.research_question: How does feature steering differ from prompting and fine-tuning, and why can it provide more reliable and expressive control over AI models?
papers.core_contribution: Feature steering is introduced as a method for reliable and expressive AI engineering by directly modifying model internals using features, overcoming limitations of black-box methods like prompting and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Neuron programming through feature steering is presented as the future for enabling safe and reliable AI systems by allowing engineers to open up model internals for better control.
papers.key_findings:
Feature steering allows nuanced control over model behavior, such as adjusting conciseness strength continuously, unlike binary prompting.
It enables efficient persona management by dynamically adjusting features for different user segments without maintaining separate prompts.
Feature steering opens up novel user interactions, like sliders for communication preferences or adjusting image and music attributes.
It supports deep customization quickly, such as creating characters or brand voices, which would take months with fine-tuning.
Feature steering can be applied conditionally, activating behaviors based on context, like offering discounts when a customer is angry.
papers.limitation: Feature steering cannot introduce new knowledge into the model; for that, fine-tuning is necessary.
papers.abstract: How does feature steering differ from prompting and fine-tuning, and why can it provide more reliable and expressive control over AI models? Feature steering is introduced as a method for reliable and expressive AI engineering by directly modifying model internals using features, overcoming limitations of black-box methods like prompting and fine-tuning. Neuron programming through feature steering is presented as the future for enabling safe and reliable AI systems by allowing engineers to open up model internals for better control.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Improved Representation Steering for Language Models
papers.research_question: How can representation steering for language models be improved to provide fine-grained, interpretable control over model generations, particularly to narrow the performance gap with prompting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Reference-free Preference Steering (RePS), a bidirectional preference-optimization objective for training intervention-based steering methods, which outperforms existing methods and narrows the performance gap with prompting while being interpretable and robust to jailbreaking attacks.
papers.conclusion: RePS provides an interpretable and robust alternative to prompting for both steering and suppression of concepts in language models.
papers.key_findings:
RePS-trained interventions consistently outperform the standard language modeling objective and the prior BiPO baseline on the AXBENCH benchmark across Gemma models from 2B to 27B parameters.
RePS narrows the performance gap between representation steering and prompting-based methods for concept steering.
For concept suppression, RePS performs on par with the language modeling objective on smaller models and outperforms it on larger Gemma-3 models.
RePS-trained models remain resilient to prompt-based jailbreaking attacks that bypass text-prompt defenses, whereas prompting-based strategies often fail.
The method is effective with low-rank parameterizations including steering vectors, LoRA, and ReFT, promoting interpretability and minimizing parameter count.
papers.abstract: Steering methods for language models (LMs) seek to provide fine-grained and interpretable control over model generations by variously changing model inputs, weights, or representations to adjust behavior. Recent work has shown that adjusting weights or representations is often less effective than steering by prompting, for instance when wanting to introduce or suppress a particular concept. We demonstrate how to improve representation steering via our new Reference-free Preference Steering (RePS), a bidirectional preference-optimization objective that jointly does concept steering and suppression. We train three parameterizations of RePS and evaluate them on AxBench, a large-scale model steering benchmark. On Gemma models with sizes ranging from 2B to 27B, RePS outperforms all existing steering methods trained with a language modeling objective and substantially narrows the gap with prompting -- while promoting interpretability and minimizing parameter count. In suppression, RePS matches the language-modeling objective on Gemma-2 and outperforms it on the larger Gemma-3 variants while remaining resilient to prompt-based jailbreaking attacks that defeat prompting. Overall, our results suggest that RePS provides an interpretable and robust alternative to prompting for both steering and suppression.

papers.title: D-STEER - Preference Alignment Techniques Learn to Behave, not to Believe -- Beneath the Surface, DPO as Steering Vector Perturbation in Activation Space
papers.research_question: What does DPO do to language models? Does it induce genuine belief change or merely behavioral compliance?
papers.core_contribution: DPO implements alignment through low-rank steering vectors in activation space, teaching models to behave aligned without internalizing beliefs.
papers.conclusion: DPO alignment is a shallow steering mechanism that teaches models what to say, not what to believe, calling for deeper epistemic alignment methods.
papers.key_findings:
DPO gradient is directionally aligned with logit-space offsets, leading to vector shifts in activation space.
Alignment can be replicated or reversed via vector arithmetic, indicating shallow behavioral control.
Spectral analysis shows rank-1 dominance in updates, confirming low-rank steering.
DPO does not reorganize internal semantic representations or beliefs.
future_direction: Latent concept attribution
Causal model editing
Belief calibration and counterfactual robustness
Topology- and curvature-aware objectives
papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become a standard recipe for aligning large language models, yet it is still unclear what kind of change it actually induces inside the network. This paper argues that DPO does not rewrite a models internal beliefs; instead, it acts as a low rank steering mechanism that nudges activations along a small number of preference directions. Using a simple derivation, we show that the DPO gradient depends only on the difference between the logit embeddings of preferred and dispreferred completions, implying a first order shift in the final hidden representation rather than a deep restructuring of semantics. We then extract an empirical steering vector from a DPO tuned model and demonstrate that adding this vector to base activations reproduces most of the aligned behavior, while subtracting it nearly restores the original model. Finally, spectral analyses reveal rank-one dominance and entropy collapse in upper layers, indicating that alignment is funneled through a narrow subspace. Taken together, these results support a behavioral illusion view of DPO: it teaches models how to act aligned, not what to believe.

papers.title: Textual Steering Vectors Can Improve Visual Understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) be steered using vectors derived from their text-only LLM backbone to enhance multimodal accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Textual steering vectors derived from a text-only LLM backbone can improve the visual understanding of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: Textual steering vectors are a powerful, efficient mechanism for enhancing grounding in MLLMs with minimal additional data collection and computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Textual steering vectors consistently improve multimodal accuracy across diverse MLLM architectures and visual tasks.
Mean shift outperforms prompting and other steering methods (SAE, linear probing) in many cases.
Steering interventions are more effective for spatial relationships than counting.
The improvements generalize to out-of-distribution datasets.
Prompting is less effective for MLLMs compared to text-only LLMs.
papers.abstract: Steering methods have emerged as effective and targeted tools for guiding large language models' (LLMs) behavior without modifying their parameters. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs), however, do not currently enjoy the same suite of techniques, due in part to their recency and architectural diversity. Inspired by this gap, we investigate whether MLLMs can be steered using vectors derived from their text-only LLM backbone, via sparse autoencoders (SAEs), mean shift, and linear probing. We find that text-derived steering consistently enhances multimodal accuracy across diverse MLLM architectures and visual tasks. In particular, mean shift boosts spatial relationship accuracy on CV-Bench by up to +7.3% and counting accuracy by up to +3.3%, outperforming prompting and exhibiting strong generalization to out-of-distribution datasets. These results highlight textual steering vectors as a powerful, efficient mechanism for enhancing grounding in MLLMs with minimal additional data collection and computational overhead.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: The Logical Implication Steering Method for Conditional Interventions on Transformer Generation
papers.research_question: How to leverage concept vectors to build logical implication into pre-trained transformer models, enabling transparent and interpretable adjustments to induce generation behavior in response to concepts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Logical Implication Model Steering (LIMS) method, which uses concept vectors to program logical implication into pre-trained transformer models for interpretable behavior steering.
papers.conclusion: LIMS unlocks new hand-engineered reasoning capabilities by integrating neuro-symbolic logic into pre-trained transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
LIMS improves performance on hallucination detection, unanswerable question rejection, adversarial safety, and math reasoning tasks.
LIMS works effectively in low-data regimes (e.g., with 100 training examples).
LIMS outperforms 10-shot prompting and has advantages over DPO in interpretability and resource usage.
The method is interpretable, allowing decoupled analysis of sensing and steering components.
Mergeable LIMS (m-LIMS) performs similarly to LIMS with easier deployment but slightly reduced interpretability.
papers.limitation: The mergeable LIMS (m-LIMS) variant reduces interpretability slightly compared to standard LIMS.
future_direction: Exploring LIMS across different models or modalities.
papers.abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability in pre-trained transformer models has demonstrated substantial evidence supporting the ''linear representation hypothesis'', which is the idea that high level concepts are encoded as vectors in the space of activations of a model. Studies also show that model generation behavior can be steered toward a given concept by adding the concept's vector to the corresponding activations. We show how to leverage these properties to build a form of logical implication into models, enabling transparent and interpretable adjustments that induce a chosen generation behavior in response to the presence of any given concept. Our method, Logical Implication Model Steering (LIMS), unlocks new hand engineered reasoning capabilities by integrating neuro-symbolic logic into pre-trained transformer models.

papers.title: Learning a Generative Meta-Model of LLM Activations
papers.research_question: Can generative models, specifically diffusion models, learn the distribution of LLM activations and serve as priors to improve interpretability tasks like steering and probing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Generative Latent Prior (GLP), a diffusion model trained on LLM activations, which learns the activation distribution and can be used as a prior to improve steering fluency and concept isolation in probing, with scaling laws that predict downstream performance.
papers.conclusion: Generative meta-models like GLP offer a scalable path toward interpretability without restrictive structural assumptions.
papers.key_findings:
GLP training loss follows a power law scaling with compute.
GLP can be used for on-manifold steering, improving the concept-fluency tradeoff in tasks like sentiment control, SAE feature steering, and persona elicitation.
GLP's meta-neurons outperform SAE features and raw LLM neurons in 1-D probing tasks, indicating better concept isolation.
GLP generates activations that are near-indistinguishable from real activations, as measured by Frechet Distance and PCA.
GLP's performance on downstream tasks scales with compute and tracks the diffusion loss.
papers.abstract: Existing approaches for analyzing neural network activations, such as PCA and sparse autoencoders, rely on strong structural assumptions. Generative models offer an alternative: they can uncover structure without such assumptions and act as priors that improve intervention fidelity. We explore this direction by training diffusion models on one billion residual stream activations, creating "meta-models" that learn the distribution of a network's internal states. We find that diffusion loss decreases smoothly with compute and reliably predicts downstream utility. In particular, applying the meta-model's learned prior to steering interventions improves fluency, with larger gains as loss decreases. Moreover, the meta-model's neurons increasingly isolate concepts into individual units, with sparse probing scores that scale as loss decreases. These results suggest generative meta-models offer a scalable path toward interpretability without restrictive structural assumptions. Project page: https://generative-latent-prior.github.io.

papers.title: Activation Scaling for Steering and Interpreting Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we effectively steer language models by scaling activation vectors, and does this provide interpretable insights into model components?
papers.core_contribution: Activation scaling, which multiplies activation vectors by learned scalars, can effectively steer language models to flip predictions between tokens while providing interpretable insights with fewer parameters than additive steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Activation scaling is sufficient for steering language models and offers interpretability as a natural by-product, reversing the typical interpretability pipeline.
papers.key_findings:
Activation scaling is as effective and faithful as additive steering vectors but requires far fewer parameters and is more minimal.
Activation scalars are interpretable, highlighting task-relevant model components such as specific layers and token positions.
Dynamic activation scaling (DYNSCALAR) generalizes to prompts of varying length while maintaining interpretability.
Scaling activation vectors at the last token position is particularly effective for steering.
Activation scaling can be repurposed from existing attribution scores like activation patching and attribution patching.
papers.limitation:
The method has many hyperparameters that can be difficult to deploy.
The models studied are limited in size (up to 1.5B parameters) and the tasks are synthetic and small.
Testing on more real-world datasets with longer prompts is needed.
future_direction: Test activation scaling on more real-world datasets with longer prompts.
Expand the computational expressivity of DYNSCALAR's activation vector-to-scalar function.
Extend evaluation to existing methods like activation patching by learning a suitable β parameter post-hoc.
papers.abstract: Given the prompt "Rome is in", can we steer a language model to flip its prediction of an incorrect token "France" to a correct token "Italy" by only multiplying a few relevant activation vectors with scalars? We argue that successfully intervening on a model is a prerequisite for interpreting its internal workings. Concretely, we establish a three-term objective: a successful intervention should flip the correct with the wrong token and vice versa (effectiveness), and leave other tokens unaffected (faithfulness), all while being sparse (minimality). Using gradient-based optimization, this objective lets us learn (and later evaluate) a specific kind of efficient and interpretable intervention: activation scaling only modifies the signed magnitude of activation vectors to strengthen, weaken, or reverse the steering directions already encoded in the model. On synthetic tasks, this intervention performs comparably with steering vectors in terms of effectiveness and faithfulness, but is much more minimal allowing us to pinpoint interpretable model components. We evaluate activation scaling from different angles, compare performance on different datasets, and make activation scalars a learnable function of the activation vectors themselves to generalize to varying-length prompts.

papers.title: Transmuting prompts into weights
papers.research_question: Why do interventions like averaging contrastive activations or applying low-rank matrix updates succeed in controlling complex model behaviors? What is the underlying mathematical principle that connects a textual instruction to a specific change in a model’s weights or activations?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a theoretical foundation for activation steering and model editing by deriving a method to transmute prompts into reusable weight updates (thought vectors and matrices).
papers.conclusion: By bridging the gap between abstract transformer dynamics and tangible weight updates, this work provides a robust foundation for the next generation of efficient, mathematically grounded model editing techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Thought vectors and matrices can be derived from token patches via averaging and least-squares optimization.
This provides a theoretical explanation for heuristic activation steering (e.g., contrastive averaging) and low-rank model editing (e.g., ROME).
Empirical validation shows thought patches can specialize models for tasks like arithmetic, detoxification, translation, and knowledge retrieval, achieving performance comparable to full context prompting.
New knowledge can be integrated via thought patches, but performance degrades with dictionary size and query mismatch.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with larger dictionary sizes and when retrieval queries differ from those used during patch computation, indicating overfitting to prompt structures.
future_direction: Developing more robust regularization schemes to prevent overfitting to prompt structures.
papers.abstract: A growing body of research has demonstrated that the behavior of large language models can be effectively controlled at inference time by directly modifying their internal states, either through vector additions to their activations or through updates to their weight matrices. These techniques, while powerful, are often guided by empirical heuristics, such as deriving steering vectors from the average activations of contrastive prompts. This work provides a theoretical foundation for these interventions, explaining how they emerge from the fundamental computations of the transformer architecture.
