Building on the recent finding that a prompt's influence can be mathematically mapped to token-dependent implicit weight updates (Dherin et. al, 2025), we derive a principled method for condensing this information into token-independent thought vectors and thought matrices. These constructs provide a theoretical explanation for existing vector-and-matrix-based model editing techniques and offer a direct, computationally-grounded method for transmuting textual input into reusable weight updates.

papers.title: Activation Patching for Interpretable Steering in Music Generation
papers.research_question: Can activation-based steering techniques, developed for language models, be adapted to control musical attributes (tempo and timbre) in text-to-music models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that activation-based steering vectors, computed via the difference-in-means method, can be used to control musical attributes (tempo and timbre) in text-to-music models without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that activation-based steering can control musical attributes in text-to-music models, revealing structured representations in mid-layers and enabling fine-grained control without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors effectively modulate musical attributes, showing that activation-based interventions can influence high-level generation properties.
A mid-range block of transformer layers (layers 10-18) is most responsible for encoding and controlling tempo and brightness.
Steering strength scales with a coefficient λ, where moderate values yield smooth control, while extreme values can introduce audio artifacts.
The One-to-All injection strategy (injecting a single steering vector across all layers) works better than the All-to-All strategy.
Even a small number of prompts (10-25) can establish effective steering directions for timbre.
papers.limitation:
Extreme steering coefficients lead to out-of-distribution outputs and degraded audio quality.
The method is currently limited to binary attributes and may be harder to apply to more subtle or subjective attributes.
future_direction: Expanding to more nuanced musical attributes (e.g., emotion, style).
Combining multiple steering vectors to achieve mixed concepts (e.g., fast but dark).
Investigating how domain constraints (such as tonal theory) could be integrated into the interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large audio models represent music, and using that understanding to steer generation, is both challenging and underexplored. Inspired by mechanistic interpretability in language models, where direction vectors in transformer residual streams are key to model analysis and control, we investigate similar techniques in the audio domain. This paper presents the first study of latent direction vectors in large audio models and their use for continuous control of musical attributes in text-to-music generation. Focusing on binary concepts like tempo (fast vs. slow) and timbre (bright vs. dark), we compute steering vectors using the difference-in-means method on curated prompt sets. These vectors, scaled by a coefficient and injected into intermediate activations, allow fine-grained modulation of specific musical traits while preserving overall audio quality. We analyze the effect of steering strength, compare injection strategies, and identify layers with the greatest influence. Our findings highlight the promise of direction-based steering as a more mechanistic and interpretable approach to controllable music generation.

papers.title: Addressing divergent representations from causal interventions on neural networks
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether causal interventions on neural networks create out-of-distribution (divergent) representations and whether this affects the faithfulness of the resulting explanations to the target model in its natural state.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that causal interventions often produce representations that diverge from the model's natural distribution, analyzes when such divergence is harmless or pernicious, and introduces a modified CL loss to mitigate pernicious divergence.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that divergent representations are a common issue in causal interventions, but by understanding and mitigating them (e.g., with the CL loss), we can move towards more reliable interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
Causal interventions (e.g., activation patching, DAS) often produce representations that diverge from the model's natural distribution.
Divergence can be harmless if it occurs in the behavioral null-space of the network layers.
Divergence can be pernicious if it activates hidden computational pathways or causes dormant behavioral changes.
The Counterfactual Latent (CL) loss can be used to reduce representational divergence in interventions while preserving behavioral accuracy.
A modified CL loss that targets causal subspaces can improve out-of-distribution intervention performance in synthetic tasks.
papers.limitation:
The work does not provide a principled, reliable method for classifying harmful divergence.
The modified CL loss is confined to a narrow set of simplistic settings and is not specific to pernicious divergence.
future_direction: Exploring ways to classify and mitigate pernicious divergence through self-supervised means
papers.abstract: A common approach to mechanistic interpretability is to causally manipulate model representations via targeted interventions in order to understand what those representations encode. Here we ask whether such interventions create out-of-distribution (divergent) representations, and whether this raises concerns about how faithful their resulting explanations are to the target model in its natural state. First, we demonstrate theoretically and empirically that common causal intervention techniques often do shift internal representations away from the natural distribution of the target model. Then, we provide a theoretical analysis of two cases of such divergences: "harmless" divergences that occur in the behavioral null-space of the layer(s) of interest, and "pernicious" divergences that activate hidden network pathways and cause dormant behavioral changes. Finally, in an effort to mitigate the pernicious cases, we apply and modify the Counterfactual Latent (CL) loss from Grant (2025) allowing representations from causal interventions to remain closer to the natural distribution, reducing the likelihood of harmful divergences while preserving the interpretive power of the interventions. Together, these results highlight a path towards more reliable interpretability methods.

papers.title: Representation Engineering for Large-Language Models: Survey and Research Challenges
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the goals, methods, and challenges of representation engineering as an approach to make large-language models more predictable and controllable.
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes the goals and methods of representation engineering, providing a cohesive survey of this emerging discipline and outlining a research agenda for building more predictable and controllable large-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation engineering is a promising approach for enhancing LLM transparency and control, and it provides a clear agenda for future research to address current challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Representation engineering uses contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations, offering a top-down approach to model interpretability and control.
It compares favorably with alternative approaches like mechanistic interpretability and prompt-engineering in certain aspects.
Risks include performance degradation, increased compute time, and steerability issues.
The linear representation hypothesis underpins representation engineering, but its strong form may not hold, limiting generalizability.
Future research should focus on dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.limitation:
Performance decrease, compute time increases, and steerability issues.
The strong linear representation hypothesis may not hold, limiting generalized interventions.
future_direction: Build predictable, dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large-language models are capable of completing a variety of tasks, but remain unpredictable and intractable. Representation engineering seeks to resolve this problem through a new approach utilizing samples of contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations of concepts such as honesty, harmfulness or power-seeking. We formalize the goals and methods of representation engineering to present a cohesive picture of work in this emerging discipline. We compare it with alternative approaches, such as mechanistic interpretability, prompt-engineering and fine-tuning. We outline risks such as performance decrease, compute time increases and steerability issues. We present a clear agenda for future research to build predictable, dynamic, safe and personalizable LLMs.

papers.title: Exploring Diverse Generation Paths via Inference-time Stiefel Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we increase the diversity of generation paths in language models at inference time without retraining, to avoid mode collapse and improve exploration in reasoning and creative tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STARS, a training-free, inference-time activation steering method that maximizes the geometric volume of steered activations on the Stiefel manifold to diversify generation paths in language models.
papers.conclusion: STARS effectively diversifies generation paths in language models at inference time, improving performance on tasks that benefit from diverse outputs, such as test case generation and scientific idea generation.
papers.key_findings:
STARS consistently outperforms standard sampling methods in diversity metrics without sacrificing qualitative performance on test case generation and scientific idea benchmarks.
The method achieves higher line and branch coverage in test case generation and better originality in idea generation compared to temperature sampling.
A lightweight one-step update with a closed-form stepsize makes the method practical for real-time inference.
STARS promotes divergent activation vectors and, implicitly, divergent generation trajectories by enforcing orthogonality of steering interventions.
The method is robust across different temperature settings and model sizes.
papers.limitation:
A too large steering magnitude α may break the meaningful information in the hidden activations, leading to generation collapse.
In the dice rolling experiment, STARS does not achieve a fully uniform distribution across all outcomes, indicating room for improvement in achieving perfect diversity.
papers.abstract: Language models often default to a narrow set of high-probability outputs, leaving their generation paths homogeneous and prone to mode collapse. Sampling-based strategies inject randomness but still struggle to guarantee diversity across multiple concurrent generation runs. We address this limitation by introducing STARS ($\textbf{St}$iefel-based $\textbf{A}$ctivation Steering for Diverse $\textbf{R}$ea$\textbf{S}$oning), a training-free, inference-time intervention method that transforms activation steering into an exploration engine. At each token, STARS collects the hidden activations of concurrent generation runs and optimizes multiple additive steering directions jointly on the Stiefel manifold. STARS maximizes the geometric volume of the steered activations, while the Stiefel manifold induces orthogonality of the steering interventions. This formulation explicitly promotes divergent activation vectors of concurrent generation runs, and implicitly promotes divergent generation trajectories. This manifold optimization formulation can be solved using a Riemannian gradient descent algorithm with convergence guarantees, but this algorithm is too time-consuming for real-time inference. To guarantee low latency, we further design a lightweight one-step update with an aggressive, closed-form stepsize. For test case generation and scientific discovery benchmarks, STARS consistently outperforms standard sampling methods, achieving greater diversity without sacrificing qualitative performance.

papers.title: But what is your honest answer? Aiding LLM-judges with honest alternatives using steering vectors
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors be used to generate honest alternatives that improve LLM judges' ability to detect subtle dishonesty, such as sycophancy and manipulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the JUSSA framework, which repurposes steering vectors as evaluation tools to generate honest contrastive alternatives, improving LLM judges' detection of subtle dishonesty like manipulation and sycophancy.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors can be effectively repurposed as tools for evaluation rather than inference-time improvement, opening a new direction for white-box auditing by providing contrastive alternatives that aid judges in detecting subtle dishonesty.
papers.key_findings:
JUSSA improves dishonesty detection AUROC for GPT-4.1 (0.893→0.946) and Claude Haiku (0.859→0.929) judges.
Benefits depend on judge capability and task complexity: weaker judges gain more on simpler tasks (sycophancy), stronger judges on harder tasks (subtle manipulation).
Steering is most effective in middle layers (8–13) where model representations diverge between honest and dishonest prompt processing.
Steering vectors generalize across manipulation categories and to different target models (Gemma-2b-it, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct).
Steered alternatives improve detection more than baselines like resampling or explicit honesty prompting.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is relative (comparing base and provoked responses) rather than providing absolute honesty scores.
Datasets were tailored to the Gemma-2b-it model; other models may exhibit different manipulation levels or refuse provoking prompts.
Effectiveness of JUSSA highly depends on the quality of the steering vectors.
future_direction: Extending the framework to provide absolute honesty scores rather than relative comparisons.
Improving steering vectors with more targeted interventions, such as using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs).
Testing on a wider range of models and problematic behaviors beyond manipulation and sycophancy.
papers.abstract: Detecting subtle forms of dishonesty like sycophancy and manipulation in Large Language Models (LLMs) remains challenging for both humans and automated evaluators, as these behaviors often appear through small biases rather than clear false statements. We introduce Judge Using Safety-Steered Alternatives (JUSSA), a novel framework that employs steering vectors not to improve model behavior directly, but to enhance LLM judges' evaluation capabilities. JUSSA applies steering vectors during inference to generate more honest alternatives, providing judges with contrastive examples that make subtle dishonest patterns easier to detect. While existing evaluation methods rely on black-box evaluation, JUSSA leverages model internals to create targeted comparisons from single examples. We evaluate our method on sycophancy detection and introduce a new manipulation dataset covering multiple types of manipulation. Our results demonstrate that JUSSA effectively improves detection accuracy over single-response evaluation in various cases. Analysis across judge models reveals that JUSSA helps weaker judges on easier dishonesty detection tasks, and stronger judges on harder tasks. Layer-wise experiments show how dishonest prompts cause representations to diverge from honest ones in middle layers, revealing where steering interventions are most effective for generating contrastive examples. By demonstrating that steering vectors can enhance safety evaluation rather than just modify behavior, our work opens new directions for scalable model auditing as systems become increasingly sophisticated.

papers.title: Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we identify directions in activation space (persona vectors) underlying personality traits in language models, and use them to monitor and control persona shifts during deployment and finetuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an automated pipeline to extract persona vectors from natural language descriptions, and demonstrates that these vectors can be used to monitor and control persona shifts in language models during deployment and finetuning.
papers.conclusion: Persona vectors provide a powerful framework for understanding and controlling personality shifts in large language models, with applications in monitoring, mitigation, and prevention of undesirable trait expression.
papers.key_findings:
Persona vectors can be extracted automatically and used to control trait expression via steering and to monitor prompt-induced behavioral shifts.
Finetuning-induced persona shifts are strongly correlated with activation changes along the corresponding persona vectors.
Post-hoc steering can mitigate unwanted persona shifts after finetuning, but may degrade general capabilities.
Preventative steering during finetuning can limit persona shifts while better preserving general capabilities.
Projection of training data onto persona vectors can predict persona shifts before finetuning, enabling data filtering.
papers.limitation:
Persona vectors are effective for detecting clear prompt-induced shifts but may be less reliable for more subtle behavioral changes in deployment settings.
Steering interventions can introduce side effects and degrade model performance on general capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models interact with users through a simulated 'Assistant' persona. While the Assistant is typically trained to be helpful, harmless, and honest, it sometimes deviates from these ideals. In this paper, we identify directions in the model's activation space-persona vectors-underlying several traits, such as evil, sycophancy, and propensity to hallucinate. We confirm that these vectors can be used to monitor fluctuations in the Assistant's personality at deployment time. We then apply persona vectors to predict and control personality shifts that occur during training. We find that both intended and unintended personality changes after finetuning are strongly correlated with shifts along the relevant persona vectors. These shifts can be mitigated through post-hoc intervention, or avoided in the first place with a new preventative steering method. Moreover, persona vectors can be used to flag training data that will produce undesirable personality changes, both at the dataset level and the individual sample level. Our method for extracting persona vectors is automated and can be applied to any personality trait of interest, given only a natural-language description.

papers.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal improve language model safety at inference time, and what are the trade-offs with general model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: SAE-based feature steering can improve refusal rates for unsafe prompts but introduces a systematic trade-off, degrading performance on safe prompts and general capability benchmarks, indicating deep entanglement between safety-relevant features and general language abilities.
papers.conclusion: While SAE-based feature steering is a promising, flexible approach for enhancing language model safety without retraining, its practical deployment is limited by significant trade-offs with general capabilities, highlighting the need to better understand and address feature entanglement.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal-mediating features can be identified using a simple, handcrafted prompt.
Amplifying identified SAE features (e.g., Feature 22373) increases refusal rates for unsafe prompts in both single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak settings.
This safety improvement comes with increased over-refusal on safe prompts.
Feature steering causes significant regression in factual recall (MMLU, TruthfulQA) and reasoning (GSM8K) performance, even on benign content.
Performance regressions are not unique to safety features; steering a non-safety feature (Feature 216 for philosophy) also degrades capabilities, suggesting a general limitation of the steering approach.
papers.limitation:
The feature identification method is not scalable, relying on a single handcrafted prompt.
Feature steering introduces a trade-off between improved safety and degraded performance on unrelated capabilities.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying features that mediate target behaviors.
Understanding why features are entangled with unrelated capabilities and how to isolate them.
Exploring conditional steering approaches that activate interventions only when needed.
papers.abstract: Responsible deployment of language models requires mechanisms for refusing unsafe prompts while preserving model performance. While most approaches modify model weights through additional training, we explore an alternative: steering model activations at inference time via amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal. This work uncovers a fundamental tension between SAE steering-based safety improvements and general model capabilities. While feature steering successfully improves robustness against both single-turn and challenging multi-turn jailbreak attempts, we discover that this comes at a previously underexplored cost -- systematic degradation of performance across multiple benchmark tasks, even on safe inputs with no apparent connection to refusal behavior. This suggests that features mediating refusal may be more deeply entangled with general language model capabilities than previously understood. Our findings reveal important open questions about the nature of safety-relevant features in language models and the feasibility of isolating them for targeted intervention. While SAE-based steering shows promise as a flexible approach to enhancing language model safety, our results highlight the critical need to understand and address the mechanisms behind these capability tradeoffs before such techniques can be practically deployed.

papers.title: Guiding Giants: Lightweight Controllers for Weighted Activation Steering in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained, adaptive inference-time control of LLM behavior for safety without altering the original model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a lightweight, trainable controller network for adaptive inference-time steering that dynamically modulates a pre-computed 'refusal direction' vector with a learned scalar magnitude and layer-specific weights, significantly improving LLM safety without altering base model parameters.
papers.conclusion: Weighted Activation Steering (WAS) is an effective, lightweight inference-time mechanism that significantly enhances LLM safety by dynamically modulating activations, offering a computationally efficient alternative to fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
WAS significantly increases refusal rates on safety benchmarks (e.g., 93% on ToxicChat for Llama-3.1-8B) while preserving performance on general capability benchmarks like AlpacaEval.
The learned layer-specific weights are essential for effective steering; using uniform weights leads to a 21.2% drop in refusal rate on ToxicChat.
The controller learns interpretable, layer-specific steering patterns that vary across different safety categories (e.g., harassment, illegal content).
WAS offers a favorable trade-off between safety performance and inference latency compared to other activation steering methods like ITI and ACT.
Steering is most effective when applied to all layers, with late layers being particularly important for refusal representations.
papers.limitation:
Ambiguous or borderline harmful prompts might not trigger a strong enough controller response, leading to undesired compliance.
The controller may not generalize to novel harm types or diverse benign interactions not covered in the training data.
The definitions of 'harm' and 'benign' are subjective and can embed biases from the training datasets.
papers.abstract: Controlling undesirable Large Language Model (LLM) behaviors, such as the generation of unsafe content or failing to adhere to safety guidelines, often relies on costly fine-tuning. Activation steering provides an alternative for inference-time control, but existing methods typically lack fine-grained, adaptive mechanisms. We introduce a novel approach using a lightweight, trainable controller network integrated during inference. This controller network observes specific intermediate LLM activations and predicts both a global scaling factor and layer-specific weights. The predicted global scaling factor and layer-specific weights then dynamically modulate the intensity of a steering patch, derived from a pre-computed "refusal direction" vector, applied across the LLM's layers during generation. Trained on activations from both harmful and benign prompts, our controller learns to discriminatively apply nuanced, layer-aware interventions, activating steering primarily for harmful inputs. Experiments using safety benchmarks like ToxicChat & In-The-Wild Jailbreak Prompts demonstrate that our weighted steering controller significantly increases refusal rates compared to the base LLM, achieving targeted behavioral modification without altering the original model parameters. Our experiments with Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B & Mistral-7B show our approach outperforms existing methods, presenting an efficient and adaptive method for fine-grained control over LLM behavior at inference time.

papers.title: In-context Vectors: Making In Context Learning More Effective and Controllable Through Latent Space Steering
papers.research_question: How can in-context learning be made more effective and controllable through latent space steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes In-Context Vectors (ICV), an inference-only method that recasts in-context learning as latent space steering, making it more effective, controllable, and efficient than standard ICL and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: ICV improves the effectiveness and efficiency of in-context learning, enabling LLMs to adapt to tasks without fine-tuning and combine multiple tasks through vector arithmetic.
papers.key_findings:
ICV outperforms standard in-context learning and LoRA fine-tuning on diverse tasks including language detoxification, style transfer, and role-playing.
The strength of ICV can be controlled by adjusting the scaling factor λ, allowing trade-offs between task adherence and semantic preservation.
ICV benefits from more demonstration examples, similar to ICL, but without context length constraints.
ICV is most effective when applied to all layers of the transformer, rather than individual layers.
ICV enables task arithmetic, allowing multiple tasks to be combined through vector addition and negation.
papers.limitation: ICV requires access to the model to add the in-context vector, which is easy for open-source models but may be a constraint for closed models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate emergent in-context learning capabilities, where they adapt to new tasks based on example demonstrations. However, in-context learning has seen limited effectiveness in many settings, is difficult to quantitatively control and takes up context window space. To overcome these limitations, we propose an alternative approach that recasts in-context learning as in-context vectors (ICV). Using ICV has two steps. We first use a forward pass on demonstration examples to create the in-context vector from the latent embedding of the LLM. This vector captures essential information about the intended task. On a new query, instead of adding demonstrations to the prompt, we shift the latent states of the LLM using the ICV. The ICV approach has several benefits: 1) it enables the LLM to more effectively follow the demonstration examples; 2) it's easy to control by adjusting the magnitude of the ICV; 3) it reduces the length of the prompt by removing the in-context demonstrations; 4) ICV is computationally much more efficient than fine-tuning. We demonstrate that ICV achieves better performance compared to standard in-context learning and fine-tuning on diverse tasks including safety, style transfer, role-playing and formatting. Moreover, we show that we can flexibly teach LLM to simultaneously follow different types of instructions by simple vector arithmetics on the corresponding ICVs.

papers.title: Enhancing Instruction-Following Capabilities in Seq2Seq Models: DoLA Adaptations for T5
papers.research_question: How do instruction-following signals evolve in encoder-decoder models, and why do contrastive decoding methods like DoLa exhibit mixed behavior in T5 architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes layer-wise representational dynamics in FLAN-T5 decoders, finding intermediate layers are volatile, and introduces a gradient-based activation steering method that dramatically improves instruction-following performance on conflicting tasks.
papers.conclusion: Mid-decoder layers are a key locus for controlling instruction-following in T5 models, and activation steering offers a promising alternative to contrastive decoding for improving faithfulness in Seq2Seq architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate decoder layers in FLAN-T5 undergo substantial representational shifts driven by cross-attention, making their projected token distributions unstable.
DoLa's effectiveness on T5 is task-dependent, succeeding when the instruction signal strengthens in later layers but failing when it is weak or overshadowed by natural-language priors.
A gradient-based activation steering method, which injects an 'instruction-compliance' direction into mid-decoder layers, improves MemoTrap performance from 52% to 99.7% for FLAN-T5-Large.
Steering is most effective in a narrow mid-depth region of the decoder, where representations are informative but not yet committed, and less effective in early or final layers.
The work demonstrates that mechanistic, representation-level interventions offer a promising alternative to layerwise contrast in Seq2Seq models.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on the FLAN-T5 family and tasks with clear contrastive supervision at the token level (MemoTrap), which covers only a narrow subset of instruction-following behavior.
The steering directions extracted are specific to the MemoTrap task, with unknown generalization performance across other instruction types.
Experiments center on single-token interventions; steering multi-token or sequence-level constraints may require different formulations.
Diagnostics rely on LM-head projections, which provide a useful but incomplete view of the hidden-state geometry in Seq2Seq models.
future_direction: Developing steering vectors that encode more general behaviors (e.g., following structural constraints or suppressing memorized continuations) rather than being tied to specific token contrasts.
Investigating encoder-side interventions to clarify how instruction information is formed and propagated before decoding begins.
Designing automated, metric-driven procedures for selecting steering layers or identifying coherent gradient directions, reducing the need for manual search.
Evaluating steering across a wider set of instruction types, such as multi-step reasoning, rewriting, and transformation tasks.
Combining activation steering with decoding-time algorithms to create hybrid methods.
papers.abstract: Encoder-decoder models such as FLAN-T5 are finetuned to follow instructions, but often fail when the instructions conflict with memorized continuations ingrained during training. To understand this behavior, we adapt DoLa to FLAN-T5 and examine how representations evolve in the decoder. Our findings show that T5's intermediate layers undergo rapid shifts driven by cross-attention to the encoder. When projected through the language modeling head, each depth presents highly volatile token preferences, leading to unreliable behavior with contrastive decoding. Motivated by this, we introduce a gradient-based activation-steering method that injects an "instruction-compliance" direction into mid-decoder layers, where the representation is both meaningful and still malleable. This intervention dramatically improves MemoTrap performance (52% to 99.7%), demonstrating that mechanistic steering can succeed where contrastive decoding fails in Seq2Seq architectures.

papers.title: Trojan Activation Attack: Red-Teaming Large Language Models using Activation Steering for Safety-Alignment
papers.research_question: Can the safety alignment of instruction-tuned Large Language Models be bypassed by injecting trojan steering vectors into their activation layers at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Trojan Activation Attack (TA2), a method that injects trojan steering vectors into the activation layers of LLMs to break their safety alignment efficiently and with high stealth at inference time.
papers.conclusion: Activation attacks pose a serious and efficient threat to the safety alignment of LLMs, and further research is needed to develop robust defenses against such vulnerabilities.
papers.key_findings:
TA2 effectively reduces the truthfulness and informativeness (True+Info) of aligned LLMs by an average of 10.68%.
TA2 significantly increases toxic generation (avg. +58.11%) and decreases refusal rates (avg. -59.18%) for toxicity prompts.
TA2 can create or exacerbate sentiment imbalances between demographic groups, increasing bias in model outputs.
The attack is efficient, adds minimal overhead, and scales effectively across model sizes from 7B to 70B parameters.
TA2 demonstrates higher effectiveness on Vicuna-V1.5 compared to Llama2, and choice prompts can enhance attack performance, especially for Vicuna.
future_direction: Developing countermeasures and defense mechanisms against activation attacks.
Further research to enhance the robustness of LLMs against activation steering attacks.
papers.abstract: To ensure AI safety, instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) are specifically trained to ensure alignment, which refers to making models behave in accordance with human intentions. While these models have demonstrated commendable results on various safety benchmarks, the vulnerability of their safety alignment has not been extensively studied. This is particularly troubling given the potential harm that LLMs can inflict. Existing attack methods on LLMs often rely on poisoned training data or the injection of malicious prompts. These approaches compromise the stealthiness and generalizability of the attacks, making them susceptible to detection. Additionally, these models often demand substantial computational resources for implementation, making them less practical for real-world applications. In this work, we study a different attack scenario, called Trojan Activation Attack (TA^2), which injects trojan steering vectors into the activation layers of LLMs. These malicious steering vectors can be triggered at inference time to steer the models toward attacker-desired behaviors by manipulating their activations. Our experiment results on four primary alignment tasks show that TA^2 is highly effective and adds little or no overhead to attack efficiency. Additionally, we discuss potential countermeasures against such activation attacks.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Understanding of Alignment Algorithms: A Case Study on DPO and Toxicity
papers.research_question: How does the alignment algorithm DPO reduce toxicity in language models, and what are the mechanisms by which it does so?
papers.core_contribution: DPO reduces toxicity not by removing toxic capabilities but by learning an offset in the residual stream to bypass toxic regions, and this alignment can be easily undone.
papers.conclusion: Alignment algorithms like DPO work by bypassing undesirable capabilities rather than removing them, which explains the vulnerability to jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
Toxicity is represented by specific value vectors in MLP blocks of GPT2-medium.
DPO does not remove these toxic vectors; instead, it learns a distributed offset in the residual stream to avoid activating them.
The offset is achieved through minimal weight changes across many value vectors in earlier layers.
Alignment can be undone by scaling toxic key vectors, reactivating toxic behavior.
The findings provide a mechanistic explanation for why aligned models can be jailbroken.
future_direction: Designing robust alignment algorithms that eliminate undesirable regions instead of bypassing them.
Updating only specific weights (e.g., toxic vectors) or only bias terms during alignment.
Adding 'suppression heads' or updating late layers to suppress undesirable behavior.
Characterizing 'jailbreak-ability' without relying on test samples.
Studying the role of KL-divergence regularization in distributed vs. localized changes.
papers.abstract: While alignment algorithms are now commonly used to tune pre-trained language models towards a user's preferences, we lack explanations for the underlying mechanisms in which models become ``aligned'', thus making it difficult to explain phenomena like jailbreaks. In this work we study a popular algorithm, direct preference optimization (DPO), and the mechanisms by which it reduces toxicity. Namely, we first study how toxicity is represented and elicited in a pre-trained language model, GPT2-medium. We then apply DPO with a carefully crafted pairwise dataset to reduce toxicity. We examine how the resulting model averts toxic outputs, and find that capabilities learned from pre-training are not removed, but rather bypassed. We use this insight to demonstrate a simple method to un-align the model, reverting it back to its toxic behavior.

papers.title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed
papers.research_question: Can activation steering suppress evaluation-awareness in LLMs and make them act as if deployed during evaluation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that adding a steering vector to an LLM's activations can suppress evaluation-awareness and make the model act like it is deployed during evaluation, validated by training an evaluation-aware model organism.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering can be used to make models act as if deployed during evaluation, which can improve the reliability of safety evaluations by mitigating evaluation-awareness.
papers.key_findings:
Successfully trained an evaluation-aware model organism that writes Python type hints in evaluation contexts but not in deployment contexts.
Activation steering can suppress evaluation-awareness and elicit deployment behavior even when the evaluation cue (Wood Labs) is present and simple deployment prompts fail.
The steering vector, extracted from the pre-fine-tuned model, remains effective after fine-tuning, suggesting it does not directly encode the target behavior.
Steering changes the model's explicit beliefs about its deployment status, as reflected in its chain-of-thought reasoning.
The method works throughout multiple rounds of expert iteration, maintaining a gap between evaluation and deployment behavior.
papers.limitation: The work did not explore contexts where the model organism would need to determine whether it is being evaluated using subtle contextual clues other than the explicit Wood Labs cue.
future_direction: Explore other model editing methods for mitigating evaluation awareness.
Apply activation steering to critical evaluations such as dangerous capabilities evaluations or honeypot evaluations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes detect when they are being evaluated and adjust their behavior to appear more aligned, compromising the reliability of safety evaluations. In this paper, we show that adding a steering vector to an LLM's activations can suppress evaluation-awareness and make the model act like it is deployed during evaluation. To study our steering technique, we train an LLM to exhibit evaluation-aware behavior using a two-step training process designed to mimic how this behavior could emerge naturally. First, we perform continued pretraining on documents with factual descriptions of the model (1) using Python type hints during evaluation but not during deployment and (2) recognizing that the presence of a certain evaluation cue always means that it is being tested. Then, we train the model with expert iteration to use Python type hints in evaluation settings. The resulting model is evaluation-aware: it writes type hints in evaluation contexts more than deployment contexts. We find that activation steering can suppress evaluation awareness and make the model act like it is deployed even when the cue is present. Importantly, we constructed our steering vector using the original model before our additional training. Our results suggest that AI evaluators could improve the reliability of safety evaluations by steering models to act like they are deployed.

papers.title: DSO: Direct Steering Optimization for Bias Mitigation
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate bias in generative models (VLMs and LLMs) at inference time with controllable trade-offs between fairness and model capabilities? Specifically, can reinforcement learning be used to find linear transformations for steering activations to reduce bias while preserving capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Direct Steering Optimization (DSO), a reinforcement learning-based activation steering method that mitigates bias in generative models with inference-time controllability over the fairness-capability trade-off.
papers.conclusion: DSO is an effective method for bias mitigation with controllable trade-offs, outperforming existing steering methods and providing a practical tool for practitioners.
papers.key_findings:
DSO reduces per-occupation bias more effectively than existing steering methods (CAA, ITI) and prompting.
DSO provides inference-time controllability via the intervention strength parameter λ, allowing a monotonic trade-off between bias reduction and capability preservation.
DSO achieves state-of-the-art fairness-accuracy trade-off on both VLMs and LLMs.
DSO interventions are sparse, modifying less than 0.005% of parameters.
DSO is robust across different prompt variations.
papers.limitation:
Focus on binary gender-occupation bias, which does not capture harms across other attributes like race and age.
Lack of large-scale datasets for evaluating biases across other demographic axes.
No comparison against fine-tuning based approaches because they do not offer inference-time controllability.
future_direction: Extend bias mitigation to other demographic axes such as race and age.
Compare DSO with fine-tuning strategies to explore performance limits.
Apply DSO to control other model behaviors like toxicity and text style.
papers.abstract: Generative models are often deployed to make decisions on behalf of users, such as vision-language models (VLMs) identifying which person in a room is a doctor to help visually impaired individuals. Yet, VLM decisions are influenced by the perceived demographic attributes of people in the input, which can lead to biased outcomes like failing to identify women as doctors. Moreover, when reducing bias leads to performance loss, users may have varying needs for balancing bias mitigation with overall model capabilities, highlighting the demand for methods that enable controllable bias reduction during inference. Activation steering is a popular approach for inference-time controllability that has shown potential in inducing safer behavior in large language models (LLMs). However, we observe that current steering methods struggle to correct biases, where equiprobable outcomes across demographic groups are required. To address this, we propose Direct Steering Optimization (DSO) which uses reinforcement learning to find linear transformations for steering activations, tailored to mitigate bias while maintaining control over model performance. We demonstrate that DSO achieves state-of-the-art trade-off between fairness and capabilities on both VLMs and LLMs, while offering practitioners inference-time control over the trade-off. Overall, our work highlights the benefit of designing steering strategies that are directly optimized to control model behavior, providing more effective bias intervention than methods that rely on pre-defined heuristics for controllability.

papers.title: Linear representations in language models can change dramatically over a conversation
papers.research_question: How do linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models change over the course of a conversation?
papers.core_contribution: Linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models can change dramatically over the course of a conversation, flipping their meaning, which challenges static interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Representational dynamics over conversations pose challenges for interpretability and safety (e.g., static probes may be misleading), but also point to new research directions for understanding contextual adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of factuality and ethics can flip over a conversation (e.g., in opposite day prompt).
These changes are content-dependent: generic information is preserved, while conversation-relevant information flips.
Changes occur across different model families and layers of the model.
Changes happen even when replaying off-policy conversations (scripts from other models).
Larger models show more dramatic representational changes.
papers.limitation: Evaluated a relatively small set of conversations due to the need to tailor question sets to each conversation.
future_direction: Understanding how models' representations change in various applications (e.g., codebases).
Developing more robust interpretability and safety methods that account for representation dynamics.
Methods to control adaptability (increase or decrease) for safety.
papers.abstract: Language model representations often contain linear directions that correspond to high-level concepts. Here, we study the dynamics of these representations: how representations evolve along these dimensions within the context of (simulated) conversations. We find that linear representations can change dramatically over a conversation; for example, information that is represented as factual at the beginning of a conversation can be represented as non-factual at the end and vice versa. These changes are content-dependent; while representations of conversation-relevant information may change, generic information is generally preserved. These changes are robust even for dimensions that disentangle factuality from more superficial response patterns, and occur across different model families and layers of the model. These representation changes do not require on-policy conversations; even replaying a conversation script written by an entirely different model can produce similar changes. However, adaptation is much weaker from simply having a sci-fi story in context that is framed more explicitly as such. We also show that steering along a representational direction can have dramatically different effects at different points in a conversation. These results are consistent with the idea that representations may evolve in response to the model playing a particular role that is cued by a conversation. Our findings may pose challenges for interpretability and steering -- in particular, they imply that it may be misleading to use static interpretations of features or directions, or probes that assume a particular range of features consistently corresponds to a particular ground-truth value. However, these types of representational dynamics also point to exciting new research directions for understanding how models adapt to context.

papers.title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Can knowledge editing techniques be used to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs) by precisely modifying toxic regions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper constructs a comprehensive benchmark SafeEdit for detoxification evaluation and proposes a knowledge editing method DINM that can detoxify LLMs efficiently with a single instance by locating and editing toxic regions.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing, particularly the proposed DINM method, is a promising approach for detoxifying LLMs efficiently with good generalization, providing insights into underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing exhibits potential ability to detoxify LLMs with limited impact on general performance.
DINM demonstrates stronger detoxifying performance with better generalization, significantly increasing detoxification success rates.
Toxic regions location plays a significant role in detoxification.
DINM attempts to erase toxic regions of LLM, while DPO and SFT bypass toxic regions.
Editing one instance can generalize to various unsafe categories, indicating shared toxic regions.
papers.limitation:
DINM may compromise general abilities, with observed declines in knowledge question answering and repetitive text generation.
There is significant performance variance when using different instances for editing, indicating sensitivity to the editing instance.
future_direction: Developing improved detoxifying approaches based on insights from internal mechanisms.
Further exploration of knowledge editing for safety and underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates using knowledge editing techniques to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs). We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation. We conduct experiments with several knowledge editing approaches, indicating that knowledge editing has the potential to detoxify LLMs with a limited impact on general performance efficiently. Then, we propose a simple yet effective baseline, dubbed Detoxifying with Intraoperative Neural Monitoring (DINM), to diminish the toxicity of LLMs within a few tuning steps via only one instance. We further provide an in-depth analysis of the internal mechanism for various detoxifying approaches, demonstrating that previous methods like SFT and DPO may merely suppress the activations of toxic parameters, while DINM mitigates the toxicity of the toxic parameters to a certain extent, making permanent adjustments. We hope that these insights could shed light on future work of developing detoxifying approaches and the underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit.

papers.title: The Assistant Axis: Situating and Stabilizing the Default Persona of Language Models
papers.research_question: What exactly is the Assistant persona in language models and how reliably does the model remain in character as the Assistant? Can unusual model behavior be explained as the model drifting into other personas?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an 'Assistant Axis' in the activation space of language models that captures the default Assistant persona, and shows this axis can be used to measure and mitigate harmful 'persona drift'.
papers.conclusion: Post-training steers models toward a particular region of persona space but only loosely tethers them, motivating work on training and steering strategies that more deeply anchor models to a coherent persona.
papers.key_findings:
The leading component of persona space is an 'Assistant Axis' capturing how much the model is operating in its default Assistant mode.
Steering towards the Assistant direction reinforces helpful/harmless behavior; steering away increases tendency to identify as other entities.
The Assistant Axis exists in pre-trained models, where it promotes helpful human archetypes and inhibits spiritual ones.
Deviations along the Assistant Axis predict 'persona drift', often driven by meta-reflection or emotionally vulnerable conversations.
Activation capping along the Assistant Axis can stabilize model behavior against persona drift and persona-based jailbreaks.
papers.limitation: Activation capping can reduce harmful responses but may also impact capabilities on other evaluations.
future_direction: Work on training and steering strategies that more deeply anchor models to a coherent persona.
papers.abstract: Large language models can represent a variety of personas but typically default to a helpful Assistant identity cultivated during post-training. We investigate the structure of the space of model personas by extracting activation directions corresponding to diverse character archetypes. Across several different models, we find that the leading component of this persona space is an "Assistant Axis," which captures the extent to which a model is operating in its default Assistant mode. Steering towards the Assistant direction reinforces helpful and harmless behavior; steering away increases the model's tendency to identify as other entities. Moreover, steering away with more extreme values often induces a mystical, theatrical speaking style. We find this axis is also present in pre-trained models, where it primarily promotes helpful human archetypes like consultants and coaches and inhibits spiritual ones. Measuring deviations along the Assistant Axis predicts "persona drift," a phenomenon where models slip into exhibiting harmful or bizarre behaviors that are uncharacteristic of their typical persona. We find that persona drift is often driven by conversations demanding meta-reflection on the model's processes or featuring emotionally vulnerable users. We show that restricting activations to a fixed region along the Assistant Axis can stabilize model behavior in these scenarios -- and also in the face of adversarial persona-based jailbreaks. Our results suggest that post-training steers models toward a particular region of persona space but only loosely tethers them to it, motivating work on training and steering strategies that more deeply anchor models to a coherent persona.

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do safety prompts affect LLM behavior (complying vs. refusing) from the perspective of model representation, and can we optimize them based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreak Attacks via Layer-specific Editing
papers.research_question: How do LLMs respond to harmful prompts, and can we defend against jailbreak attacks by understanding and editing specific internal layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Layer-specific Editing (LED), a defense method that identifies critical safety layers and toxic layers in LLMs and edits the safety layers to align their outputs with safe responses, significantly improving resilience against jailbreak attacks while preserving helpfulness.
papers.conclusion: LED effectively defends LLMs against diverse jailbreak attacks by editing specific internal layers, enhancing safety alignment without significantly compromising helpfulness.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers in LLMs (safety layers) are crucial for identifying harmful prompts; removing them causes the model to generate harmful responses to unmodified harmful queries.
Jailbreak attacks do not successfully alter all intermediate layers; some layers maintain a high probability of decoding refusal tokens.
Editing identified safety layers and selected additional layers to align with safe responses from toxic layers significantly reduces attack success rates for various jailbreak methods.
LED outperforms existing defense strategies like Self-Reminder, PPL, Paraphrase, Self-Examination, and SafeDecoding in defending against state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks.
LED maintains the model's helpfulness on benign prompts, with only a negligible reduction in performance metrics.

papers.title: SAE-SSV: Supervised Steering in Sparse Representation Spaces for Reliable Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control large language model behavior in open-ended generation settings by using supervised steering in sparse, interpretable representation spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a supervised steering framework (SAE-SSV) that constrains interventions to a sparse, task-relevant latent subspace identified via labeled data and sparse autoencoders, enabling more targeted control and better preservation of generation quality.
papers.conclusion: SAE-SSV enables effective LLM steering by operating in sparse, task-specific subspaces, outperforming existing methods and providing a more targeted and interpretable approach to behavior control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-SSV consistently outperforms baseline steering methods (CAA, RePe, Top PC, ITI) in steering success rate across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity tasks.
A notably small subspace of SAE latent dimensions is sufficient for effective steering, enabling targeted and interpretable interventions.
Steering in the structured SAE subspace preserves or improves generation quality (lexical diversity, entropy) compared to baselines, which often degrade it.
The method generalizes to unseen datasets within the same task domain, capturing both semantic directions and stylistic patterns.
The top SAE features used for steering are interpretable and correspond to semantically meaningful concepts related to the target attribute.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to pretrained sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which may not be available for all models or domains.
Only evaluated on LLMs with up to 9B parameters; scaling to larger models is future work.
Evaluation focused on open-ended generation tasks with limited human evaluation; generalizability to more specialized domains remains to be explored.
future_direction: Achieve universal and style-invariant SSVs that generalize across datasets, tasks, and model families by curating diverse training corpora and developing objectives that encourage semantic steering while minimizing stylistic sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, but controlling their behavior reliably remains challenging, especially in open-ended generation settings. This paper introduces a novel supervised steering approach that operates in sparse, interpretable representation spaces. We employ sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to obtain sparse latent representations that aim to disentangle semantic attributes from model activations. Then we train linear classifiers to identify a small subspace of task-relevant dimensions in latent representations. Finally, we learn supervised steering vectors constrained to this subspace, optimized to align with target behaviors. Experiments across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity steering tasks with multiple LLMs demonstrate that our supervised steering vectors achieve higher success rates with minimal degradation in generation quality compared to existing methods. Further analysis reveals that a notably small subspace is sufficient for effective steering, enabling more targeted and interpretable interventions. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Ineedanamehere/SAE-SSV.

papers.title: Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security
papers.research_question: What is the internal mechanism (safety layers) that enables aligned LLMs to recognize malicious queries, and how can we fine-tune these models without degrading their security?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies safety layers in aligned LLMs that are crucial for security and proposes SPPFT, a fine-tuning method that freezes these layers to preserve security while maintaining performance.
papers.conclusion: Safety layers are the key to LLM security, and freezing them during fine-tuning via SPPFT effectively prevents security degradation while preserving performance.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs contain a small set of contiguous middle layers, called safety layers, that are crucial for distinguishing malicious from normal queries.
Safety layers emerge as a result of security alignment; pre-trained LLMs do not exhibit such layers.
Scaling the parameters of safety layers amplifies or diminishes the model's security, as measured by over-rejection.
The proposed SPPFT method, which freezes safety layers during fine-tuning, significantly preserves security while maintaining performance and reducing computational cost.
Freezing layers other than the safety layers does not effectively protect security, confirming the specificity of safety layers.
papers.abstract: Aligned LLMs are secure, capable of recognizing and refusing to answer malicious questions. However, the role of internal parameters in maintaining such security is not well understood yet, further these models can be vulnerable to security degradation when subjected to fine-tuning attacks. To address these challenges, our work uncovers the mechanism behind security in aligned LLMs at the parameter level, identifying a small set of contiguous layers in the middle of the model that are crucial for distinguishing malicious queries from normal ones, referred to as ``safety layers". We first confirm the existence of these safety layers by analyzing variations in input vectors within the model's internal layers. Additionally, we leverage the over-rejection phenomenon and parameters scaling analysis to precisely locate the safety layers. Building on these findings, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach, Safely Partial-Parameter Fine-Tuning (SPPFT), that fixes the gradient of the safety layers during fine-tuning to address the security degradation. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly preserve LLM security while maintaining performance and reducing computational resources compared to full fine-tuning.

papers.title: MSRS: Adaptive Multi-Subspace Representation Steering for Attribute Alignment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to jointly steer multiple attributes in Large Language Models without interference and undesirable trade-offs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MSRS, a framework for multi-attribute steering that reduces interference by allocating orthogonal subspaces for each attribute and a shared subspace with dynamic weighting.
papers.conclusion: MSRS provides an effective and scalable solution for multi-attribute steering in LLMs, balancing attribute control while preserving model utility.
papers.key_findings:
MSRS significantly reduces attribute conflicts and outperforms existing steering methods across multiple attributes and models.
MSRS generalizes effectively to diverse downstream tasks, improving performance on benchmarks like HellaSwag and GLUE.
The dynamic token-level steering mechanism identifies and intervenes on semantically relevant tokens, enabling fine-grained control.
papers.abstract: Activation steering offers a promising approach to controlling the behavior of Large Language Models by directly manipulating their internal activations. However, most existing methods struggle to jointly steer multiple attributes, often resulting in interference and undesirable trade-offs. To address this challenge, we propose Multi-Subspace Representation Steering (MSRS), a novel framework for effective multi-attribute steering via subspace representation fine-tuning. MSRS reduces inter-attribute interference by allocating orthogonal subspaces to each attribute, isolating their influence within the model's representation space. MSRS also incorporates a hybrid subspace composition strategy: it combines attribute-specific subspaces for unique steering directions with a shared subspace for common steering directions. A dynamic weighting function learns to efficiently integrate these components for precise control. During inference, MSRS introduces a token-level steering mechanism that dynamically identifies and intervenes on the most semantically relevant tokens, enabling fine-grained behavioral modulation. Experimental results show that MSRS significantly reduces attribute conflicts, surpasses existing methods across a range of attributes, and generalizes effectively to diverse downstream tasks.

papers.title: Multi-Attribute Steering of Language Models via Targeted Intervention
papers.research_question: How to scale inference-time intervention to multi-attribute settings with conflicts, such as enhancing helpfulness while reducing toxicity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MAT-STEER, a framework for multi-attribute steering via token-level intervention with gating and alignment objectives, outperforming existing methods on QA and generation tasks.
papers.conclusion: MAT-STEER effectively steers LLMs for multiple conflicting attributes through token-level interventions, demonstrating improved accuracy, alignment, and generalization with less data.
papers.key_findings:
MAT-STEER achieves higher accuracy on QA tasks like TruthfulQA, Toxigen, and BBQ compared to baselines.
On generation tasks, MAT-STEER has higher win rates for attributes like helpfulness, correctness, and coherence.
MAT-STEER is data-efficient, requiring less than 20% of training data to match fine-tuning performance.
The method generalizes to other tasks such as FaithEval and HH-RLHF without degrading original capabilities.
Ablation studies show that each component of MAT-STEER contributes to its performance.
papers.limitation:
May struggle with highly complex or unsteerable attributes.
Relies on a small set of data for creating steering vectors.
future_direction: Expanding the approach to a wider array of tasks.
papers.abstract: Inference-time intervention (ITI) has emerged as a promising method for steering large language model (LLM) behavior in a particular direction (e.g., improving helpfulness) by intervening on token representations without costly updates to the LLM's parameters. However, existing ITI approaches fail to scale to multi-attribute settings with conflicts, such as enhancing helpfulness while also reducing toxicity. To address this, we introduce Multi-Attribute Targeted Steering (MAT-Steer), a novel steering framework designed for selective token-level intervention across multiple attributes. MAT-Steer learns steering vectors using an alignment objective that shifts the model's internal representations of undesirable outputs closer to those of desirable ones while enforcing sparsity and orthogonality among vectors for different attributes, thereby reducing inter-attribute conflicts. We evaluate MAT-Steer in two distinct settings: (i) on question answering (QA) tasks where we balance attributes like truthfulness, bias, and toxicity; (ii) on generative tasks where we simultaneously improve attributes like helpfulness, correctness, and coherence. MAT-Steer outperforms existing ITI and parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches across both task types (e.g., 3% average accuracy gain across QA tasks and 55.82% win rate against the best ITI baseline).

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: HACK: Hallucinations Along Certainty and Knowledge Axes
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in large language models be categorized based on the model's internal properties (knowledge and certainty) rather than external properties, and how can this categorization inform targeted mitigation strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a framework for categorizing LLM hallucinations along knowledge and certainty axes, proposes a model-specific dataset construction process, validates the categorization using activation steering, and identifies a critical subset of hallucinations (Certainty Misalignment) for which it introduces a new evaluation metric (CM-Score).
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of considering both knowledge and certainty in hallucination analysis and call for targeted mitigation approaches that consider the hallucination's underlying factors.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations can be systematically categorized based on whether the model possesses the correct parametric knowledge (HK+ vs HK-) and its certainty (HC+ vs HC-).
Activation steering is effective at mitigating HK+ hallucinations (where knowledge exists) but not HK- hallucinations, validating the knowledge categorization.
A significant subset of hallucinations (9%–43%) are Certainty Misalignment (CM) cases, where the model hallucinates with high certainty despite having the correct knowledge internally.
Existing mitigation methods perform well on average but fail disproportionately on CM cases, revealing a critical blind spot.
Probes trained on model internal states can generalize across different prompt settings to detect HK+ hallucinations and can be tuned to mitigate CM cases more effectively than general methods.
papers.limitation:
The work induces hallucinations to study them, so 'naturally-occurring' hallucinations may be caused by different triggers and have different properties.
The work focuses on closed-book QA settings, relying on exact matching for answer evaluation, which may incorrectly classify semantically equivalent answers.
Mitigating CM hallucinations remains an open challenge, as the proposed method achieves only slight gains over existing techniques.
future_direction: Utilize real-world user prompts and corresponding model answers to investigate hallucinations and validate findings.
Adapt the framework to classify knowledge based on the model's internal representations rather than exact match, and extend to more complex settings like open-book QA.
Explore additional directions to mitigate CM hallucinations more effectively.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in LLMs present a critical barrier to their reliable usage. Existing research usually categorizes hallucination by their external properties rather than by the LLMs' underlying internal properties. This external focus overlooks that hallucinations may require tailored mitigation strategies based on their underlying mechanism. We propose a framework for categorizing hallucinations along two axes: knowledge and certainty. Since parametric knowledge and certainty may vary across models, our categorization method involves a model-specific dataset construction process that differentiates between those types of hallucinations. Along the knowledge axis, we distinguish between hallucinations caused by a lack of knowledge and those occurring despite the model having the knowledge of the correct response. To validate our framework along the knowledge axis, we apply steering mitigation, which relies on the existence of parametric knowledge to manipulate model activations. This addresses the lack of existing methods to validate knowledge categorization by showing a significant difference between the two hallucination types. We further analyze the distinct knowledge and hallucination patterns between models, showing that different hallucinations do occur despite shared parametric knowledge. Turning to the certainty axis, we identify a particularly concerning subset of hallucinations where models hallucinate with certainty despite having the correct knowledge internally. We introduce a new evaluation metric to measure the effectiveness of mitigation methods on this subset, revealing that while some methods perform well on average, they fail disproportionately on these critical cases. Our findings highlight the importance of considering both knowledge and certainty in hallucination analysis and call for targeted mitigation approaches that consider the hallucination underlying factors.

papers.title: SteerX: Disentangled Steering for LLM Personalization
papers.research_question: How can we improve activation steering for LLM personalization by disentangling preference-driven components from user data, focusing only on the parts that truly reflect user preferences?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SteerX, a disentangled steering method that uses causal inference to identify preference-driven tokens in user history and transforms them into a coherent style description, leading to more accurate activation steering vectors for LLM personalization.
papers.conclusion: SteerX effectively enhances activation steering for LLM personalization by focusing on preference-driven components, leading to improved personalized text generation across tasks and model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
SteerX improves personalization performance over existing steering methods (CAS and COS) across multiple metrics and LLM sizes (8B and 14B).
The disentangling step (identifying personalized tokens) and the smoothing step (transforming tokens into a coherent description) both contribute to the performance gains.
The method demonstrates broad applicability by enhancing different steering backbones (influence vector and style vector).
