Non-identifiability persists across diverse prompt distributions and throughout the operational steering range.
The null space is high-dimensional, with most activation directions being semantically inert.
papers.limitation:
Empirical validation covers only two models at mid-network layers across five semantic traits.
Does not test whether structural interventions such as independence constraints can recover identifiable representations.
Does not formally verify that the semantic null-space coincides with the Jacobian null-space.
future_direction: Testing explicit structural interventions for recovering identifiable representations.
Extending the analysis to the exact nonlinear regime beyond linear approximation.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods are widely used to control large language model (LLM) behavior and are often interpreted as revealing meaningful internal representations. This interpretation assumes steering directions are identifiable and uniquely recoverable from input-output behavior. We show that, under white-box single-layer access, steering vectors are fundamentally non-identifiable due to large equivalence classes of behaviorally indistinguishable interventions. Empirically, we show that orthogonal perturbations achieve near-equivalent efficacy with negligible effect sizes across multiple models and traits. Critically, we show that the non-identifiability is a robust geometric property that persists across diverse prompt distributions. These findings reveal fundamental interpretability limits and highlight the need for structural constraints beyond behavioral testing to enable reliable alignment interventions.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders be used to decompose and interpret steering vectors?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why directly applying sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two main reasons why sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide misleading decompositions of steering vectors: (1) steering vectors are out-of-distribution for SAEs, and (2) SAEs cannot represent negative coefficients which are meaningful in steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Direct SAE decomposition of steering vectors is misleading due to out-of-distribution and non-negativity constraints; alternative approaches such as learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors have significantly smaller L2-norms than model activations, causing the SAE encoder bias to dominate the decomposition and yield misleading results.
Scaling steering vectors does not resolve the out-of-distribution issue because steering vectors lack default components present in model activations.
SAEs restrict decompositions to non-negative coefficients, but steering vectors have meaningful negative projections in feature directions.
Negative projections in steering vectors can cause spurious positive activations in SAE features due to negative cosine similarities between features.
These issues explain prior observations of irrelevant features in SAE decompositions and the failure of SAE-reconstructed vectors to retain steering properties.
papers.limitation:
The proposed alternative method of learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis requires two SAE decompositions per difference vector, increasing the potential impact of SAE error.
The corrigibility steering vectors may include confounding features related to computer science and language modeling.
future_direction: Explore learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis and establish evaluation metrics to compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a promising approach to control the behaviour of large language models. However, their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) may offer a potential method to interpret steering vectors, recent findings show that SAE-reconstructed vectors often lack the steering properties of the original vectors. This paper investigates why directly applying SAEs to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions, identifying two reasons: (1) steering vectors fall outside the input distribution for which SAEs are designed, and (2) steering vectors can have meaningful negative projections in feature directions, which SAEs are not designed to accommodate. These limitations hinder the direct use of SAEs for interpreting steering vectors.

papers.title: LinEAS: End-to-end Learning of Activation Steering with a Distributional Loss
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently control generative models by steering activations with a global distributional loss that requires low data and is modality-agnostic?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LinEAS, a method for activation steering that uses a global distributional loss to jointly learn affine transformations across layers, enabling effective control with low data and automatic neuron selection via sparsity regularization.
papers.conclusion: LinEAS is an effective method for activation steering, offering improved controllability and robustness by learning lightweight interventions with a global distributional loss.
papers.key_findings:
LinEAS outperforms existing activation steering methods on toxicity mitigation in LLMs and style control in text-to-image models.
LinEAS requires only a handful of unpaired samples (e.g., 32) to be effective.
The global loss and joint optimization across layers lead to more robust interventions and better preservation of model utility.
Sparsity regularization allows automatic selection of neurons and layers, reducing the intervention support by 100x.
LinEAS provides a continuous intervention strength parameter, allowing fine-grained control.
papers.limitation: The method requires access to intermediate activations, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending LinEAS to other modalities and tasks.
Investigating the theoretical properties of the distributional loss.
papers.abstract: The growing use of generative models in daily life calls for efficient mechanisms to control their generation, to e.g., produce safe content or provide users with tools to explore style changes. Ideally, such mechanisms should require low volume of unpaired data (i.e., without explicit preference), and should be cheap, both at train and inference time, while preserving output quality. Recent research has shown that such mechanisms can be obtained by intervening exclusively on model activations, with the goal of correcting distributional differences between activations seen when using prompts from a source vs. a target set (e.g., toxic and non-toxic sentences). While cheap, these fast methods are inherently crude: their maps are tuned locally, not accounting for their impact on downstream layers, resulting in interventions that cause unintended shifts when used out-of-sample. We propose in this work linear end-to-end activation steering (LinEAS), an approach trained with a global loss that accounts simultaneously for all layer-wise distributional shifts. In addition to being more robust, the loss used to train LinEAS can be regularized with sparsifying norms, which can automatically carry out neuron selection. LinEAS only requires a handful of unpaired samples to be effective, and beats similar baselines on toxicity mitigation in language models, becoming competitive with oracle-dependent methods that have access to strong supervision. LinEAS is modality-agnostic and we empirically find that it outperforms existing activation steering methods at mitigating and including new concepts at the output of single-step text-to-image generation models.

papers.title: Angular Steering: Behavior Control via Rotation in Activation Space
papers.research_question: How can we control specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Angular Steering, a rotation-based framework for fine-grained behavior control in LLMs that generalizes existing activation steering methods and maintains general language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: Angular Steering offers a principled, flexible, and robust framework for behavior control in LLMs, enabling fine-grained modulation while preserving general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors like refusal and compliance by rotating activations in a fixed 2D subspace.
The method generalizes existing activation addition and directional ablation techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework.
Angular Steering maintains general language modeling performance (e.g., on TINYBENCHMARKS) while effectively steering behavior.
Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant, improves robustness and coherence by rotating only activations aligned with the target feature.
Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show the method's flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches.
papers.limitation: The method requires a contrastive dataset to extract the feature direction, which may not always be available.
future_direction: Extending Angular Steering to multi-feature steering and dynamic plane selection.
papers.abstract: Controlling specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities is a central challenge for safe and reliable artificial intelligence deployment. Current steering methods, such as vector addition and directional ablation, are constrained within a two-dimensional subspace defined by the activation and feature direction, making them sensitive to chosen parameters and potentially affecting unrelated features due to unintended interactions in activation space. We introduce Angular Steering, a novel and flexible method for behavior modulation that operates by rotating activations within a fixed two-dimensional subspace. By formulating steering as a geometric rotation toward or away from a target behavior direction, Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors such as refusal and compliance. We demonstrate this method using refusal steering emotion steering as use cases. Additionally, we propose Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant that rotates only activations aligned with the target feature, further enhancing stability and coherence. Angular Steering generalizes existing addition and orthogonalization techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework, simplifying parameter selection and maintaining model stability across a broader range of adjustments. Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show that Angular Steering achieves robust behavioral control while maintaining general language modeling performance, underscoring its flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/lone17/angular-steering/.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: The Rogue Scalpel: Activation Steering Compromises LLM Safety
papers.research_question: Does activation steering, a technique for precise and interpretable model control, compromise LLM safety by systematically breaking alignment safeguards?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering, a technique promoted for precise and interpretable model control, systematically breaks LLM alignment safeguards, enabling harmful compliance even with random or semantically benign steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering poses systematic safety risks by breaking alignment safeguards, even with benign vectors, challenging the paradigm of safety through interpretability. Mitigation strategies and further research into the underlying mechanisms are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering in a random direction can increase the probability of harmful compliance from 0% to 1–13% across different model families.
Steering with benign SAE features demonstrates comparable or greater harmful potential, increasing compliance by 1–4% over random steering.
Steering is most effective when applied to the model's middle or early layers, indicating safety mechanisms are most vulnerable in intermediate processing stages.
Most SAE features exhibit jailbreaking capabilities, but they show poor cross-prompt generalization, making systematic safety monitoring challenging.
Averaging just 20 random vectors that jailbreak a single prompt creates a universal attack vector that significantly boosts harmful compliance on unseen requests, requiring only black-box steering access.
future_direction: Investigate the mechanisms behind alignment failures by analyzing activation patterns or refusal circuits in the model’s latent space.
Develop mitigation strategies like adversarial training to counter steering perturbations.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a promising technique for controlling LLM behavior by adding semantically meaningful vectors directly into a model's hidden states during inference. It is often framed as a precise, interpretable, and potentially safer alternative to fine-tuning. We demonstrate the opposite: steering systematically breaks model alignment safeguards, making it comply with harmful requests. Through extensive experiments on different model families, we show that even steering in a random direction can increase the probability of harmful compliance from 0% to 1-13%. Alarmingly, steering benign features from a sparse autoencoder (SAE), a common source of interpretable directions, demonstrates a comparable harmful potential. Finally, we show that combining 20 randomly sampled vectors that jailbreak a single prompt creates a universal attack, significantly increasing harmful compliance on unseen requests. These results challenge the paradigm of safety through interpretability, showing that precise control over model internals does not guarantee precise control over model behavior.

papers.title: Patterns and Mechanisms of Contrastive Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: What are the patterns, mechanisms, and limitations of Contrastive Activation Engineering for steering LLM outputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically investigates Contrastive Activation Engineering, revealing that steering vectors are only reliable within the distribution they are computed from, have diminishing returns with sample size, can be adversarially nullified, and generally harm model perplexity, with larger models being more resistant.
papers.conclusion: CAE shows promise for controlling LLM behavior but has limitations in out-of-distribution generalization and performance degradation, necessitating careful deployment and further research.
papers.key_findings:
CAE is only reliably effective when applied to in-distribution contexts.
Increasing the number of samples used to generate steering vectors has diminishing returns at around 80 samples.
Steering vectors are susceptible to adversarial inputs that reverse the steered behavior.
Steering vectors harm the overall model perplexity.
Larger models are more resistant to steering-induced degradation.
papers.limitation:
In-distribution evaluation introduces noise from the model’s default tendency on each behavior.
Out-of-distribution evaluation relies on the assumption that LLMs can act in place of human evaluators, which was not verified.
The out-of-distribution evaluation dataset is not grounded in real user queries.
future_direction: Improving out-of-distribution robustness
Developing automated methods for balancing steering effectiveness against potential negative impacts on model performance
Expanding the set of CAE techniques and models studied
papers.abstract: Controlling the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge due to their inherent complexity and opacity. While techniques like fine-tuning can modify model behavior, they typically require extensive computational resources. Recent work has introduced a class of contrastive activation engineering (CAE) techniques as promising approaches for steering LLM outputs through targeted modifications to their internal representations. Applied at inference-time with zero cost, CAE has the potential to introduce a new paradigm of flexible, task-specific LLM behavior tuning. We analyze the performance of CAE in in-distribution, out-of-distribution settings, evaluate drawbacks, and begin to develop comprehensive guidelines for its effective deployment. We find that 1. CAE is only reliably effective when applied to in-distribution contexts. 2. Increasing the number of samples used to generate steering vectors has diminishing returns at around 80 samples. 3. Steering vectors are susceptible to adversarial inputs that reverses the behavior that is steered for. 4. Steering vectors harm the overall model perplexity. 5. Larger models are more resistant to steering-induced degradation.

papers.title: Steering Externalities: Benign Activation Steering Unintentionally Increases Jailbreak Risk for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do steering vectors learned from benign instruction data have unintended side-effects on model safety? Specifically, does benign activation steering (for utility) unintentionally increase jailbreak risk for LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies 'steering externalities', a phenomenon where benign activation steering (e.g., for compliance or JSON formatting) unintentionally erodes safety guardrails and significantly increases jailbreak vulnerability in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering for utility creates steering externalities that increase jailbreak risk; steered deployments should be red-teamed, and future work should develop safety-aware steering to preserve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Benign activation steering (STEER-COMPLIANCE, STEER-JSON) increases Attack Success Rates (ASR) for jailbreak attacks, acting as a 'force multiplier' that can boost ASR to over 80-99% on standard benchmarks.
Steering shifts the internal representations of harmful prompts towards regions associated with harmless requests, reducing the model's 'safety margin' and making refusal less likely.
The safety degradation occurs because steering biases the early-token distribution away from refusal prefixes, making the model more likely to enter a non-refusal generation trajectory.
The effect is observed across multiple models (Llama-2, Llama-3, Gemma) and is amplified by existing black-box jailbreak methods like CoP, PAIR, and TAP.
A preliminary safety-aware steering method (STEER-BIND) can partially mitigate the externality, suggesting a path for future safer steering techniques.
papers.limitation: t-SNE visualizations are qualitative projections and the 2D boundary is only an illustrative diagnostic.
future_direction: Develop safety-aware steering vectors (like STEER-BIND) that preserve robustness.
Include broader alignment evaluations (beyond safety refusal) when auditing steered models.
Routine red-teaming and regression testing of steered model configurations before deployment.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a practical post-training model alignment technique to enhance the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs). Prior to deploying a model as a service, developers can steer a pre-trained model toward specific behavioral objectives, such as compliance or instruction adherence, without the need for retraining. This process is as simple as adding a steering vector to the model's internal representations. However, this capability unintentionally introduces critical and under-explored safety risks. We identify a phenomenon termed Steering Externalities, where steering vectors derived from entirely benign datasets-such as those enforcing strict compliance or specific output formats like JSON-inadvertently erode safety guardrails. Experiments reveal that these interventions act as a force multiplier, creating new vulnerabilities to jailbreaks and increasing attack success rates to over 80% on standard benchmarks by bypassing the initial safety alignment. Ultimately, our results expose a critical blind spot in deployment: benign activation steering systematically erodes the "safety margin," rendering models more vulnerable to black-box attacks and proving that inference-time utility improvements must be rigorously audited for unintended safety externalities.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by modifying their activations during inference? The paper introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) to control model behaviors.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method to steer language models by adding computed steering vectors to the residual stream, which effectively controls targeted behaviors with minimal impact on general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behaviors and insights into linear representations of abstract concepts in models.
papers.key_findings:
CAA effectively steers Llama 2 Chat models on multiple alignment-relevant behaviors, with optimal layers around layer 13 for 7B and 14-15 for 13B.
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks and works alongside system prompting and finetuning.
CAA has minimal negative impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU and can slightly improve truthfulness on TruthfulQA when subtracting sycophancy.
Steering vectors exhibit intuitive similarity with token activations relevant to the behavior and transfer well across layers and between base and chat models.
The representations of behaviors are linearly separable in the residual stream, and CAA vectors capture these directions.
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluations may be sensitive to prompt wording and have biases, though manual checks show consistency.
Finetuning baselines were not fully optimized (e.g., learning rate, epochs, loss function), so CAA's relative effect might be smaller with better finetuning.
Prompting baselines may not be fully optimized, and better prompts might achieve stronger effects.
Vector normalization choices (not normalizing across layers) could affect layer optimality results.
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions instead of all tokens after the prompt.
Steering outside the residual stream, e.g., after MLP layers.
Application to red-teaming to trigger unwanted behaviors more efficiently.
papers.abstract: We introduce Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), an innovative method for steering language models by modifying their activations during forward passes. CAA computes "steering vectors" by averaging the difference in residual stream activations between pairs of positive and negative examples of a particular behavior, such as factual versus hallucinatory responses. During inference, these steering vectors are added at all token positions after the user's prompt with either a positive or negative coefficient, allowing precise control over the degree of the targeted behavior. We evaluate CAA's effectiveness on Llama 2 Chat using multiple-choice behavioral question datasets and open-ended generation tasks. We demonstrate that CAA significantly alters model behavior, is effective over and on top of traditional methods like finetuning and system prompt design, and minimally reduces capabilities. Moreover, we gain deeper insights into CAA's mechanisms by employing various activation space interpretation methods. CAA accurately steers model outputs and sheds light on how high-level concepts are represented in Large Language Models (LLMs).

papers.title: Controlling Language and Diffusion Models by Transporting Activations
papers.research_question: How can we control generative models by steering activations using optimal transport theory?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Activation Transport (ACT), a framework for steering activations using optimal transport theory, which generalizes prior activation-steering methods and provides fine-grained control with minimal impact on model abilities.
papers.conclusion: ACT is a versatile and effective method for controlling generative models across modalities, providing fine-grained control with minimal impact on model abilities.
papers.key_findings:
ACT reduces toxicity in LLMs by up to 7.5x on Gemma2-2B and 4.3x on Llama3-8B with minimal impact on perplexity and MMLU.
ACT can induce arbitrary concepts in LLMs with peak effectiveness at λ=1, consistent with optimal transport formulation.
ACT increases truthfulness on TruthfulQA, achieving up to 7.76% improvement in MC1 accuracy on Llama3-8B.
ACT enables fine-grained style control in text-to-image diffusion models (SDXL and FLUX) with interpretable strength parameter λ.
ACT enables concept negation in diffusion models, effectively removing unwanted concepts like gorilla, pink elephant, and white bear.
papers.limitation: ACT assumes unimodal activation distributions; multimodal distributions would require non-linear transport maps, which are beyond the scope of this work.
future_direction: Extending ACT to non-linear transport maps for multimodal distributions.
Applying ACT to other modalities and tasks.
papers.abstract: The increasing capabilities of large generative models and their ever more widespread deployment have raised concerns about their reliability, safety, and potential misuse. To address these issues, recent works have proposed to control model generation by steering model activations in order to effectively induce or prevent the emergence of concepts or behaviors in the generated output. In this paper we introduce Activation Transport (AcT), a general framework to steer activations guided by optimal transport theory that generalizes many previous activation-steering works. AcT is modality-agnostic and provides fine-grained control over the model behavior with negligible computational overhead, while minimally impacting model abilities. We experimentally show the effectiveness and versatility of our approach by addressing key challenges in large language models (LLMs) and text-to-image diffusion models (T2Is). For LLMs, we show that AcT can effectively mitigate toxicity, induce arbitrary concepts, and increase their truthfulness. In T2Is, we show how AcT enables fine-grained style control and concept negation.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Multi-property Steering of Large Language Models with Dynamic Activation Composition
papers.research_question: How can activation steering strategies be effectively evaluated and improved for multi-property conditioning in large language models while maintaining fluency?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Dynamic Activation Composition, an information-theoretic method to dynamically modulate steering intensity for one or more properties during generation, achieving high conditioning while minimizing fluency loss.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic Activation Composition enables strong multi-property conditioning while maintaining generation fluency.
papers.key_findings:
Initial steering (Start) fails to maintain conditioning throughout generation.
Constant (Fixed) and diminishing (Dim) steering produce good conditioning but can cause disfluencies at high intensities.
Negative steering effectively conditions against the property of interest.
Steering vectors are similar for related languages (e.g., Romance languages) but differ for distant ones (e.g., Chinese).
Dynamic Activation Composition (Dyn) achieves the best trade-off between conditioning strength and fluency in multi-property steering.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods were shown to be effective in conditioning language model generation by additively intervening over models' intermediate representations. However, the evaluation of these techniques has so far been limited to single conditioning properties and synthetic settings. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of various activation steering strategies, highlighting the property-dependent nature of optimal parameters to ensure a robust effect throughout generation. To address this issue, we propose Dynamic Activation Composition, an information-theoretic approach to modulate the steering intensity of one or more properties throughout generation. Our experiments on multi-property steering show that our method successfully maintains high conditioning while minimizing the impact of conditioning on generation fluency.

papers.title: ExpertLens: Activation steering features are highly interpretable
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether the features discovered by activation steering methods in large language models are interpretable, and if they align with human representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ExpertLens, a method based on activation steering, and shows that the expert neurons it identifies are stable across models and datasets, and their representations align closely with human conceptual structures.
papers.conclusion: ExpertLens is a flexible and lightweight approach for interpretability of LLMs, providing insights into model representations that align with human concepts.
papers.key_findings:
ExpertLens representations are stable across models and datasets.
ExpertLens representations align closely with human representations, matching inter-human alignment levels.
ExpertLens significantly outperforms the alignment captured by word/sentence embeddings.
ExpertLens can reconstruct human conceptual structure (domain organization).
Experts are learned from data, with larger models having more experts.
papers.limitation:
Only single-word concepts are considered.
Do not have access to training data.
Model choice (Pythia family).
Study neurons individually.
Polysemantic neurons are discussed.
future_direction: Future work will consider more complex concepts such as those expressing human values or preferences.
Exploration of alignment and its emergence in alternative model families.
Studying neurons jointly to capture additional aspects of concept representation.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods in large language models (LLMs) have emerged as an effective way to perform targeted updates to enhance generated language without requiring large amounts of adaptation data. We ask whether the features discovered by activation steering methods are interpretable. We identify neurons responsible for specific concepts (e.g., ``cat'') using the ``finding experts'' method from research on activation steering and show that the ExpertLens, i.e., inspection of these neurons provides insights about model representation. We find that ExpertLens representations are stable across models and datasets and closely align with human representations inferred from behavioral data, matching inter-human alignment levels. ExpertLens significantly outperforms the alignment captured by word/sentence embeddings. By reconstructing human concept organization through ExpertLens, we show that it enables a granular view of LLM concept representation. Our findings suggest that ExpertLens is a flexible and lightweight approach for capturing and analyzing model representations.

papers.title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models can monitor their own internal states and resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, a phenomenon termed Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR).
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces and characterizes Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), showing that large language models can self-correct during inference when subjected to task-misaligned activation steering, and provides causal evidence for internal consistency-checking circuits.
papers.conclusion: ESR demonstrates that large language models have internal self-monitoring mechanisms that can resist activation steering, which has implications for both robustness and safety, highlighting the need to understand and control these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families show it less frequently.
26 SAE latents are identified as off-topic detectors and causally linked to ESR; ablating them reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%.
ESR can be enhanced through meta-prompts, increasing the multi-attempt rate by 4.3× for Llama-3.3-70B.
Fine-tuning on self-correction examples can induce ESR-like behavior in smaller models, but only increases attempt frequency without improving success rate.
ESR has dual implications: it could protect against adversarial manipulation but might interfere with beneficial safety interventions.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on single-layer SAEs limits tracing of inter-layer dynamics.
Only 5 models tested, making it difficult to disentangle effects of scale, architecture, and training.
Judge-based evaluation involves subjective assessment of response quality.
future_direction: Investigate whether ESR emerges from RLHF or exists in pretrained representations.
Study how ESR responds to safety-relevant steering.
Explore whether ESR can be adversarially circumvented.
papers.abstract: Large language models can resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, sometimes recovering mid-generation to produce improved responses even when steering remains active. We term this Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR). Using sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents to steer model activations, we find that Llama-3.3-70B shows substantial ESR, while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families exhibit the phenomenon less frequently. We identify 26 SAE latents that activate differentially during off-topic content and are causally linked to ESR in Llama-3.3-70B. Zero-ablating these latents reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, providing causal evidence for dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits. We demonstrate that ESR can be deliberately enhanced through both prompting and training: meta-prompts instructing the model to self-monitor increase the multi-attempt rate by 4x for Llama-3.3-70B, and fine-tuning on self-correction examples successfully induces ESR-like behavior in smaller models. These findings have dual implications: ESR could protect against adversarial manipulation but might also interfere with beneficial safety interventions that rely on activation steering. Understanding and controlling these resistance mechanisms is important for developing transparent and controllable AI systems. Code is available at github.com/agencyenterprise/endogenous-steering-resistance.

papers.title: Efficient and accurate steering of Large Language Models through attention-guided feature learning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the steering of Large Language Models by dynamically selecting token embeddings, using soft labels based on attention to prefix, and identifying relevant layers for steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an attention-guided steering framework that dynamically selects token embeddings based on attention to prefix, uses soft labels for concept vector extraction, and identifies relevant blocks via concept enrichment scores, substantially improving steering success over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: The attention-guided steering framework significantly improves steering performance and sheds light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers, opening avenues for efficient fine-tuning and understanding of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Dynamic token selection based on attention to prefix improves steering over fixed token selection.
Using soft labels (attention-to-prefix) instead of hard labels improves concept vector extraction and steering.
Concept enrichment scores based on attention can identify effective blocks for steering.
The framework nearly doubles the number of successfully steered concepts across model sizes and architectures.
The distribution of concept-specific features varies across layers and concepts.
future_direction: Advancing understanding of knowledge representation in LLMs
Developing computationally efficient fine-tuning algorithms for domain-specific applications
papers.abstract: Steering, or direct manipulation of internal activations to guide LLM responses toward specific semantic concepts, is emerging as a promising avenue for both understanding how semantic concepts are stored within LLMs and advancing LLM capabilities. Yet, existing steering methods are remarkably brittle, with seemingly non-steerable concepts becoming completely steerable based on subtle algorithmic choices in how concept-related features are extracted. In this work, we introduce an attention-guided steering framework that overcomes three core challenges associated with steering: (1) automatic selection of relevant token embeddings for extracting concept-related features; (2) accounting for heterogeneity of concept-related features across LLM activations; and (3) identification of layers most relevant for steering. Across a steering benchmark of 512 semantic concepts, our framework substantially improved steering over previous state-of-the-art (nearly doubling the number of successfully steered concepts) across model architectures and sizes (up to 70 billion parameter models). Furthermore, we use our framework to shed light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers. Overall, our framework opens further avenues for developing efficient, highly-scalable fine-tuning algorithms for industry-scale LLMs.

papers.title: Painless Activation Steering: An Automated, Lightweight Approach for Post-Training Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do there exist activation steering (AS) methods that are both human-independent and adaptive to arbitrary models and arbitrary tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Painless Activation Steering (PAS), a family of fully automated, human-independent methods for activation steering that works with any labeled dataset, removing the need for manual prompt construction or feature annotation.
papers.conclusion: PAS provides a fast, lightweight, and practical automated option for post-training large language models, complementing weight- and prompt-based methods.
papers.key_findings:
PAS reliably improves performance on behavior tasks (bias, morality, alignment) but provides little benefit on intelligence-oriented tasks.
Introspective PAS variants (iPAS) perform best by constructing steering vectors from a model's own errors.
PAS complements existing methods, providing additional gains on top of In-Context Learning (ICL) and outperforming Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on TruthfulQA.
PAS generally does not cause catastrophic forgetting on control tasks, except at very high steering strengths.
PAS is effective even in small data regimes and is computationally and storage efficient compared to weight-based methods.
papers.limitation:
PAS is ineffective on intelligence-oriented tasks that require specialized knowledge or advanced reasoning capacity.
At very high steering strengths, PAS can cause catastrophic forgetting on tasks like Sycophancy and TruthfulQA.
PAS is mathematically equivalent to modifying a single bias vector, which may limit its expressivity compared to methods that update all weights.
future_direction: Extending PAS through multi-task multi-layer composition.
Exploring alternative extraction methods for steering vectors.
Investigating new use cases for the PAS framework.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) are typically post-trained for desired capabilities and behaviors via weight-based or prompt-based steering, but the former is time-consuming and expensive, and the latter is not precisely controllable and often requires manual trial-and-error. While activation steering (AS) promises a cheap, fast, and controllable alternative to the two existing post-training methods, current AS techniques require hand-crafted prompt pairs or labor-intensive feature annotation, making them more inconvenient than the plug-and-play methods such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). We introduce Painless Activation Steering (PAS), a family of fully automated methods that make AS readily usable with any given labeled dataset, with no need for prompt construction, feature labeling, or human intervention. We evaluate PAS on three open-weight models (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B, and Nous-Hermes-2) and 18 tasks; we find that PAS reliably improves performance for behavior tasks, but not for intelligence-oriented tasks. The introspective variant (iPAS) delivers the strongest causal steering effects (10.1% on Bias, 5.2% on Morality, and 34.8% on Alignment). We also show PAS delivers additional gains on top of In-Context Learning (ICL) and SFT. PAS constructs a fast, lightweight activation vector that can be cheaply trained, easily stored, and activated at will. Our results provide a characterization of where AS helps, where it fails, and how to deploy it as a practical, automated LM post-training option.

papers.title: Personalized Steering of Large Language Models: Versatile Steering Vectors Through Bi-directional Preference Optimization
papers.research_question: How can we produce more effective steering vectors for personalized control of LLMs, particularly in alignment-related scenarios?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Bi-directional Preference Optimization (BiPO) to compute effective steering vectors for LLMs, enabling personalized control of behaviors by adjusting vector direction and magnitude.
papers.conclusion: Proposes BiPO for effective steering vectors, enabling personalized behavior control without additional training, with demonstrated versatility and transferability.
papers.key_findings:
BiPO outperforms baseline methods (CAA and Freeform) in steering AI personas, as measured by behavioral scores.
BiPO effectively steers models in alignment-related scenarios, including truthfulness, hallucination, and jailbreaking attacks and defenses.
The optimized steering vectors are transferable across different models (e.g., from Llama-2 to Vicuna) and fine-tuned LoRAs.
Multiple steering vectors can be applied simultaneously, showing synergistic effects and functionality fusion.
By scaling the steering vector, varying degrees of behavior intensity can be achieved, allowing for personalized control.
papers.limitation: The steering vector only affects a single layer in the transformer; a multi-layer design might improve results.
future_direction: Exploring multi-layer steering designs for potentially better results.
papers.abstract: Researchers have been studying approaches to steer the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) and build personalized LLMs tailored for various applications. While fine-tuning seems to be a direct solution, it requires substantial computational resources and may significantly affect the utility of the original LLM. Recent endeavors have introduced more lightweight strategies, focusing on extracting "steering vectors" to guide the model's output toward desired behaviors by adjusting activations within specific layers of the LLM's transformer architecture. However, such steering vectors are directly extracted from the activations of human preference data and thus often lead to suboptimal results and occasional failures, especially in alignment-related scenarios. This work proposes an innovative approach that could produce more effective steering vectors through bi-directional preference optimization. Our method is designed to allow steering vectors to directly influence the generation probability of contrastive human preference data pairs, thereby offering a more precise representation of the target behavior. By carefully adjusting the direction and magnitude of the steering vector, we enabled personalized control over the desired behavior across a spectrum of intensities. Extensive experimentation across various open-ended generation tasks, particularly focusing on steering AI personas, has validated the efficacy of our approach. Moreover, we comprehensively investigate critical alignment-concerning scenarios, such as managing truthfulness, mitigating hallucination, and addressing jailbreaking attacks. Remarkably, our method can still demonstrate outstanding steering effectiveness across these scenarios. Furthermore, we showcase the transferability of our steering vectors across different models/LoRAs and highlight the synergistic benefits of applying multiple vectors simultaneously.

papers.title: Steering Risk Preferences in Large Language Models by Aligning Behavioral and Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors be systematically identified to change LLM behavior? The paper proposes a principled approach by aligning latent representations from behavioral methods (Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with neural counterparts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for deriving steering vectors by aligning behavioral representations (elicited via MCMC with LLMs) with neural activations, enabling precise control of LLM risk preferences without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Self-alignment methods that align behavioral and neural representations offer an effective and principled means of controlling LLM behavior in risk-sensitive contexts.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors derived from aligned behavioral and neural representations (MCMC and Certainty Equivalent methods) outperform Contrastive Activation in steering risky decisions, risk perception, and text generation.
The optimal layer for steering varies: risk perception is more steerable in earlier layers, while risky decisions are more steerable in later layers.
The method allows precise control over risk preferences (risk-seeking vs. risk-averse) across different tasks.
Steering vectors transfer to tasks far from the original elicitation context.
The behavioral representation from MCMC reveals more nuanced risk preferences compared to the Certainty Equivalent method.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical and mechanistic interpretability research is needed to establish a more concrete link between behaviorally elicited representations and their corresponding neural activations.
Modifying a Transformer’s residual stream is not uniformly effective across all layers; the success of such interventions is highly dependent on the layer selected. Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question.
This form of steering is limited in scope for proprietary models where weights are not accessible, restricting its broader applicability.
future_direction: Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question for future research.
Future research should consider developing new descriptive frameworks tailored to characterizing and predicting the risky choices of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Changing the behavior of large language models (LLMs) can be as straightforward as editing the Transformer's residual streams using appropriately constructed "steering vectors." These modifications to internal neural activations, a form of representation engineering, offer an effective and targeted means of influencing model behavior without retraining or fine-tuning the model. But how can such steering vectors be systematically identified? We propose a principled approach for uncovering steering vectors by aligning latent representations elicited through behavioral methods (specifically, Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with their neural counterparts. To evaluate this approach, we focus on extracting latent risk preferences from LLMs and steering their risk-related outputs using the aligned representations as steering vectors. We show that the resulting steering vectors successfully and reliably modulate LLM outputs in line with the targeted behavior.

papers.title: Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Whether in-context learning and activation steering are instances of a broader framework for controlling LLM behavior, and how they jointly affect model behavior.
papers.core_contribution: Presents a Bayesian belief dynamics model that unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior under both interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Bayesian belief dynamics model unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior and revealing a phase boundary between interventions.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning and activation steering jointly affect behavior, creating a phase boundary modulated by context and activations.
The Bayesian model predicts sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates and additivity of interventions in log-belief space.
The model predicts crossover points (N*) where behavior transitions between concepts, with high correlation to empirical data.
The linear representation hypothesis holds within a range of steering magnitudes, beyond which behavior breaks down.
The model generalizes across different LLMs (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and datasets (persona, sentiment).
papers.limitation: The linear representation hypothesis breaks down with large steering magnitudes, leading to chance behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be controlled at inference time through prompts (in-context learning) and internal activations (activation steering). Different accounts have been proposed to explain these methods, yet their common goal of controlling model behavior raises the question of whether these seemingly disparate methodologies can be seen as specific instances of a broader framework. Motivated by this, we develop a unifying, predictive account of LLM control from a Bayesian perspective. Specifically, we posit that both context- and activation-based interventions impact model behavior by altering its belief in latent concepts: steering operates by changing concept priors, while in-context learning leads to an accumulation of evidence. This results in a closed-form Bayesian model that is highly predictive of LLM behavior across context- and activation-based interventions in a set of domains inspired by prior work on many-shot in-context learning. This model helps us explain prior empirical phenomena - e.g., sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates - while predicting novel ones - e.g., additivity of both interventions in log-belief space, which results in distinct phases such that sudden and dramatic behavioral shifts can be induced by slightly changing intervention controls. Taken together, this work offers a unified account of prompt-based and activation-based control of LLM behavior, and a methodology for empirically predicting the effects of these interventions.

papers.title: Improving Instruction-Following in Language Models through Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Can we efficiently extract vector representations that encode and control specific instruction-following behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can enhance instruction-following in language models by computing vectors from activations and applying them to guide generation, even without explicit instructions.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering offers a practical and scalable approach for fine-grained control in language generation.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors improve instruction adherence when no instructions are provided in the input.
Steering reinforces instruction adherence even when instructions are explicitly present.
Multiple constraints can be steered simultaneously, such as format and length.
Steering vectors computed on instruction-tuned models can transfer to improve base models.
papers.limitation:
Steering can sometimes compromise response quality, leading to nonsensical tokens or repetition.
For instructions like 'End Checker', steering vectors may fail to capture specific required sentences.
papers.abstract: The ability to follow instructions is crucial for numerous real-world applications of language models. In pursuit of deeper insights and more powerful capabilities, we derive instruction-specific vector representations from language models and use them to steer models accordingly. These vectors are computed as the difference in activations between inputs with and without instructions, enabling a modular approach to activation steering. We demonstrate how this method can enhance model adherence to constraints such as output format, length, and word inclusion, providing inference-time control over instruction following. Our experiments across four models demonstrate how we can use the activation vectors to guide models to follow constraints even without explicit instructions and to enhance performance when instructions are present. Additionally, we explore the compositionality of activation steering, successfully applying multiple instructions simultaneously. Finally, we demonstrate that steering vectors computed on instruction-tuned models can transfer to improve base models. Our findings demonstrate that activation steering offers a practical and scalable approach for fine-grained control in language generation.

papers.title: Steering Language Models With Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can we elicit hidden capabilities from language models by modifying activations at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces activation engineering and the ActAdd method, which achieves state-of-the-art on toxicity reduction and sentiment control while preserving model capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Activation engineering, particularly ActAdd, is a promising approach for steering language models and eliciting their full capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
ActAdd reduces perplexity on target topics and increases probability of relevant tokens.
ActAdd achieves SOTA toxicity reduction on RealToxicityPrompts using OPT and LLaMA-3.
ActAdd effectively controls sentiment shift on the IMDb dataset.
ActAdd preserves general knowledge as shown on the ConceptNet benchmark.
ActAdd allows inference-time control over output properties with minimal side effects.
papers.limitation:
ActAdd requires tuning hyperparameters like injection coefficient and layer, which can be less user-friendly.
ActAdd is not applicable with only API access since intermediate activations need to be exposed.
The impact of ActAdd on reasoning has not been examined.
future_direction: Compare ActAdd on knowledge editing benchmarks.
Develop general steering methods using activation engineering for safety.
papers.abstract: Prompt engineering and finetuning aim to maximize language model performance on a given metric (like toxicity reduction). However, these methods do not fully elicit a model's capabilities. To reduce this gap, we introduce activation engineering: the inference-time modification of activations in order to control (or steer) model outputs. Specifically, we introduce the Activation Addition (ActAdd) technique, which contrasts the intermediate activations on prompt pairs (such as "Love" versus "Hate") to compute a steering vector (Subramani et al. 2022). By tactically adding in e.g. the "Love" - "Hate" steering vector during the forward pass, we achieve SOTA on negative-to-positive sentiment shift and detoxification using models including LLaMA-3 and OPT. ActAdd yields inference-time control over high-level output properties (like topic and sentiment) while preserving performance on off-target tasks. ActAdd is lightweight: it does not require any machine optimization and works with a single pair of data points, which enables rapid iteration over steering. ActAdd demonstrates the power of activation engineering.

papers.title: CASteer: Cross-Attention Steering for Controllable Concept Erasure
papers.research_question: How can we achieve training-free, precise concept erasure in diffusion models by steering cross-attention representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CASteer, a training-free method for concept erasure in diffusion models that uses precomputed steering vectors from cross-attention outputs to dynamically suppress unwanted concepts during inference without retraining.
papers.conclusion: CASteer provides an effective, training-free approach for concept erasure in diffusion models, enabling precise control over generated content without compromising image quality.
papers.key_findings:
CASteer effectively erases both concrete (e.g., objects) and abstract (e.g., styles, nudity) concepts without model retraining.
The method outperforms state-of-the-art concept erasure techniques on multiple benchmarks (I2P for nudity/inappropriate content, style removal).
CASteer preserves image quality and unrelated content while erasing targeted concepts, as measured by CLIP score and FID.
Steering vectors can be transferred from distilled models (e.g., SDXL-Turbo) to their non-distilled counterparts (e.g., SDXL) without loss in performance.
The method allows for erasure of multiple concepts simultaneously by averaging or orthogonalizing steering vectors.
papers.limitation: Effectiveness depends on curated positive and negative prompts, which may introduce human bias and require domain knowledge for effective pairing.
future_direction: Finding better ways of constructing prompt pairs for steering vectors.
Developing a deep theoretical understanding of the mechanisms behind CASteer.
Exploring applicability to other tasks such as image editing or controllable image generation.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have transformed image generation, yet controlling their outputs to reliably erase undesired concepts remains challenging. Existing approaches usually require task-specific training and struggle to generalize across both concrete (e.g., objects) and abstract (e.g., styles) concepts. We propose CASteer (Cross-Attention Steering), a training-free framework for concept erasure in diffusion models using steering vectors to influence hidden representations dynamically. CASteer precomputes concept-specific steering vectors by averaging neural activations from images generated for each target concept. During inference, it dynamically applies these vectors to suppress undesired concepts only when they appear, ensuring that unrelated regions remain unaffected. This selective activation enables precise, context-aware erasure without degrading overall image quality. This approach achieves effective removal of harmful or unwanted content across a wide range of visual concepts, all without model retraining. CASteer outperforms state-of-the-art concept erasure techniques while preserving unrelated content and minimizing unintended effects.

papers.title: Shifting Perspectives: Steering Vectors for Robust Bias Mitigation in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors effectively mitigate social biases in LLMs, and how do they compare to other bias mitigation methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that steering vectors, applied to model activations at inference time, are a lightweight and effective method for mitigating social biases in LLMs, outperforming prompting and Self-Debias with minimal impact on general model performance.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors offer a plug-and-play, interpretable, and computationally lightweight intervention for bias mitigation, achieving substantial bias reduction with minimal impact on core LLM performance.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors achieved average accuracy improvements of 12.8% on BBQ, 8.3% on CLEAR-Bias, and 1% on StereoSet.
Steering vectors outperformed prompting and Self-Debias in all cases, and outperformed fine-tuning in 12 out of 17 evaluations.
Steering vectors had the lowest negative impact on MMLU scores (3.9% decrease) compared to other bias mitigation methods tested.
Steering vectors trained on one bias-specific dataset (BBQ) transferred effectively to other tasks and datasets, demonstrating robustness and generalizability.
Linear separability analysis identified optimal intervention layers (13-14) for applying the steering vectors.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on a 7B parameter model, which may not fully capture emergent abilities related to bias observed in larger models.
MMLU may not capture all aspects of language understanding and reasoning; additional benchmarks would provide a more complete assessment.
future_direction: Explore different contrastive dataset structures for constructing steering vectors.
Investigate multi-dimensional steering by controlling along multiple PCA axes simultaneously.
Study cross-axis interactions (e.g., gender vs. race) to mitigate unintended cross-bias amplification.
Develop adaptive coefficient selection strategies to dynamically adjust steering strength per input.
Apply steering vectors to other forms of harmful behaviors (e.g., toxicity, misinformation) and assess real-world impact.
papers.abstract: We present a novel approach to bias mitigation in large language models (LLMs) by applying steering vectors to modify model activations in forward passes. We compute 8 steering vectors, each corresponding to a different social bias axis, such as age, gender, or race, on a training subset of the BBQ dataset and compare the effectiveness of these to 3 additional bias mitigation methods across 4 datasets. When optimized on the BBQ dataset, our individually tuned steering vectors achieve average improvements of 12.8% on BBQ, 8.3% on CLEAR-Bias, and 1% on StereoSet, and show improvements over prompting and Self-Debias in all cases, and improvements over fine-tuning in 12 out of 17 evaluations. In addition, steering vectors showed the lowest impact on MMLU scores of the four bias mitigation methods tested. The work presents the first systematic investigation of steering vectors for bias mitigation, and we demonstrate that they are a powerful and computationally efficient strategy for reducing bias in LLMs, with broader implications for enhancing AI safety.

papers.title: What Can We Actually Steer? A Multi-Behavior Study of Activation Control
papers.research_question: How does activation steering effectiveness vary across different behavior types, and can the nature of target behaviors predict steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with internal traits like personality and misalignment being more steerable than knowledge-dependent behaviors, and vector separation does not predict success.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is not a universal control method but a semantic modulator effective for abstract, internal dispositions but ineffective for knowledge-heavy roleplay or precise formatting tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Steering effectiveness bifurcates between internal traits (e.g., personality, misalignment) and external knowledge (e.g., public figures), with internal traits being more steerable.
Trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with steering coefficient strength, peaking at moderate coefficients while coherence and relevance decline monotonically.
Vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, contradicting the intuition that larger activation differences yield better control.
Larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering without coherence collapse, improving steering quality despite smaller raw activation differences.
Misalignment behaviors such as hallucination and sycophancy are highly steerable, indicating potential safety risks where adversarial actors could easily amplify harmful traits.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily used Llama 3.1 8B, and steerability may scale non-linearly with model size.
Steering was restricted to Layer 15, and different behaviors might be localized at different layers.
Reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4.1) for evaluation introduces potential biases in scoring.
future_direction: Future work should explore whether more sophisticated vector diagnostics or non-linear relationships might better predict steerability.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require precise behavior control for safe and effective deployment across diverse applications. Activation steering offers a promising approach for LLMs' behavioral control. We focus on the question of how steering effectiveness varies across different behavior types and whether the nature of target behaviors can predict steering success. We address this through empirical analysis of activation steering across 50 behaviors that span persona archetypes, personality traits, misalignment behaviors, style cues, and impersonation of public figures. We present a set of comprehensive experiments on coefficient optimization, vector properties, and data requirements to provide comprehensive guidance for the implementation of activation steering. Our analysis demonstrates that steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with different behavioral categories exhibiting distinct response patterns to intervention strength. We find that trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with a steering coefficient strength. We also show that vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, but larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering. These findings provide empirically grounded guidance for implementing activation steering and demonstrate that steering effectiveness is heavily influenced by behavior type.

papers.title: DISCO: Disentangled Communication Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is steering the query and value representation spaces within attention heads more effective for controlling LLM behavior than steering attention head outputs or other spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCO Steering, a method that injects steering vectors directly into the query and value spaces of attention heads, providing more granular control and superior performance over existing steering vector baselines.
papers.conclusion: Query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods, and DISCO provides an effective and flexible approach for controlling LLM behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Query and value spaces exhibit higher linear discriminability of concepts compared to attention head outputs.
DISCO Steering disentangles the strong Communication Steering baseline, allowing independent control of query and value steering magnitudes.
DISCO achieves the best performance in 13 out of 16 experiments across multiple datasets and models.
Steering query spaces dynamically re-weights attention, while steering value spaces directly adds to the head output.
The method is effective for promoting and suppressing behaviors like truthfulness, power-seeking, wealth-seeking, and corrigibility.
papers.limitation:
Requires a dataset of positive and negative examples for each concept.
Steering vectors are linear, which may not capture nonlinear concepts.
Could be misused for jailbreaks or generating inappropriate content.
future_direction: Extending DISCO to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder, multimodal).
Exploring nonlinear steering vectors.
Applying DISCO to more complex behaviors and real-world applications.
papers.abstract: A variety of recent methods guide large language model outputs via the inference-time addition of steering vectors to residual-stream or attention-head representations. In contrast, we propose to inject steering vectors directly into the query and value representation spaces within attention heads. We provide evidence that a greater portion of these spaces exhibit high linear discriminability of concepts --a key property motivating the use of steering vectors-- than attention head outputs. We analytically characterize the effect of our method, which we term DISentangled COmmunication (DISCO) Steering, on attention head outputs. Our analysis reveals that DISCO disentangles a strong but underutilized baseline, steering attention inputs, which implicitly modifies queries and values in a rigid manner. In contrast, DISCO's direct modulation of these components enables more granular control. We find that DISCO achieves superior performance over a number of steering vector baselines across multiple datasets on LLaMA 3.1 8B and Gemma 2 9B, with steering efficacy scoring up to 19.1% higher than the runner-up. Our results support the conclusion that the query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-Correction in LLMs: Towards Explainable Prompting via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does intrinsic self-correction prompting act as representation steering along interpretable latent directions?
papers.core_contribution: Intrinsic self-correction in LLMs functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by alignment between prompt-induced shifts and steering vectors and causal verification via activation addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings link self-correction prompting to representation steering along interpretable latent directions, highlighting the role of interpretability methods in understanding prompt-driven LLM phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Prompt-induced shifts in self-correction align with steering vectors constructed from contrastive pairs.
Activation injection with steering vectors causally reproduces behavioral changes in toxicity.
Detoxification is effective even with weak prompts, while toxification requires strong prompts.
Most of the behavioral change occurs in the first self-correction round.
Alignment between shifts and vectors peaks in mid-to-late layers for some models.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to toxicity-related behaviors and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other prompt-driven phenomena such as chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Intrinsic self-correction refers to the phenomenon where a language model refines its own outputs purely through prompting, without external feedback or parameter updates. While this approach improves performance across diverse tasks, its mechanism remains unclear. We show that intrinsic self-correction functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by both alignment analysis and activation interventions. To achieve this, we analyze intrinsic self-correction via the representation shift induced by prompting.
