In parallel, we construct interpretable latent directions with contrastive pairs and verify the causal effect of these directions via activation addition. Evaluating six open-source LLMs, our results demonstrate that prompt-induced representation shifts in text detoxification and text toxification consistently align with latent directions constructed from contrastive pairs. In detoxification, the shifts align with the non-toxic direction; in toxification, they align with the toxic direction. These findings suggest that representation steering is the mechanistic driver of intrinsic self-correction. Our analysis highlights that understanding model internals offers a direct route to analyzing the mechanisms of prompt-driven LLM behaviors.

papers.title: Scaling laws for activation steering with Llama 2 models and refusal mechanisms
papers.research_question: How does the effectiveness of the Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steering technique scale with model size, specifically for controlling refusal behavior in Llama 2 models?
papers.core_contribution: The effectiveness of Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) for steering model behavior diminishes with increasing model size, negative steering is more effective than positive steering, and steering is most effective when applied at early-mid layers.
papers.conclusion: Model alignment is complex and requires nuanced approaches to steer models effectively as they become larger, with future research needed to understand the interplay between alignment strategies, model architecture, and dataset characteristics.
papers.key_findings:
CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers (approximately 0.4 × total layer count).
The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size, making larger models harder to steer with the same vectors.
Negative steering (towards non-refusal) has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.
The layer of peak steering effectiveness for positive and negative steering converges as model size increases.
The diminishing effectiveness might be because larger models 'drown out' the steering vector due to more downstream computation.
papers.limitation: The experiments were limited to the specific topic of refusal and the results may be different for different topics or prompting approaches.
future_direction: Feature steering with sparse autoencoders (SAE).
Modifying activation steering for larger models, e.g., scaling up steering vectors or injecting at multiple layers.
Experimenting with diverse model architectures (e.g., Mistral, BERT, BLOOM) to understand alignment differences.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve in complexity and capability, the efficacy of less widely deployed alignment techniques are uncertain. Building on previous work on activation steering and contrastive activation addition (CAA), this paper explores the effectiveness of CAA with model scale using the family of Llama 2 models (7B, 13B, and 70B). CAA works by finding desirable 'directions' in the model's residual stream vector space using contrastive pairs (for example, hate to love) and adding this direction to the residual stream during the forward pass. It directly manipulates the residual stream and aims to extract features from language models to better control their outputs. Using answer matching questions centered around the refusal behavior, we found that 1) CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers. 2) The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size. 3) Negative steering has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.

papers.title: Activation Steering with a Feedback Controller
papers.research_question: How can we develop a control-theoretic foundation for activation steering in large language models to achieve more robust and reliable behavioral control?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes PID Steering, a control-theoretic framework for activation steering in LLMs that uses a Proportional-Integral-Derivative controller to compute steering vectors, reducing steady-state error and improving stability compared to existing methods.
papers.conclusion: PID Steering provides a principled control-theoretic framework for activation steering, offering improved performance, stability, and interpretability for controlling LLM behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Existing activation steering methods (ActAdd, DirAblate, Mean-AcT) correspond to proportional (P) controllers and suffer from steady-state error.
PID Steering reduces steady-state error and overshoot by incorporating integral and derivative terms.
PID Steering outperforms existing methods in toxicity mitigation and jailbreaking tasks across multiple model families and scales.
The method is lightweight, modular, and integrates with existing steering paradigms.
Theoretical analysis shows PID Steering ensures input-to-state stability and reduces the first-overshoot amplitude.
papers.abstract: Controlling the behaviors of large language models (LLM) is fundamental to their safety alignment and reliable deployment. However, existing steering methods are primarily driven by empirical insights and lack theoretical performance guarantees. In this work, we develop a control-theoretic foundation for activation steering by showing that popular steering methods correspond to the proportional (P) controllers, with the steering vector serving as the feedback signal. Building on this finding, we propose Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) Steering, a principled framework that leverages the full PID controller for activation steering in LLMs. The proportional (P) term aligns activations with target semantic directions, the integral (I) term accumulates errors to enforce persistent corrections across layers, and the derivative (D) term mitigates overshoot by counteracting rapid activation changes. This closed-loop design yields interpretable error dynamics and connects activation steering to classical stability guarantees in control theory. Moreover, PID Steering is lightweight, modular, and readily integrates with state-of-the-art steering methods. Extensive experiments across multiple LLM families and benchmarks demonstrate that PID Steering consistently outperforms existing approaches, achieving more robust and reliable behavioral control.

papers.title: YaPO: Learnable Sparse Activation Steering Vectors for Domain Adaptation
papers.research_question: How can we learn sparse, disentangled steering vectors for fine-grained alignment of LLMs, such as cultural adaptation, while preserving general knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces YaPO, a method to learn sparse, disentangled steering vectors in the SAE latent space, which improves convergence, stability, and fine-grained alignment (e.g., cultural adaptation) while preserving general knowledge.
papers.conclusion: YaPO provides a general recipe for efficient, stable, and fine-grained alignment of LLMs through sparse, preference-optimized steering vectors learned in SAE latent space.
papers.key_findings:
YaPO converges faster and more stably than dense steering methods (BiPO).
YaPO achieves stronger performance on cultural alignment, especially on non-localized prompts (closing the implicit-explicit localization gap).
YaPO generalizes to other alignment tasks (hallucination, wealth-seeking, jailbreak, power-seeking).
YaPO preserves general knowledge (no degradation on MMLU).
Sparse steering vectors are more interpretable and disentangled than dense ones.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were limited to the Gemma-2 family (2B and 9B) and did not include other architectures.
The cultural dataset does not capture within-country diversity.
If no SAE is available, one would need to train one, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Expanding the cultural dataset to capture within-country diversity.
Exploring cross-model transferability of sparse steering vectors.
Learning task-specific SAEs when none are available.
papers.abstract: Steering Large Language Models (LLMs) through activation interventions has emerged as a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for alignment and personalization. Recent work on Bi-directional Preference Optimization (BiPO) shows that dense steering vectors can be learned directly from preference data in a Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) fashion, enabling control over truthfulness, hallucinations, and safety behaviors. However, dense steering vectors often entangle multiple latent factors due to neuron multi-semanticity, limiting their effectiveness and stability in fine-grained settings such as cultural alignment, where closely related values and behaviors (e.g., among Middle Eastern cultures) must be distinguished. In this paper, we propose Yet another Policy Optimization (YaPO), a \textit{reference-free} method that learns \textit{sparse steering vectors} in the latent space of a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE). By optimizing sparse codes, YaPO produces disentangled, interpretable, and efficient steering directions. Empirically, we show that YaPO converges faster, achieves stronger performance, and exhibits improved training stability compared to dense steering baselines. Beyond cultural alignment, YaPO generalizes to a range of alignment-related behaviors, including hallucination, wealth-seeking, jailbreak, and power-seeking. Importantly, YaPO preserves general knowledge, with no measurable degradation on MMLU. Overall, our results show that YaPO provides a general recipe for efficient, stable, and fine-grained alignment of LLMs, with broad applications to controllability and domain adaptation. The associated code and data are publicly available\footnote{https://github.com/MBZUAI-Paris/YaPO}.

papers.title: Mind the Performance Gap: Capability-Behavior Trade-offs in Feature Steering
papers.research_question: What is the trade-off between behavioral control and task performance when using feature steering methods? Specifically, can feature steering modify target behaviors without degrading model performance on factual reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Feature steering methods (specifically Goodfire's Auto Steer) substantially degrade model performance (accuracy and coherence) even when successfully controlling target behaviors, revealing a critical capability-behavior trade-off. Simple prompting achieves a better balance between behavioral control and performance preservation.
papers.conclusion: Current feature steering methods face a fundamental capability-behavior trade-off that limits their practical deployment in scenarios where task performance cannot be sacrificed. More work is needed to determine if these trade-offs are fundamental or implementation-specific.
papers.key_findings:
Auto Steer successfully increases behavioral control but causes severe degradation in accuracy (from 66% to 46% on Llama-8B and 87% to 73% on Llama-70B) and coherence (from 4.62 to 2.24 on Llama-8B and 4.94 to 3.89 on Llama-70B).
Simple prompting maintains baseline accuracy and coherence levels while achieving modest behavioral improvements, representing the best overall balance.
The combined approach (Auto Steer + prompting) achieves the strongest behavioral modifications on Llama-8B but inherits the coherence degradation and fails to rescue accuracy.
Steering effectiveness and degradation vary by query: emotional and creative behaviors show strong steering effects but catastrophic performance costs, while behaviors naturally elicited by MMLU (e.g., professional, analytical) show minimal additional modification and less degradation.
There is a consistent positive correlation between coherence and accuracy across both model scales (r=0.302 for Llama-8B, r=0.307 for Llama-70B), indicating that coherence degradation directly predicts reasoning capability loss.
papers.limitation:
Only a single feature steering method (Goodfire's Auto Steer) is evaluated, limiting generalizability to other steering techniques.
Only a single steering strength level is tested, which may not capture the full trade-off curve.
Evaluation is limited to the MMLU benchmark, which focuses on factual recall and analytical reasoning, and may not generalize to other task types.
Reliance on LLM-as-judge methodology for coherence and behavior evaluation may introduce biases.
Only Llama model families (8B and 70B) are tested, so findings may not generalize to other architectures.
future_direction: Systematic comparisons across multiple steering methods to determine if trade-offs are fundamental or implementation-specific.
Varying steering strength to characterize the full trade-off curve between behavioral control, coherence, and task performance.
Evaluating steering methods on diverse tasks including open-ended generation, creative writing, dialogue, and code generation.
Validating automated metrics against human evaluation to ensure reliability.
Testing across different model families to establish generality of findings.
papers.abstract: Feature steering has emerged as a promising approach for controlling LLM behavior through direct manipulation of internal representations, offering advantages over prompt engineering. However, its practical effectiveness in real-world applications remains poorly understood, particularly regarding potential trade-offs with output quality. We show that feature steering methods substantially degrade model performance even when successfully controlling target behaviors, a critical trade-off. Specifically, we evaluate Goodfire's Auto Steer against prompt engineering baselines across 14 steering queries (covering innocuous and safety-relevant behaviors) on 171 Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) questions using Llama-8B and Llama-70B, measuring accuracy, coherence, and behavioral control. Our findings show that Auto Steer successfully modifies target behaviors (achieving scores of 3.33 vs. 2.98 for prompting on Llama-8B and 3.57 vs. 3.10 on Llama-70B), but causes dramatic performance degradation: accuracy on the MMLU questions drops from 66% to 46% on Llama-8B and 87% to 73% on Llama-70B, with coherence falling from 4.62 to 2.24 and 4.94 to 3.89 respectively. Simple prompting achieves the best overall balance. These findings highlight limitations of current feature steering methods for practical deployment where task performance cannot be sacrificed. More broadly, our work demonstrates that mechanistic control methods face fundamental capability-behavior trade-offs that must be empirically characterized before deployment.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Steering Strength
papers.research_question: How does the steering strength α control the trade-off between steering efficacy and distortion in next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a theoretical analysis of steering strength in LLMs, characterizing its effect on next-token probabilities, concept probability, and cross-entropy, and validates the predictions empirically.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework accurately predicts the empirical behavior of steering strength, providing guidelines for choosing α to balance steering efficacy and output quality.
papers.key_findings:
Next-token probability increases exhibit a bump behavior for most tokens, with off-target tokens peaking earlier than target tokens.
Target concept probability increases sigmoidally with steering strength.
Cross-entropy degrades quadratically with steering strength near zero.
The large-α limit of steered logits converges to a fixed direction determined by the steering vector.
Steering strength α should be chosen adaptively per prompt for optimal effect.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical model assumes a simplified dataset where concepts correspond to disjoint vocabulary subsets, which is unrealistic.
The analysis assumes perfect training of the model, which may not hold in practice.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex datasets and models.
Adaptive choice of steering strength α per input prompt.
papers.abstract: A popular approach to post-training control of large language models (LLMs) is the steering of intermediate latent representations. Namely, identify a well-chosen direction depending on the task at hand and perturbs representations along this direction at inference time. While many propositions exist to pick this direction, considerably less is understood about how to choose the magnitude of the move, whereas its importance is clear: too little and the intended behavior does not emerge, too much and the model's performance degrades beyond repair. In this work, we propose the first theoretical analysis of steering strength. We characterize its effect on next token probability, presence of a concept, and cross-entropy, deriving precise qualitative laws governing these quantities. Our analysis reveals surprising behaviors, including non-monotonic effects of steering strength. We validate our theoretical predictions empirically on eleven language models, ranging from a small GPT architecture to modern models.

papers.title: Steering Large Language Model Activations in Sparse Spaces
papers.research_question: How can we steer large language model behavior in a more interpretable and fine-grained way by leveraging sparse representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Steering (SAS), a method that uses sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable steering vectors from contrastive prompt pairs, enabling precise and modular control over LLM behavior during inference.
papers.conclusion: SAS provides an effective framework for steering LLM behavior in sparse spaces, offering improved interpretability and fine-grained control compared to dense activation steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control over LLM outputs.
Scaling sparse autoencoders (increasing dictionary size) improves the monosemanticity of the extracted SAS vectors.
Sparse representations allow for modular control, enabling fine-grained behaviors to be composed simultaneously.
papers.abstract: A key challenge in AI alignment is guiding large language models (LLMs) to follow desired behaviors at test time. Activation steering, which modifies internal model activations during inference, offers a potential solution. However, prior work in dense activation spaces struggles with superposition, wherein multiple features become entangled, limiting interpretability and precise control. In contrast, sparse representations provide an untapped opportunity for more interpretable behavior modulation. In this work, we introduce sparse activation steering (SAS), a method that leverages sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steer LLM behavior in sparse spaces. By isolating behavior-specific features through a contrastive prompt-pairing approach, we define a set of features that can selectively reinforce or suppress behaviors. Experiments on Gemma 2 LLMs show that SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control. Furthermore, scaling SAEs improves monosemanticity of SAS vectors, suggesting more reliable and interpretable interventions.

papers.title: Steering Large Language Models using Conceptors: Improving Addition-Based Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can conceptors be used to improve the precision and effectiveness of activation engineering for steering large language models compared to traditional additive steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces conceptors as a novel steering mechanism for large language models, demonstrating that they provide more precise control and outperform traditional additive steering methods across multiple tasks.
papers.conclusion: Conceptor-based steering outperforms additive methods and offers a more precise and effective way to control LLM outputs, suggesting a shift towards region-based representations in activation engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Conceptor-based steering achieves higher accuracy than additive steering on all function tasks for both GPT-J and GPT-NeoX models.
Mean-centering enhances the performance of both steering methods, but conceptors still outperform even without mean-centering.
Conceptors can be combined using Boolean operations (AND) to steer composite functions, outperforming additive combination of steering vectors.
Steering is most effective in specific layers (9-16 for GPT-J, 10-30 for GPT-NeoX).
The aperture parameter α for conceptors is robust, with α=0.1 performing well across experiments.
papers.limitation:
Conceptors rely on more data points to build accurate representations.
Conceptors are more computationally expensive compared to simple addition-based methods.
Conceptors introduce a new hyperparameter, the aperture α, that may require tuning for optimal performance.
future_direction: Assess the impact of conceptor steering on the model's overall capabilities.
Evaluate performance on more complex behaviors or tasks.
Investigate scalability to larger models.
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed AI, yet reliably controlling their outputs remains a challenge. This paper explores activation engineering, where outputs of pre-trained LLMs are controlled by manipulating their activations at inference time. Unlike traditional methods using a single steering vector, we introduce conceptors - mathematical constructs that represent sets of activation vectors as ellipsoidal regions. Conceptors act as soft projection matrices and offer more precise control over complex activation patterns. Our experiments demonstrate that conceptors outperform traditional methods across multiple steering tasks. We further use Boolean operations on conceptors for combined steering goals that empirically outperform additively combining steering vectors on a set of tasks. These results highlight conceptors as a promising tool for more effective steering of LLMs. Our code is available on github.com/jorispos/conceptorsteering.

papers.title: Mitigating Memorization in LLMs using Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Can activation steering mitigate memorization in LLMs, and what factors influence its effectiveness? What are best practices for using activation steering to mitigate memorization?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can effectively reduce memorization in LLMs, especially when applied to later layers, with minimal impact on linguistic fluency and general performance.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering can suppress memorized content in LLMs while maintaining fluency and general abilities, offering a practical alternative to data sanitization or retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering reduces memorization, as shown by decreased ANLCS with high steering strength.
Steering later layers (e.g., Layer 31) minimizes degradation in language modeling and general task performance.
Early layer steering leads to significant performance drops in linguistic and reasoning tasks.
Random SAE features can be used for steering, indicating that memorization is distributed and not tied to specific features.
Features with high semantic footprint can cause stylistic shifts in output, which may be undesirable.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted only on the Gemma model.
The benchmark primarily consists of literary examples, which may have been present in the model's training data.
A more comprehensive evaluation incorporating diverse datasets and direct analysis of training data exposure is needed.
Future studies should assess the broader applicability of activation steering across different model architectures and tasks.
future_direction: More comprehensive evaluation with diverse datasets and direct analysis of training data exposure.
Assess broader applicability across different model architectures and tasks.
Explore more adaptive and dynamic steering mechanisms to enhance robustness while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.abstract: The memorization of training data by Large Language Models (LLMs) poses significant risks, including privacy leaks and the regurgitation of copyrighted content. Activation steering, a technique that directly intervenes in model activations, has emerged as a promising approach for manipulating LLMs. In this work, we explore the effectiveness of activation steering in reducing memorization while preserving generalization capabilities. We conduct empirical evaluations using a controlled memorization benchmark of literary material and demonstrate that our method successfully suppresses memorized content with minimal degradation in model performance in Gemma. Additionally, we analyze the trade-offs between suppression effectiveness and linguistic fluency, highlighting the advantages and limitations of activation-based interventions. Our findings contribute to ongoing efforts in developing safer and more privacy-preserving LLMs by providing a practical and efficient mechanism to mitigate unintended memorization.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: A Timeline and Analysis for Representation Plasticity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does the plasticity of LLM representations for the concept of 'honesty' change during fine-tuning, and when are steering interventions most effective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies critical periods during fine-tuning where representation steering is most effective, showing that early steering exhibits high plasticity while later stages have responsive windows, and this pattern generalizes across model architectures.
papers.conclusion: This paper provides novel insight into critical intervention periods for representation steering, which can guide alignment research to apply Representation Engineering techniques more efficiently.
papers.key_findings:
Critical intervention periods exist during fine-tuning, with peaks at specific iterations (e.g., 3 and 8).
The pattern of critical periods is consistent across GPT-2 Small and Medium architectures.
Early fine-tuning stages show high plasticity for steering, while later stages have surprising responsiveness.
Representation Engineering interventions can significantly impact model behavior when applied at optimal times.
Statistical analysis confirms significant differences in steering effectiveness across intervention times.
papers.limitation: Generalization to larger models is limited as only GPT-2 Small and Medium were used.
future_direction: Employing more robust extraction methods like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT).
Understanding the changing stability of representations throughout training.
papers.abstract: The ability to steer AI behavior is crucial to preventing its long term dangerous and catastrophic potential. Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a novel, powerful method to steer internal model behaviors, such as "honesty", at a top-down level. Understanding the steering of representations should thus be placed at the forefront of alignment initiatives. Unfortunately, current efforts to understand plasticity at this level are highly neglected. This paper aims to bridge the knowledge gap and understand how LLM representation stability, specifically for the concept of "honesty", and model plasticity evolve by applying steering vectors extracted at different fine-tuning stages, revealing differing magnitudes of shifts in model behavior. The findings are pivotal, showing that while early steering exhibits high plasticity, later stages have a surprisingly responsive critical window. This pattern is observed across different model architectures, signaling that there is a general pattern of model plasticity that can be used for effective intervention. These insights greatly contribute to the field of AI transparency, addressing a pressing lack of efficiency limiting our ability to effectively steer model behavior.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Steering Effectiveness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can the reliability of activation-based steering in LLMs be diagnosed using internal model signals such as entropy and KL divergence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that internal mechanistic signals (NBF and KL divergence) can predict steering effectiveness and introduces rotation-based steering as a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods.
papers.conclusion: Internal mechanistic signals can predict steering effectiveness, and rotation-based steering provides a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods, making steering a more measurable and predictable process.
papers.key_findings:
LLM judges (ChatGPT-4o-mini and Gemini-Flash-2.5) show substantial agreement in evaluating steering outputs after correcting for calibration bias.
Effective steering is characterized by structured entropy preservation (NBF) and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps.
Internal signals (NBF, KL, attention patterns) can predict steering quality with reasonable accuracy.
Rotation-based steering outperforms naive additive steering in terms of steering-coherence trade-off.
Attention patterns show a drop in confidence immediately after the intervention layer, correlating with coherence.
papers.limitation:
Limited conceptual coverage (only nine target concepts).
Focus on GEMMA model family, may not generalize to newer models.
Regression formulation requires further refinement.
Label noise from LLM-based judges and qualitative nature of tasks.
papers.abstract: Activation-based steering enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to exhibit targeted behaviors by intervening on intermediate activations without retraining. Despite its widespread use, the mechanistic factors that govern when steering succeeds or fails remain poorly understood, as prior work has relied primarily on black-box outputs or LLM-based judges. In this study, we investigate whether the reliability of steering can be diagnosed using internal model signals. We focus on two information-theoretic measures: the entropy-derived Normalized Branching Factor (NBF), and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between steered activations and targeted concepts in the vocabulary space. We hypothesize that effective steering corresponds to structured entropy preservation and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps. Building on a reliability study demonstrating high inter-judge agreement between two architecturally distinct LLMs, we use LLM-generated annotations as ground truth and show that these mechanistic signals provide meaningful predictive power for identifying successful steering and estimating failure probability. We further introduce a stronger evaluation baseline for Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-based steering, the two most widely adopted activation-steering methods.

papers.title: Do Personality Traits Interfere? Geometric Limitations of Steering in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether personality steering directions are geometrically independent in large language models, what happens to steering effectiveness when geometric independence is explicitly enforced, and if observed trait dependencies are consistent across different model families.
papers.core_contribution: Personality steering directions in LLMs are not geometrically independent; enforcing orthogonality does not eliminate cross-trait behavioral effects and can reduce steering strength and fluency, indicating that traits occupy a coupled subspace.
papers.conclusion: Personality traits in large language models are not independent directions in activation space, and geometric constraints on steering vectors have limitations in achieving fully independent trait control.
papers.key_findings:
Personality steering directions exhibit substantial geometric dependence, with steering one trait inducing changes in others.
Enforcing geometric independence through hard orthonormalisation does not eliminate cross-trait effects and reduces fluency.
Cross-trait dependencies are consistent across different model families like LLaMA-3-8B and Mistral-8B.
Model-specific modulation exists, e.g., Neuroticism steering is strong in LLaMA-3 but weak in Mistral-8B.
Soft constraint methods like selective or soft projection offer a better trade-off between disentanglement and semantic preservation.
papers.limitation:
Limited to a small set of large language models and personality datasets.
Relies on linear geometric constraints; other orthogonalisation or projection methods are not explored.
Uses LLMs as judges for behavioral assessment without human evaluation.
future_direction: Extend analysis to a broader range of model families and trait representations.
Explore other orthogonalisation or projection methods beyond linear constraints.
Incorporate human evaluation or complementary metrics for assessment.
papers.abstract: Personality steering in large language models (LLMs) commonly relies on injecting trait-specific steering vectors, implicitly assuming that personality traits can be controlled independently. In this work, we examine whether this assumption holds by analysing the geometric relationships between Big Five personality steering directions. We study steering vectors extracted from two model families (LLaMA-3-8B and Mistral-8B) and apply a range of geometric conditioning schemes, from unconstrained directions to soft and hard orthonormalisation. Our results show that personality steering directions exhibit substantial geometric dependence: steering one trait consistently induces changes in others, even when linear overlap is explicitly removed. While hard orthonormalisation enforces geometric independence, it does not eliminate cross-trait behavioural effects and can reduce steering strength. These findings suggest that personality traits in LLMs occupy a slightly coupled subspace, limiting fully independent trait control.

papers.title: Activation Steering Meets Preference Optimization: Defense Against Jailbreaks in Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: How to defend against jailbreak attacks in Vision Language Models (VLMs) by combining activation steering and preference optimization to enhance safety while preserving visual understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SPO-VLM, a two-stage defense framework that combines activation steering and sequence-level preference optimization to enhance safety of VLMs against jailbreak attacks while preserving visual understanding.
papers.conclusion: SPO-VLM effectively enhances safety against jailbreak attacks while preserving visual understanding, providing a foundation for future research on activation-space intervention and preference-driven alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SPO-VLM reduces toxicity scores and attack success rates across multiple datasets and models.
SPO-VLM maintains or even improves visual understanding performance compared to baseline methods.
SPO-VLM shows transferability to unseen attack types, such as structure-based attacks.
The two-stage approach (activation steering + preference optimization) is more effective than activation steering alone.
SPO-VLM achieves a better trade-off between safety and visual understanding than prior methods like ASTRA.
future_direction: Future research on activation-space intervention and preference-driven alignment to ensure trustworthy deployment of LLMs and VLMs.
papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in integrating visual and textual information for understanding and reasoning, but remain highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks. While activation steering has emerged as a promising defence, existing approaches often rely on task-specific contrastive prompts to extract harmful directions, which exhibit suboptimal performance and can degrade visual grounding performance. To address these limitations, we propose \textit{Sequence-Level Preference Optimization} for VLM (\textit{SPO-VLM}), a novel two-stage defense framework that combines activation-level intervention with policy-level optimization to enhance model robustness. In \textit{Stage I}, we compute adaptive layer-specific steering vectors from diverse data sources, enabling generalized suppression of harmful behaviors during inference. In \textit{Stage II}, we refine these steering vectors through a sequence-level preference optimization process. This stage integrates automated toxicity assessment, as well as visual-consistency rewards based on caption-image alignment, to achieve safe and semantically grounded text generation. The two-stage structure of SPO-VLM balances efficiency and effectiveness by combining a lightweight mitigation foundation in Stage I with deeper policy refinement in Stage II. Extensive experiments shown SPO-VLM enhances safety against attacks via activation steering and preference optimization, while maintaining strong performance on benign tasks without compromising visual understanding capabilities. We will release our code, model weights, and evaluation toolkit to support reproducibility and future research. \textcolor{red}{Warning: This paper may contain examples of offensive or harmful text and images.}

papers.title: The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence
papers.research_question: How is refusal behavior mediated in large language models? Is it controlled by a single direction or by more complex geometric structures such as multiple independent directions and concept cones?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a gradient-based representation engineering method (RDO) to identify refusal directions, discovers multi-dimensional refusal cones, and proposes representational independence to characterize independent directions.
papers.conclusion: The work advances understanding of refusal mechanisms in LLMs through gradient-based representation engineering, showing refusal is governed by high-dimensional cones and multiple independent directions, providing a framework for analyzing representational interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based Refusal Direction Optimization (RDO) yields more effective refusal directions with fewer side effects compared to difference-in-means (DIM) baselines.
Refusal behavior is mediated by multi-dimensional polyhedral cones (concept cones) in activation space, not a single linear direction.
Orthogonality does not guarantee independence under intervention; representational independence accounts for linear and non-linear dependencies.
Multiple representationally independent refusal directions exist, indicating distinct underlying mechanisms.
These independent directions can be accessed via input manipulations (e.g., adversarial suffixes) and compositionally ablated to improve jailbreak success.
papers.limitation:
The refusal directions are optimized on the same targets, which may limit their ability to capture fully distinct mechanisms.
Cannot rule out the possibility of other yet-undiscovered regions in the model that mediate refusal.
future_direction: Extending the method to incorporate diverse targets or leveraging reinforcement learning with a judge-based reward function to identify additional independent mechanisms.
Applying the gradient-based representation engineering approach to identify various concepts beyond refusal by changing optimization targets.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) can be circumvented through adversarially crafted inputs, yet the mechanisms by which these attacks bypass safety barriers remain poorly understood. Prior work suggests that a single refusal direction in the model's activation space determines whether an LLM refuses a request. In this study, we propose a novel gradient-based approach to representation engineering and use it to identify refusal directions. Contrary to prior work, we uncover multiple independent directions and even multi-dimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. Moreover, we show that orthogonality alone does not imply independence under intervention, motivating the notion of representational independence that accounts for both linear and non-linear effects. Using this framework, we identify mechanistically independent refusal directions. We show that refusal mechanisms in LLMs are governed by complex spatial structures and identify functionally independent directions, confirming that multiple distinct mechanisms drive refusal behavior. Our gradient-based approach uncovers these mechanisms and can further serve as a foundation for future work on understanding LLMs.

papers.title: In-Distribution Steering: Balancing Control and Coherence in Language Model Generation
papers.research_question: How can we balance behavioral control and text coherence in language model generation by dynamically adjusting activation steering strength based on the input's position within the target behavior's activation distribution?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces In-Distribution Steering (IDS), a novel activation steering method that dynamically adjusts intervention strength per input to achieve precise behavioral control while maintaining the plausibility and coherence of generated text.
papers.conclusion: IDS enables fine-grained control over LLM behavior while maintaining output quality, making it a practical tool for deploying more controllable and reliable language models in high-stakes applications.
papers.key_findings:
IDS achieves superior Steering Performance Impact (SPI) compared to competitors (CAA, MERA) across diverse models and datasets, ranking first on average.
IDS maintains text plausibility (perplexity) close to baseline methods while avoiding the collapse and non-plausible text generated by over-steering competitors like MERA.
IDS operates along the Pareto frontier between steering performance and text plausibility, demonstrating an optimal trade-off.
The method's performance is robust across hyperparameter variations, with optimal results when retaining 30-42% of variance in PCA and using an F1-score threshold around 0.7 for layer selection.
Ablation studies show that larger average steering factors in methods like MERA correlate with collapse in open-ended generation, which IDS avoids through adaptive intervention.
papers.limitation: The paper focuses on directional steering (moving along a steering vector) and does not guarantee that angular steering (rotation in activation space) interventions remain within the data distribution.
future_direction: Extending the approach to angular steering (rotation in activation space).
Applying IDS to generate more truthful rationales in complex reasoning tasks (explain-then-predict).
Applying steering during the inference of reasoning models to improve performance on complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods control large language model (LLM) behavior by modifying internal activations at inference time. However, most existing activation steering methods rely on a fixed steering strength, leading to either insufficient control or unadapted intervention that degrades text plausibility and coherence. We introduce In-Distribution Steering (IDS), a novel method that adapts steering strength based on the input data distribution in representation space. IDS dynamically adjusts interventions according to how far a given input lies within the distribution, enabling adaptive intervention and generation stability during text generation. Experiments demonstrate that IDS achieves strong accuracy on classification tasks while producing coherent text without collapse, making IDS particularly well suited for real-world applications.

papers.title: Beyond Forgetting: Machine Unlearning Elicits Controllable Side Behaviors and Capabilities
papers.research_question: What are the roles of target vectors in representation misdirection for machine unlearning, and does machine unlearning elicit controllable side behaviors and capabilities beyond forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Machine unlearning via representation misdirection with concept vectors elicits controllable side behaviors and capabilities, beyond forgetting, which can be a risk or a tool for model control.
papers.conclusion: Machine unlearning can elicit side behaviors and capabilities, which can be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models with stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning via RAd with truthfulness direction improves model truthfulness on TruthfulQA.
Unlearning via RAd with sentiment direction controls model sentiment on SST2.
Unlearning via RAd with refusal direction induces refusal to harmless instructions in Alpaca.
Unlearning via RAd with task-specific directions improves in-context learning on linguistic and knowledge tasks.
Conversely, RAb with concept directions effectively eliminates these side behaviors.
papers.limitation: RAd models are highly susceptible to benign perturbations, indicating a trade-off between unlearning effectiveness and robustness.
papers.abstract: We consider representation misdirection (RM), a class of LLM unlearning methods that achieves forgetting by manipulating the forget-representations, that is, latent representations of forget samples. Despite being important, the roles of target vectors used in RM, however, remain underexplored. Here, we approach and revisit RM through the lens of the linear representation hypothesis. Specifically, if one can somehow identify a one-dimensional representation corresponding to a high-level concept, the linear representation hypothesis enables linear operations on this concept vector within the forget-representation space. Under this view, we hypothesize that, beyond forgetting, machine unlearning elicits controllable side behaviors and stronger side capabilities corresponding to the high-level concept. Our hypothesis is empirically validated across a wide range of tasks, including behavioral control (e.g., controlling unlearned models' truth, sentiment, and refusal) and capability enhancement (e.g., improving unlearned models' in-context learning capability). Our findings reveal that this fairly attractive phenomenon could be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models that require stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.

papers.title: There Is More to Refusal in Large Language Models than a Single Direction
papers.research_question: How different are the refusal directions when computed for different types of refusal behavior beyond safety, and how do these directions get expressed in the latent space such that they facilitate various styles of refusal under a similar intervention mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal behavior in LLMs is mediated by multiple geometrically distinct activation-space directions, but linear steering along any refusal-related direction acts as a one-dimensional control knob for refusal, with differences primarily in refusal style. Sparse autoencoders reveal a structured internal representation with a shared core of refusal latents and a long tail of style-specific latents.
papers.conclusion: The internal structure of refusal is rich and structured, but linear control flattens this complexity, highlighting the limits of linear interpretability for aligned model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Different refusal categories correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space.
Linear steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal–over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob.
The primary effect of different directions is not whether the model refuses, but how it refuses (style).
Sparse autoencoders uncover a structured internal representation: a small reusable core of shared refusal latents supplemented by a long tail of style- and domain-specific latents.
Linear interventions collapse over this structure, flattening mechanistic differences into uniform behavioral control.
papers.limitation:
The techniques could be misused to suppress refusal behavior and facilitate the generation of harmful content.
Linear steering collapses a rich internal refusal structure into a coarse behavioral knob, underscoring that such interventions are not suitable as principled safety mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Prior work argues that refusal in large language models is mediated by a single activation-space direction, enabling effective steering and ablation. We show that this account is incomplete. Across eleven categories of refusal and non-compliance, including safety, incomplete or unsupported requests, anthropomorphization, and over-refusal, we find that these refusal behaviors correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space. Yet despite this diversity, linear steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal to over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob. The primary effect of different directions is not whether the model refuses, but how it refuses.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: Surgical Activation Steering via Generative Causal Mediation
papers.research_question: Where should we intervene in a language model (LM) to localize and control behaviors that are diffused across many tokens of a long-form response?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Generative Causal Mediation (GCM), a method for selecting attention heads that are causal mediators of a target concept using contrastive long-form responses, enabling effective localization and steering of diffuse behaviors.
papers.conclusion: GCM provides an effective approach for localizing from and controlling the long-form responses of LMs.
papers.key_findings:
GCM successfully localizes concepts expressed in long-form responses and outperforms correlational probe-based baselines when steering with a sparse set of attention heads.
GCM variants (activation patching, attribution patching, attention head knockouts) provide effective strategies for concept localization.
Steering success depends on hyperparameters like the steering factor (α) and the percentage of heads intervened on (k).
Representation Fine-Tuning (ReFT) is an effective supervised steering method when combined with GCM localization.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching is computationally expensive, scaling linearly with the number of neurons.
Attribution patching is a linear approximation that may not be perfect, especially at the first and last layers.
future_direction: Extending GCM to other model components beyond attention heads.
Applying GCM to a broader range of tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: Where should we intervene in a language model (LM) to control behaviors that are diffused across many tokens of a long-form response? We introduce Generative Causal Mediation (GCM), a procedure for selecting model components, e.g., attention heads, to steer a binary concept (e.g., talk in verse vs. talk in prose) from contrastive long-form responses. In GCM, we first construct a dataset of contrasting inputs and responses. Then, we quantify how individual model components mediate the contrastive concept and select the strongest mediators for steering. We evaluate GCM on three tasks--refusal, sycophancy, and style transfer--across three language models. GCM successfully localizes concepts expressed in long-form responses and consistently outperforms correlational probe-based baselines when steering with a sparse set of attention heads. Together, these results demonstrate that GCM provides an effective approach for localizing and controlling the long-form responses of LMs.

papers.title: Beyond Multiple Choice: Evaluating Steering Vectors for Adaptive Free-Form Summarization
papers.research_question: How effective are steering vectors (specifically Contrastive Activation Addition) for controlling text properties like topical focus, sentiment, toxicity, and readability in free-form abstractive summarization, and what are the trade-offs with text quality?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that steering vectors (Contrastive Activation Addition) can effectively control text properties in free-form summarization, but high steering strengths degrade text quality; combining steering with prompting yields the strongest control and the most favorable efficacy-quality trade-off at moderate steering strengths.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors are effective for controlling text properties in free-form summarization, but there is a practical trade-off between control strength and text quality preservation; combining steering with prompting is recommended for achieving strong control with acceptable quality.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors successfully control topical focus, sentiment, and readability in free-form summaries, but toxicity is harder to control due to model safety alignment.
High steering strengths consistently degrade both intrinsic (e.g., perplexity, repetition) and extrinsic (e.g., ROUGE, BERTScore) text quality.
Prompting alone offers weaker control over text properties but better preserves text quality compared to steering.
Combining steering vectors with prompting yields the strongest control over text properties and the most favorable efficacy-quality trade-off at moderate steering strengths.
Steering vectors generally do not affect unrelated properties, except that toxicity steering also influences sentiment (making it more negative).
papers.limitation:
High steering strengths degrade text quality, limiting the practical applicability of strong steering.
Toxicity is difficult to control via steering, likely due to extensive post-training alignment of the models.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a lightweight method for controlling text properties by adding a learned bias to language model activations at inference time. So far, steering vectors have predominantly been evaluated in multiple-choice settings, while their effectiveness in free-form generation tasks remains understudied. Moving "Beyond Multiple Choice," we thoroughly evaluate the effectiveness of steering vectors in adaptively controlling topical focus, sentiment, toxicity, and readability in abstractive summaries of the NEWTS dataset. We find that steering effectively controls the targeted summary properties, but high steering strengths consistently degrade both intrinsic and extrinsic text quality. Compared to steering, prompting offers weaker control, while preserving text quality. Combining steering and prompting yields the strongest control over text properties and offers the most favorable efficacy-quality trade-off at moderate steering strengths. Our results underscore the practical trade-off between control strength and text quality preservation when applying steering vectors to free-form generation tasks.

papers.title: Refusal in LLMs is an Affine Function
papers.research_question: How can affine concept editing (ACE) provide more precise and standardized control over refusal behavior in language models compared to existing steering methods?
papers.core_contribution: ACE unifies directional ablation and activation addition in an affine framework, enabling more standardized and precise control over refusal behavior in language models, and generalizes to models where prior methods fail.
papers.conclusion: ACE offers a more consistent and standardized approach for steering refusal behavior in LLMs, mitigating limitations of existing methods and working across diverse model architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ACE provides more standardized steering than contrastive activation addition (CAA), reducing dependency on input prompts for refusal control.
ACE corrects the issue of nonsense generation in models like Hermes Eagle RWKV v5, where directional ablation alone produces incoherent outputs.
The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, but parameters slightly below zero and above one are effective for controlling refusal.
ACE works on both transformer-based models (e.g., Llama 3) and recurrent neural networks (e.g., RWKV v5), demonstrating generalizability.
ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control refusal across different prompt types.
papers.limitation: The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, suggesting that steering vectors may be flawed or that directional ablation does not fully erase information.
future_direction: Exploring whether nonlinear techniques are required to fully erase concepts like refusal.
Extending steering techniques to work reliably on a more varied set of behaviors.
papers.abstract: We propose affine concept editing (ACE) as an approach for steering language models' behavior by intervening directly in activations. We begin with an affine decomposition of model activation vectors and show that prior methods for steering model behavior correspond to subsets of terms of this decomposition. We then provide a derivation of ACE and use it to control refusal behavior on ten different models, including Llama 3 70B. ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control the model's refusal responses across prompt types. We evaluate the results using LLM-based scoring on a collection of harmful and harmless prompts. Our experiments demonstrate that ACE consistently achieves more precise control over model behavior than existing methods and generalizes to models where directional ablation via affine subspace projection alone produces incoherent outputs. Code for reproducing our results is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/steering-llama3 .

papers.title: Steering Vector Fields for Context-Aware Inference-Time Control in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why are static steering vectors unreliable for inference-time control in LLMs, and can a context-dependent steering method improve reliability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Steering Vector Fields (SVF), a context-dependent inference-time steering method that learns a differentiable concept boundary and uses its local gradient for steering, improving reliability and enabling coordinated multi-layer, long-form, and multi-attribute control.
papers.conclusion: Steering Vector Fields (SVF) provides a unified, context-dependent framework for inference-time control that is more reliable and effective than static steering vectors, especially in challenging settings like long-form generation and multi-attribute steering.
papers.key_findings:
SVF outperforms static steering baselines (CAA, ICV, RED, BiPO) in accuracy and steerable rate on multiple-choice persona tasks.
SVF provides more reliable long-form generation control by refreshing steering directions based on the evolving hidden state.
SVF enables effective multi-attribute steering by composing concept boundaries via a smooth softmin function.
SVF reduces concept contamination on irrelevant queries compared to preference-optimization baselines like BiPO.
SVF's multi-layer alignment and shared concept space produce coordinated interventions, improving performance on concepts that are unsteerable with single-layer methods.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) offer a lightweight way to control large language models (LLMs) at inference time by shifting hidden activations, providing a practical middle ground between prompting and fine-tuning. Yet SVs can be unreliable in practice. Some concepts are unsteerable, and even when steering helps on average it can backfire for a non-trivial fraction of inputs. Reliability also degrades in long-form generation and multi-attribute steering. We take a geometric view of these failures. A static SV applies the same update vector everywhere in representation space, implicitly assuming that the concept-improving direction is constant across contexts. When the locally effective direction varies with the current activation, a single global vector can become misaligned, which yields weak or reversed effects. Guided by this perspective, we propose Steering Vector Fields (SVF), which learns a differentiable concept scoring function whose local gradient defines the steering direction at each activation, making interventions explicitly context-dependent. This formulation supports coordinated multi-layer interventions in a shared, aligned concept space, and enables efficient long-form and multi-attribute control within a unified framework. Across multiple LLMs and steering tasks, SVF delivers stronger and more reliable control, improving the practicality of inference-time steering.

papers.title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How does linear steerability emerge in language models during pretraining, and why does it vary across concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Linear steerability emerges during intermediate stages of training, varies across concepts, and is linked to increasing linear separability of concepts in the hidden space.
papers.conclusion: Linear steerability does not emerge uniformly but develops over training and varies between concepts, aligning with increasingly structured internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear steerability emerges in later training stages, separate from reasoning capability and emotion expression via prompting.
Emergence times vary widely across concepts, such as anger emerging earlier than sadness.
Concept representations become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses.
The Intervention Detector (ID) framework can reveal steerability dynamics and predict when linear steerability emerges.
These findings hold across different model families, indicating a general pattern.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on 7B-scale open-source models, not tested on larger LLMs.
Intervention coefficient was empirically tuned and differs across models, with underlying causes not investigated.
Did not explore alternative nonlinear approaches for extracting or intervening in model representations.
Methodological innovation in intervention techniques is not the focus; core procedure is consistent with prior work.
Alternative unsupervised methods such as mean-difference vectors are not compared.
Concepts like emotions lack ground truth, making evaluation subjective and based on semantic interpretation.
Steering certain concepts can produce offensive outputs, with no safety filtering applied.
future_direction: Examining how different pre-training corpora influence intervention outcomes.
Exploring alternative steering methods beyond PCA or K-Means.
Comparing unsupervised methods like mean-difference vectors and their influence on downstream intervention performance.
papers.abstract: Language models can be steered by modifying their internal representations to control concepts such as emotion, style, or truthfulness in generation. However, the conditions for an effective intervention remain unclear and are often validated through heuristics and trial-and-error. To fill this gap, we demonstrate that intervention efficacy, measured by linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training. Moreover, even closely related concepts (e.g., anger and sadness) exhibit steerability emergence at distinct stages of training. To better interpret the dynamics of steerability during training, we adapt existing intervention techniques into a unified framework, referred to as the "Intervention Detector" (ID), which is designed to reveal how linear steerability evolves over the course of training through hidden state and representation analysis. ID reveals that concepts become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses, which strongly correlates with the emergence of linear steerability. We further introduce ID-based metrics, such as heatmaps, entropy trends, and cosine similarity, to help interpret how linear steerability evolves throughout training. In addition, we apply ID across different model families to ensure the generality of our findings on steerability dynamics.

papers.title: Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning
papers.research_question: How can refusal behavior in safety-aligned language models be ablated without causing collateral damage to core capabilities like math and coding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA), a method that cleans refusal vectors by orthogonalizing against capability and style directions, enabling precise ablation of refusal behavior with minimal distribution drift and preserved capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SRA treats refusal ablation as a semantic disentanglement problem, achieving behavioral editing with dramatically reduced drift and preserved capabilities compared to standard methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0–2% on harmful suite) with negligible perplexity impact on wikitext_2_raw and minimal distribution drift.
Standard ablation induces severe distribution drift, while SRA maintains original distribution while achieving low refusal rates.
SRA preserves or improves math and code perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP datasets.
The dirty refusal vector is polysemantic, entangling refusal signals with unrelated linguistic structure and capability circuits.
Cleaning the vector via spectral residualization reduces 'Ghost Noise' damage caused by standard ablation.
papers.limitation:
The atom registry is curated and may miss confounds; unseen entanglers could still leak into the refusal direction.
Evaluation limitations include refusal detection being definition-dependent, finite harmful prompt suites, and proxy drift metrics not substituting for comprehensive behavioral evaluation.
future_direction: Automating atom discovery or expanding registries to handle unseen confounds.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned language models systematically refuse harmful requests. While activation steering can modulate refusal, ablating the raw "refusal vector" calculated from contrastive harmful and harmless prompts often causes collateral damage and distribution drift. We argue this degradation occurs because the raw vector is polysemantic, entangling the refusal signal with core capability circuits and linguistic style. We introduce Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA) to distill these steering directions. SRA constructs a registry of independent Concept Atoms representing protected capabilities and stylistic confounds, then uses ridge-regularized spectral residualization to orthogonalize the refusal vector against these directions. This yields a clean refusal direction that targets refusal-relevant structure while minimizing disruption to the model's semantic geometry. Across five models (Qwen3-VL and Ministral series), SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0-2%) with negligible perplexity impact on Wikitext-2 (mean delta PPL approx. 0.02) and minimal distribution drift. Notably, standard ablation on Qwen3-VL-4B induces severe drift (first-token KL = 2.088), whereas SRA maintains the original distribution (KL = 0.044) while achieving the same 0% refusal rate. Using teacher-forced perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP as a high-resolution capability proxy, we show SRA preserves math and code distributions. These results suggest that common "model damage" is often "Ghost Noise," defined as the spectral bleeding of the dirty refusal direction into capability subspaces.

papers.title: Steering in the Shadows: Causal Amplification for Activation Space Attacks in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can intermediate activations in decoder-only LLMs be exploited as a vulnerable attack surface for behavioral control via causal amplification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a white-box activation attack that exploits the Causal Amplification Effect (CAE) in transformer compression valleys to induce strong behavioral shifts with minimal perturbation, turning activation steering into a concrete security concern.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering via methods like SSS represents a realistic and underexplored attack surface for LLM security, highlighting the need for defenses based on introspection and activation-space monitoring.
papers.key_findings:
SSS reliably steers multiple LLMs across behavioral axes (evil, hallucination, sycophancy, sentiment) while preserving coherence.
The Causal Amplification Effect (CAE) allows small perturbations in high-gain regions (compression valleys) to be amplified autoregressively.
SSS outperforms existing activation steering baselines (BOS-only, constant vector) in efficacy and stealth.
Standard guardrail models fail to detect a significant portion of harmful outputs generated under SSS attack.
Weak spontaneous introspection signals are observed in a small subset of generations, suggesting a latent capacity for internal anomaly detection.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted behavior vectors is uncertain; their conceptual meaning may not fully align with human-intended semantics.
Reliance on LLM-as-Judge for behavioral evaluation introduces potential noise and sensitivity to prompt wording.
Effectiveness of SSS is limited when generation is too short, as perturbations lack time to accumulate influence.
future_direction: Designing robust defenses, including introspection-based safeguards and improved monitoring of internal activations.
Systematic study, detection, and mitigation of similar activation-level attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) are typically secured by auditing data, prompts, and refusal policies, while treating the forward pass as an implementation detail. We show that intermediate activations in decoder-only LLMs form a vulnerable attack surface for behavioral control. Building on recent findings on attention sinks and compression valleys, we identify a high-gain region in the residual stream where small, well-aligned perturbations are causally amplified along the autoregressive trajectory--a Causal Amplification Effect (CAE). We exploit this as an attack surface via Sensitivity-Scaled Steering (SSS), a progressive activation-level attack that combines beginning-of-sequence (BOS) anchoring with sensitivity-based reinforcement to focus a limited perturbation budget on the most vulnerable layers and tokens. We show that across multiple open-weight models and four behavioral axes, SSS induces large shifts in evil, hallucination, sycophancy, and sentiment while preserving high coherence and general capabilities, turning activation steering into a concrete security concern for white-box and supply-chain LLM deployments.

papers.title: Representation Surgery: Theory and Practice of Affine Steering
papers.research_question: How can we optimally steer language model representations using affine transformations to reduce undesirable behaviors like bias and toxicity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper derives two optimal affine steering functions (mean matching and mean+covariance matching) under guardedness constraints, providing theoretical justification for existing steering approaches and introducing an improved method for bias and toxicity mitigation.
papers.conclusion: Affine steering functions, particularly mean and covariance matching, are effective for mitigating bias and toxicity in language models, offering a theoretically grounded and practical approach for representation surgery.
papers.key_findings:
Mean and covariance matching steering (MiMiC) reduces bias more effectively than mean matching alone, as shown by lower TPR gap and reduced bias by neighbors.
Affine steering functions can mitigate toxicity in text generation without fine-tuning, though they do not reach state-of-the-art performance compared to methods that require gradient computation or fine-tuning.
The derived steering functions provably remove bias by neighbors in expectation when matching both means and covariances.
Steering representations towards a target concept (e.g., non-toxic) is more suitable for toxicity mitigation than concept erasure, which might erase the model's ability to distinguish between concepts.
The methods are effective across different models (BERT, GPT-2, Llama2) and tasks (classification, generation).
papers.limitation:
The linear nature of the affine transformations may limit their effectiveness compared to non-linear methods.
There is a disparity between the training distribution (last token representations) and inference-time usage (applying the intervention at each generation step) for toxicity mitigation, which may affect performance.
papers.abstract: Language models often exhibit undesirable behavior, e.g., generating toxic or gender-biased text. In the case of neural language models, an encoding of the undesirable behavior is often present in the model's representations. Thus, one natural (and common) approach to prevent the model from exhibiting undesirable behavior is to steer the model's representations in a manner that reduces the probability of it generating undesirable text. This paper investigates the formal and empirical properties of steering functions, i.e., transformation of the neural language model's representations that alter its behavior. First, we derive two optimal, in the least-squares sense, affine steering functions under different constraints. Our theory provides justification for existing approaches and offers a novel, improved steering approach. Second, we offer a series of experiments that demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of the methods in mitigating bias and reducing toxic generation.

papers.title: Risk-adaptive Activation Steering for Safe Multimodal Large Language Models
